title: Lighthouse scoring math and reliable measurement
summary: The mobile Performance score (Lighthouse 10 through the current 13.5.0; PSI switched to 13.x the week of 10 Oct 2025 with explicitly "no changes to the performance scoring") is a weighted mean of five metric scores: TBT 30, LCP 25, CLS 25, FCP 10, Speed Index 10 (INP is present with weight 0). Each metric score comes from a log-normal curve fixed by two control points (p10 → 0.9, median → 0.5): FCP 1800/3000 ms, SI 3387/5800 ms, LCP 2500/4000 ms, TBT 200/600 ms, CLS 0.10/0.25. The category score is rounded to two decimals, so a displayed 100 needs a weighted mean ≥ 0.995: with CLS = 0 and TBT = 0 (both score exactly 1.0, locking 55 points) you still need LCP ≲ 1.5 s, FCP ≲ 1.2 s and SI ≲ 2.0 s under simulated slow-4G/4× CPU; hitting all five "good" thresholds exactly gives only 90. In this agency's 10 home pages the points lost average LCP 16.2, TBT 11.1, SI 6.9, FCP 5.0, CLS 0.3, so the attack order for score-per-effort is LCP first, TBT second, then SI/FCP (which mostly move with the LCP/render-blocking work), with CLS as a regression guard rather than a target. Ranking does not use this score at all: Google's page-experience doc (updated 2026-09-22) says "Core Web Vitals are used by our ranking systems" and those are CrUX field p75 values over 28 days for LCP/INP/CLS; INP cannot be measured in Lighthouse and TBT is only its proxy. Measurement must be treated as a distribution: PSI and the CLI both use "simulate" throttling, which loads the page once unthrottled and multiplies observed CPU task durations by 4 (layout tasks by 2, each task capped at 10 s), so a slow or contended lab CPU inflates TBT/TTI/SI directly; take the median of 5 runs on ≥2 dedicated cores, discard any run with runWarnings (one local run reported TBT 142,018 ms because the page never went quiet within the 45 s maxWaitForLoad), and use PSI (API key mandatory: the anonymous quota returned HTTP 429 "Queries per day" today) as the reference judge. Finally, Lighthouse 13 deleted or renamed many non-scored audits (uses-optimized-images, third-party-summary, largest-contentful-paint-element, render-blocking-resources, font-display, offscreen-images…), so the plugin's existing lighthouse.sh jq fields silently degrade to 0/empty on LH 13; local runs today used LH 12.8.2 while PSI runs 13.x.
critic_notes: Method: opened every cited source that was reachable (raw GitHub, developer.chrome.com, developers.google.com, web.dev, DebugBear, Unlighthouse via curl through the proxy after WebFetch DNS failures), re-derived all curve thresholds and score scenarios with a Python port of getLogNormalScore, and recomputed per-metric points lost from the 10 local LH 12.8.2 JSON files (all figures match the researcher). The single most consequential correction: PSI mobile has run at cpuSlowdownMultiplier 1.2 (not 4) with 35 s/15 s timeouts since Dec 2024 (core/config/lr-mobile-config.js), so any 'match PSI' logic, verification step or benchmarkIndex comparison in the findings must be rewritten around calibration via the calculator formula. Second: Google says PSI API field data will be discontinued; the plugin's Field column belongs on the CrUX API. Third: LH13 insight ids differ from the blog (lcp-breakdown-insight, inp-breakdown-insight, cache-insight) and already exist in the local 12.8.2 runs. Open items I could not close: anonymous PSI still returns 429 today, so PSI's live Lighthouse version (13.4.x or 13.5.0) and benchmarkIndex remain unobserved; PR #16226/#16256 diffs were not readable from this session (GitHub access to that repo is not enabled), so the 1.2 value rests on the config file plus release notes; desktop FCP/SI curve files and the CrUX 404 behaviour were not opened. Skipped: practitioner blogs about 'realistic Elementor scores'; nothing here is Elementor-version specific, so no 4.x applicability caveat arises.

findings.claim: The mobile Performance score is round2(weighted mean) of exactly five metric scores with weights TBT 30, LCP 25, CLS 25, FCP 10, Speed Index 10 (INP weight 0); this is unchanged from Lighthouse 10 through the current 13.5.0, including the PSI switch to Lighthouse 13.
findings.detail: core/config/default-config.js on main (package.json version 13.5.0, node >=22.19) lists performance auditRefs: first-contentful-paint 10, largest-contentful-paint 25, total-blocking-time 30, cumulative-layout-shift 25, speed-index 10, interaction-to-next-paint 0; every other performance audit has weight 0 and NOT_APPLICABLE/INFORMATIVE/MANUAL audits are forced to 0. core/scoring.js: arithmeticMean = sum(score*weight)/sum(weight) then clampTo2Decimals = Math.round(val*100)/100; a single null metric score makes the category null. Displayed score = that value ×100, so 100 requires weighted mean ≥ 0.995 and 90 requires ≥ 0.895. The Lighthouse 13 blog (Published Oct 10, 2025: 'available in PageSpeed Insights within the next week', Chrome stable 143) states 'There are no changes to the performance scoring in this version of Lighthouse, which is based on the metrics rather than the audits.' The developer.chrome.com scoring page (last updated 2019-09-19) still documents the Lighthouse 10 table with the same five weights.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; the weights would only change with a Lighthouse major version that announces a scoring change (none announced for 13.x as of 13.5.0, Sept 2026).
findings.how_to_apply: Compute the score yourself from a Lighthouse JSON: sum over the five audits of audits[id].score*weight / 100; compare with categories.performance.score. In the plugin, store the weights table and emit a 'points lost per metric' column = weight*(1-score) so each run shows where the deficit is.
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.categories.performance.auditRefs[] | select(.weight>0) | {id,weight}' on any LH 12/13 JSON prints the five ids above; recompute the weighted mean and confirm it matches .categories.performance.score to 2 decimals.

findings.claim: Each metric score is a log-normal curve fixed by two control points (p10 → score 0.9, median → 0.5); the mobile points are FCP 1800/3000 ms, SI 3387/5800 ms, LCP 2500/4000 ms, TBT 200/600 ms, CLS 0.10/0.25, and from these the exact value needed for any metric score can be computed.
findings.detail: shared/statistics.js getLogNormalScore({median,p10},value): if value<=0 return 1; standardizedX = ln(value/median)*0.9061938024368232 / -ln(p10/median); score = (1-erf(standardizedX))/2 (Abramowitz-Stegun 7.1.26 erf), clamped to [0.9,1] when value<=p10, [0.5,0.9) when value<=median, [0,0.5) otherwise. Control points from core/audits/metrics/*.js (mobile): FCP p10 1800 median 3000 ('25th and 8th percentiles HTTPArchive'), speed-index 3387/5800, LCP 2500/4000 ('25th and 13th percentiles'), TBT 200/600 ('semi-arbitrarily chosen… 19 and 189 would lead to surprisingly harsh scoring'), CLS 0.1/0.25 (no mobile/desktop split). Desktop differs: FCP 934/1600, SI 1311/2300, LCP 1200/2400, TBT 150/350. Values I computed with the exact formula for metric score ≥ 0.90 / 0.95 / 0.97 / 0.99 / 0.995: FCP 1800 / 1557 / 1418 / 1187 / 1075 ms; SI 3387 / 2908 / 2634 / 2185 / 1967 ms; LCP 2500 / 2188 / 2007 / 1704 / 1555 ms; TBT 200 / 146 / 120 / 82 / 66 ms; CLS 0.100 / 0.077 / 0.065 / 0.047 / 0.040. A metric score of exactly 1.0 is reached only at value 0 (TBT 0 and CLS 0 are realistic; time metrics never are). Google's doc: 'between 0.50 and 0.92 there's a near-linear relationship', 'around a score of 0.96 is the point of diminishing returns', 'taking a score from 99 to 100 needs about the same amount of metric improvement that would take a 90 to 94'.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; control points have been stable since Lighthouse 8 (TBT/CLS) and 6 (others). Desktop runs use different curves, so a desktop number must never be compared against this table.
findings.how_to_apply: Put the table and the 20-line formula (port of getLogNormalScore) in the plugin's references and in the audit script, so the plugin reports 'LCP 2473 ms → metric score 0.90 → 2.5 points lost; to gain 2 more points LCP must reach 1704 ms'. Use --form-factor=mobile always; use --preset=desktop only for a separate desktop check.
findings.how_to_verify: Feed known values: LCP 2500 → 0.90, LCP 4000 → 0.50, TBT 0 → 1.0, CLS 0.107 → ~0.88; compare against audits[...].score in a real report (they match to 2 decimals).

findings.claim: 'Near 100' on mobile means: CLS = 0 and TBT = 0 (locks 55/100), plus LCP ≤ ~1.5 s, FCP ≤ ~1.2 s and SI ≤ ~2.0 s under simulated slow-4G/4× CPU; merely reaching all five 'good' thresholds yields exactly 90, and TBT alone decides whether 95+ is reachable.
findings.detail: Scenarios I computed with the exact curves (mobile): all five at their p10 (FCP 1.8 s, SI 3.4 s, LCP 2.5 s, TBT 200 ms, CLS 0.1) → 90. CLS 0, TBT 0, LCP 2.5 s, FCP 1.8 s, SI 3.4 s → 96 (raw 95.5). CLS 0, TBT 0, LCP 2.0 s, FCP 1.5 s, SI 2.5 s → 99 (98.6). CLS 0, TBT 0, LCP 1.5 s, FCP 1.2 s, SI 2.0 s → 100 (99.7). Even TBT 50 ms still allows 100 (99.9) with LCP 1.3/FCP 1.0/SI 1.7. CLS 0, TBT 100 ms, LCP 1.8 s, FCP 1.2 s, SI 2.2 s → 99. CLS 0.02, TBT 150, LCP 2.2, FCP 1.5, SI 2.8 → 96. Same page with TBT 300 ms → 92; TBT 600 ms → 84. Points available per metric moving from median to p10: TBT 12, LCP 10, CLS 10, FCP 4, SI 4; from p10 to ~0: TBT 3, LCP 2.5, CLS 2.5, FCP 1, SI 1. Google's own wording: 'A perfect score of 100 is extremely challenging to achieve and not expected.' For an Elementor page this translates to: hero LCP must be an immediately-discoverable static image/text (no three.js, no autoplay video, no slider), and main-thread work before TTI must be ≤ ~50–100 ms after ×4 slowdown, which the observed GTM+GA4+Ads+FB-pixel stacks rarely allow (measured TBT 215–615 ms on the 'fast' sites).
findings.breaks_when: Chasing the last 4 points (96→100) requires TBT≈0, i.e. removing/deferring tag manager, pixels, cookie banners and Elementor frontend scripts until after TTI; done naively that breaks consent logging, conversion tracking and booking widgets. Target 95–97 as the default contract, 100 only for pages with no third-party tags.
findings.how_to_apply: Set the plugin's acceptance thresholds per metric, not per score: CLS ≤ 0.02, TBT ≤ 100 ms, LCP ≤ 1.8 s, FCP ≤ 1.2 s, SI ≤ 2.2 s (→ ≥ 99 expected). Build pages so that the LCP element is in the initial HTML with fetchpriority=high and no lazy-load, fonts have font-display:swap with preloaded Greek+Latin subsets, and no third-party JS executes before TTI.
findings.how_to_verify: After each change run 5 mobile Lighthouse runs, take the median, and check the five numericValues against the thresholds above; confirm with one PSI run (lab section) that the same page scores ≥ 95 on Google's hardware.

findings.claim: On this agency's 10 home pages the points lost average LCP 16.2, TBT 11.1, SI 6.9, FCP 5.0, CLS 0.3 (of 100), so the score-per-effort order is LCP → TBT → SI/FCP, with CLS treated only as a regression guard.
findings.detail: From the local LH 12.8.2 mobile runs (points lost = weight×(1−metric score)): limnoupolis.gr 27 (LCP 7749 ms −24.2, TBT invalid −30, SI 21.5 s −10, FCP −6, CLS 0.103 −2.7); staging.limnoupolis 30 (LCP 10.2 s −25, TBT 1796 ms −27); onar-seaside-lounge 44 (LCP 16.4 s −25, TBT 615 −15.6); voreniahorizon 50 (LCP 9.0 s −24.8, TBT 428 −10.5); kand 68 (SI 11.5 s −9.5, TBT 406 −9.9, LCP 3.6 s −9.8); fagitiotiszois 68 (LCP 4.4 s −15.2, SI 11 s −9.4); cretaforums 74 (LCP 4.4 s −15.2); marakaki 74 (LCP 5.2 s −19, TBT 63 ms −0); platonos 84 (TBT 358 −8.4, SI 6.4 s −6); pallada 86 (SI 6.1 s −5.6, TBT 215 −3.6, LCP 2.47 s −2.5, FCP −2.1). Pattern: LCP is the largest single loss on 8/10 pages (hero video/3D/slider), TBT second; on the two best pages Speed Index is the biggest remaining loss even though LCP is fine, i.e. late-painting content (entrance animations, sliders) costs 5–6 points after LCP is solved. CLS is already ~0 everywhere, so any CLS regression (e.g. lazy-load raising CLS to 0.107 = metric score 0.88 = −3 points) is pure loss.
findings.breaks_when: The order flips on pages with heavy JS: when TBT is > 600 ms (TBT score 0, −30) fixing LCP alone cannot get above ~70; then TBT comes first.
findings.how_to_apply: Plugin audit output: rank the five metrics by points lost for the tested page and print the fix list in that order. Generic default order when no data: 1) LCP element (static, discoverable, preloaded, not lazy), 2) TBT (defer/delay third-party tags, remove unused JS), 3) SI/FCP (render-blocking CSS/fonts, remove entrance animations above the fold), 4) CLS guard (reserve image/iframe/banner space, no lazy-load on first-viewport media).
findings.how_to_verify: Re-run the per-metric points-lost table after each fix; the metric targeted must drop in 'points lost' while the other four stay within ±1 point across a 5-run median.

findings.claim: Google ranking uses field Core Web Vitals (CrUX 28-day p75 LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1), not the Lighthouse/PSI lab score; INP cannot be measured in the lab, where TBT is only a proxy.
findings.detail: Google Search Central 'Understanding page experience' (Last updated 2026-09-22): 'Core Web Vitals are used by our ranking systems'; 'there is no single signal'; 'trying to get a perfect score just for SEO reasons may not be the best use of your time'; 'Beyond Core Web Vitals, other page experience aspects don't directly help your website rank higher.' The CWV page (updated 2025-12-10): LCP within 2.5 s, INP under 200 ms, CLS under 0.1, 'metrics that measure real-world user experience'. web.dev/vitals (updated 2024-10-31): pass = all three good at the 75th percentile, segmented mobile/desktop; FID retired, INP stable CWV since 2024; 'Tools like Lighthouse that load pages in a simulated environment without a user cannot measure INP… TBT is a proxy for INP.' PSI 'About': field data = CrUX previous 28 days, p75 shown, categories Good/Needs Improvement/Poor with FCP 1800/3000, LCP 2500/4000, CLS 0.1/0.25, INP 200/500, TTFB 800/1800 (experimental); page-level falls back to origin-level when the URL lacks data; CWV assessment passes if LCP, CLS and INP p75 are all Good (INP optional if insufficient). web.dev lab-vs-field: Lighthouse = 'a single device… a single network… a single geographic location', cold cache, no bfcache, one fixed LCP element; field = many devices, warm caches, multiple LCP elements, 28-day distribution.
findings.breaks_when: Optimising only the lab score can leave field INP poor (e.g. heavy click handlers in booking widgets, mega-menu, JetSmartFilters) and the page still fails CWV in Search Console; conversely a page with lab TBT 300 ms may pass field INP. The lab score is a diagnostic, not the goal.
findings.how_to_apply: Plugin reporting: show two columns — Lab (Lighthouse 5-run median) and Field (PSI loadingExperience / originLoadingExperience p75 for LCP, INP, CLS, FCP, TTFB) — and declare success on field CWV 'Good', using the lab score as the day-to-day proxy. Add a field INP check (Search Console CWV report or CrUX API) to every monthly review.
findings.how_to_verify: PSI JSON: loadingExperience.overall_category == 'FAST' and each of LARGEST_CONTENTFUL_PAINT_MS, INTERACTION_TO_NEXT_PAINT, CUMULATIVE_LAYOUT_SHIFT_SCORE has category 'FAST'; Search Console → Core Web Vitals → mobile shows the URL group as Good.

findings.claim: PSI and the Lighthouse CLI default to 'simulate' throttling: one unthrottled load, then Lantern replays it with RTT 150 ms, 1.6 Mbps down / 750 kbps up and multiplies every observed CPU task by 4 (layout tasks by 2, each task capped at 10 s), so the lab machine's real CPU speed directly scales TBT, TTI and Speed Index.
findings.detail: Lighthouse core/config/constants.js: formFactor 'mobile', throttlingMethod 'simulate', throttling = mobileSlow4G, screenEmulation 412×823 @1.75 (Moto G Power), UA 'Android 11; moto g power (2022)'. Lantern Constants.ts: mobileSlow4G rttMs 150, throughputKbps 1638.4, requestLatencyMs 562.5 (150×3.75 DEVTOOLS_RTT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR), downloadThroughputKbps 1474.56 (×0.9), uploadThroughputKbps 675, cpuSlowdownMultiplier 4 — 'align with WebPageTest's Fast 3G… roughly the 75th percentile of 4G connections'. Desktop (desktopDense4G): rtt 40, 10,240 kbps, CPU ×1, 1350×940. Simulator.ts estimateCPUTimeRemaining: multiplier = didPerformLayout ? layoutTaskMultiplier : cpuSlowdownMultiplier; duration = min(round(task/1000×multiplier), DEFAULT_MAXIMUM_CPU_TASK_DURATION) with the comment 'if a task takes more than 10 seconds it's usually a sign it isn't actually CPU bound'; layoutTaskMultiplier = cpuSlowdownMultiplier × 0.5. For 'devtools'/'provided' the simulator sets cpuSlowdownMultiplier = 1 (real throttling applied during load). docs/throttling.md: PSI 'uses simulated throttling, the same default as the Lighthouse CLI'. The local runs today match exactly (configSettings.throttling rttMs 150, throughputKbps 1638.4, cpuSlowdownMultiplier 4). TBT (TotalBlockingTime.ts) is the sum of task time over 50 ms between FCP and TTI, averaged 50/50 from optimistic and pessimistic simulations.
findings.breaks_when: Comparing a local run to PSI without equal CPU power: on a contended/slow host observed tasks are longer, ×4 makes TBT and TTI balloon and the score drops although nothing on the site changed; conversely a fast M-series laptop under-reports TBT and the site then 'fails' in PSI.
findings.how_to_apply: Keep the defaults (do not pass --throttling-method=devtools when the goal is to match PSI). Record environment.benchmarkIndex with every result and only compare runs with similar benchmarkIndex; when you must correct, pass --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=<n> per the calibration table (finding on benchmarkIndex).
findings.how_to_verify: In the JSON: .configSettings.throttlingMethod == 'simulate', .configSettings.throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier == 4, .configSettings.throttling.rttMs == 150; in the PSI/HTML report footer hover 'Slow 4G throttling' and read 'CPU/Memory Power'.
findings.correction: Correct for the Lighthouse CLI/DevTools default (constants.js throttlingMethod 'simulate', Lantern mobileSlow4G rtt 150 / 1638.4 kbps / cpuSlowdownMultiplier 4, layoutTaskMultiplier 0.5×, 10 000 ms task cap all confirmed). WRONG for PSI since December 2024: core/config/lr-mobile-config.js (the config PSI/Lightrider runs) sets throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier: 1.2 with the comment 'Determined using PSI CPU benchmark median and https://lighthouse-cpu-throttling-calculator.vercel.app/'. PSI release notes, Dec 5, 2024: 'The CPU throttling factor for PageSpeed Insights has been adjusted to account for the low CPU performance benchmarks typical in PageSpeed Insights production environments ... Field data and desktop scores should not be affected.' Changelog 12.2.2 'lr: set CPU throttling based on benchmark (#16226)' and 12.2.3 note. PSI desktop still uses desktopDense4G (CPU ×1). So PSI = 1.2× on a slow machine; local CLI = 4× on a fast machine; network simulation identical. The shared conclusion (host CPU scales TBT/TTI/SI) stands.

findings.claim: Reliable lab numbers need the median of ≥5 runs on ≥2 dedicated cores with no concurrent tests; Lighthouse's own guidance is that the median of 5 is 'twice as stable as 1 run', and the representative run is picked by FCP+TTI distance, not by score.
findings.detail: docs/variability.md: variability sources ranked High = page nondeterminism (A/B, ads), local network, client hardware, client resource contention (other apps, extensions, antivirus); Medium = tier-1 network, browser nondeterminism; Low = web server. Strategies: 'run multiple times and use aggregates' (median, 90th percentile or min/max, never one run), 'the median of 5 runs is twice as stable as 1 run'; 'minimum 2 dedicated cores (4 recommended) and 2 GB RAM (4–8 GB recommended)'; 'avoid function-as-a-service platforms and burstable or shared-core instances'; 'don't run concurrent tests on one machine', scale horizontally; isolate third parties and random animations; 'if local resources are limited, use a hosted lab such as PageSpeed Insights or WebPageTest'. Example cost: m5.large/n2-standard-2 ≈ $0.10/h, ~30 s per test, ≈ $0.0008/report. Simulated throttling mitigates local/tier-1 network variance fully and hardware/contention only partially. core/lib/median-run.js computeMedianRun: distance = (medianFCP−fcp)² + (medianTTI−tti)², ties broken by lower TTI; filterToValidRuns drops runs with non-finite FCP/TTI. Lighthouse CI: collect.numberOfRuns default 3; assert.aggregationMethod ∈ median | optimistic (default) | pessimistic | median-run ('the run determined to be most representative of all runs based on key performance metrics').
findings.breaks_when: A single-run before/after comparison will show ±3–8 point swings that are noise, leading to wrong accept/reject decisions on a fix; running runs in parallel on the same box (e.g. 10 sites at once) inflates TBT on all of them.
findings.how_to_apply: lighthouserc.json: {"ci":{"collect":{"numberOfRuns":5,"url":["https://site/"],"settings":{"onlyCategories":["performance"],"formFactor":"mobile"}},"assert":{"aggregationMethod":"median-run","assertions":{"categories:performance":["error",{"minScore":0.95}],"largest-contentful-paint":["error",{"maxNumericValue":1800}],"total-blocking-time":["error",{"maxNumericValue":100}],"cumulative-layout-shift":["error",{"maxNumericValue":0.02}]}}}}; run `lhci collect` then `lhci assert`; or with the raw CLI loop 5× sequentially and pick the run flagged isRepresentativeRun / computeMedianRun. Update the plugin's lighthouse.sh to loop N=5 sequentially per URL and report median plus min–max spread.
findings.how_to_verify: Spread check: the five performance scores should sit within ~±2 of the median on a sane host; a spread > 6 points means the host or page is too noisy and the run set must be repeated or moved to PSI.

findings.claim: Lighthouse warns about a slow host only when benchmarkIndex ≤ 1000 and only in the CLI; this session's container (benchmarkIndex 1181–2065) never triggers it yet is a shared-core host, so its TBT must be treated as indicative only, and cpuSlowdownMultiplier should be calibrated from the benchmarkIndex bracket table.
findings.detail: core/gather/driver/environment.js: SLOW_CPU_BENCHMARK_INDEX_THRESHOLD = 1000; getSlowHostCpuWarning returns 'The tested device appears to have a slower CPU than…' only when settings.channel === 'cli', throttlingMethod is simulate/devtools, cpuSlowdownMultiplier equals the default, and BenchmarkIndex ≤ 1000. docs/throttling.md benchmarkIndex brackets (Chrome m86): High-End Desktop 1500–2000, Low-End Desktop 1000–1500, High-End Mobile 800–1200, Mid-Tier Mobile 125–800, Low-End Mobile < 125; recommended multiplier when host → target Mid-Tier Mobile: High-End Desktop 4× (range 2–10), Low-End Desktop 2× (1–5), High-End Mobile 2× (1–5); 'if your benchmarkIndex is at the high end of its bracket use a higher multiplier… low end, a lower multiplier'; 'You can find this value under the title CPU/Memory Power at the bottom of the Lighthouse report'; set with --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=<value>. Today's local runs: benchmarkIndex 1181 (pallada), 1512–1674 (most), 1838–2065 (limnoupolis, onar), i.e. straddling 'low-end' and 'high-end desktop' between runs on the same machine — the signature of a shared/bursting vCPU. Variability.md explicitly says to avoid 'burstable or shared-core instances'.
findings.breaks_when: Setting a lower multiplier (e.g. 2×) to 'match' PSI without knowing PSI's benchmarkIndex produces optimistic TBT that then fails in PSI; always validate against PSI before trusting a non-default multiplier.
findings.how_to_apply: Record .environment.benchmarkIndex per run. Rule for the plugin: if benchmarkIndex < 1000 or the spread across the 5 runs exceeds ~400, mark TBT/TTI/SI as 'low confidence' and use PSI for the TBT verdict; optionally pass --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier per the table only after cross-checking one page against PSI.
findings.how_to_verify: Compare the median local TBT with the PSI lab TBT for the same URL on the same day; they should agree within ~±30% when benchmarkIndex is comparable; if local TBT is 2× PSI, the host is the problem, not the site.
findings.correction: Mechanics confirmed (environment.js: SLOW_CPU_BENCHMARK_INDEX_THRESHOLD = 1000, channel must be 'cli', method simulate/devtools, default multiplier). Correction: the bracket table is coarse; use the exact piecewise formula from the calculator the Lighthouse team itself cites in lr-mobile-config.js: benchmarkIndex ≥1300 → multiplier = 3 + (bi−1300)/233; 800–1300 → 2 + (bi−800)/500; 150–800 → 1 + (bi−150)/650; <150 → 'too slow to accurately emulate'. Applied to today's container runs: 1181 → 2.8×, 1512 → 3.9×, 1674 → 4.6×, 1838 → 5.3×, 2065 → 6.3×; so the default 4× was roughly right for the mid runs and under-throttled by ~35% for the 2065 runs (onar, limnoupolis) and over-throttled for pallada (1181). The 1.2× PSI value corresponds to a PSI benchmarkIndex of ≈280 (mid-tier mobile class), so PSI hardware is ~5× slower than this container; do not expect local benchmarkIndex to ever match PSI's.

findings.claim: A run whose page never goes network/CPU-quiet within maxWaitForLoad (45 s default) yields garbage metrics (observed TBT 142,018 ms and TTI 160,917 ms on limnoupolis.gr) and carries a runWarning; such runs must be discarded, not averaged.
findings.detail: core/config/constants.js defaultSettings: maxWaitForFcp 30000, maxWaitForLoad 45000, pauseAfterFcpMs 1000, pauseAfterLoadMs 1000, networkQuietThresholdMs 1000, cpuQuietThresholdMs 1000. Local evidence: limnoupolis_gr.json runWarnings ['The page loaded too slowly to finish within the time limit. Results may be incomplete.'], TBT 142,018 ms, TTI 160,917 ms, max-potential-fid 10,000 ms, SI 21.5 s — the three.js hero keeps the main thread busy so Lantern's TTI never settles and TBT accumulates (each simulated task capped at 10 s, but many tasks). voreniahorizon_gr.json carried the same warning (TBT 428, LCP 9.0 s — also incomplete). pallada_gr.json carried a redirect warning ('your test URL … was re[directed]'), which adds a redirect hop to every time metric. Lighthouse CI example sets "maxWaitForLoad": 90000 to 'Wait up to 90s for the page to load'; CLI flag --max-wait-for-load.
findings.breaks_when: Averaging or 'median-of-5' including such runs still corrupts the result when ≥3 of 5 hit the timeout — the page itself is the problem (continuous animation loop / autoplay) and the audit must say so instead of reporting a number.
findings.how_to_apply: In lighthouse.sh: emit runWarnings in the JSON line and exclude any run with a non-empty runWarnings from the median; if all runs warn, report 'page never idles – continuous main-thread work' as a blocking finding. Always test the final URL (with www/trailing slash exactly as the server serves it) to avoid redirect warnings. Do not raise --max-wait-for-load to 'fix' the number; the warning is the finding.
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.runWarnings' is [] on every run used; TBT values are < 10,000 ms (Lantern's own per-task cap); TTI is finite and < maxWaitForLoad.
findings.correction: CLI defaults confirmed (constants.js maxWaitForFcp 30000, maxWaitForLoad 45000, pause/quiet thresholds 1000 ms) and the local evidence confirmed (limnoupolis_gr.json runWarnings 'The page loaded too slowly to finish within the time limit. Results may be incomplete.', TBT 142 017.85 ms; voreniahorizon same warning; pallada redirect warning). Correction: PSI is stricter, not equal: lr-mobile-config.js and lr-desktop-config.js set maxWaitForFcp 15 s and maxWaitForLoad 35 s, so a page that idles between 35 and 45 s passes locally but is 'incomplete' in PSI. Also PSI 'will attempt to follow 3XX redirects before handing off that URL to Lighthouse' (release note May 10, 2022), so the pallada.gr → /en/ redirect warning appears only in the CLI; the plugin should resolve redirects itself (curl -sIL) before running the CLI.

findings.claim: The PSI API call is GET https://pagespeedonline.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed?url=<URL>&strategy=mobile&category=performance&key=<KEY>; without a key it is unusable for automation — today it returned HTTP 429 'Quota exceeded … limit Queries per day' on the shared anonymous project.
findings.detail: Reference (runpagespeed): GET https://pagespeedonline.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed; query params: url (required), category enum ACCESSIBILITY | BEST_PRACTICES | PERFORMANCE | SEO (repeatable; 'if none are given, only Performance category will be run'), strategy enum DESKTOP | MOBILE ('desktop is the default' — always pass strategy=mobile), locale, utm_campaign, utm_source, captchaToken. Response: captchaResult, kind, id, loadingExperience, originLoadingExperience, analysisUTCTimestamp, lighthouseResult (LighthouseResultV5: a full Lighthouse JSON incl. lighthouseVersion, audits, categories, configSettings, environment). Get-started (Last updated 2025-08-28): 'The API can be used with or without an API key, although a key is recommended for frequent, automated queries'; legacy host https://www.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed also works; key goes in the URL ('safe for embedding in URLs'). My read-only test today without key: both calls → HTTP 429 in 0.4 s with body error.code 429, message "Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Queries' and limit 'Queries per day' of service 'pagespeedonline.googleapis.com' for consumer 'project_number:583797351490'" — the shared no-key project's daily quota was already exhausted mid-day.
findings.breaks_when: Any plugin flow that calls PSI without a key will fail nondeterministically (shared quota); omitting strategy returns desktop numbers that look ~20–30 points better and are scored on desktop curves.
findings.how_to_apply: Create a Google Cloud project, enable 'PageSpeed Insights API', create an API key, store it as PSI_API_KEY. Call: curl -sG 'https://pagespeedonline.googleapis.com/pagespeedonline/v5/runPagespeed' --data-urlencode "url=$URL" -d strategy=mobile -d category=performance -d key=$PSI_API_KEY. Read: .lighthouseResult.categories.performance.score, .lighthouseResult.lighthouseVersion, .lighthouseResult.environment.benchmarkIndex, .lighthouseResult.audits["largest-contentful-paint"].numericValue etc. Keep the full JSON (it is a normal Lighthouse report).
findings.how_to_verify: HTTP 200 with .lighthouseResult.configSettings.formFactor == 'mobile' and .lighthouseResult.configSettings.throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier == 4; .analysisUTCTimestamp is today.
findings.correction: Endpoint, parameters and defaults confirmed ('strategy ... desktop is the default'; 'if none are given, only Performance category will be run'; get-started Last updated 2025-08-28: key 'recommended for frequent, automated queries'). I repeated the anonymous call for https://pallada.gr/en/ and got HTTP 429 with the same 'Queries per day' message for project_number 583797351490, so the observation reproduces. Correction to how_to_verify: expect .lighthouseResult.configSettings.throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier == 1.2 (not 4) on mobile, and formFactor 'mobile'; a value of 4 there would mean the response did not come from PSI's Lightrider config.

findings.claim: Field data in the PSI response lives in loadingExperience (URL) and originLoadingExperience (whole origin): metrics.<NAME>.percentile is the 28-day p75, category is FAST | AVERAGE | SLOW, distributions give the Good/NI/Poor proportions, and overall_category is the CWV verdict; the URL block is absent or falls back to origin when CrUX lacks page data.
findings.detail: Get-started example JSON: loadingExperience { id, metrics { FIRST_CONTENTFUL_PAINT_MS { percentile, distributions [ {min 0,max 1000,proportion}, {min 1000,max 2500,proportion}, {min 2500,proportion} ], category 'SLOW' }, … }, overall_category, initial_url }, originLoadingExperience with the same shape; metric keys used by PSI today: FIRST_CONTENTFUL_PAINT_MS, LARGEST_CONTENTFUL_PAINT_MS, CUMULATIVE_LAYOUT_SHIFT_SCORE (CLS ×100 as integer), INTERACTION_TO_NEXT_PAINT, EXPERIMENTAL_TIME_TO_FIRST_BYTE (the doc sample still shows legacy FIRST_INPUT_DELAY_MS). PSI 'About': data = CrUX 'previous 28-day collection period', updated daily; 'PSI will fall back to origin-level granularity' when the page lacks data; 'sometimes the origin may also have insufficient data'; the aggregation passes CWV if p75 of LCP, CLS and INP are all Good (INP optional when insufficient). CrUX methodology (updated 2024-06-20): a page must be 'publicly discoverable' and 'sufficiently popular'; origins/pages with >20% ineligible traffic are excluded; query strings and fragments are stripped; iframes contribute to the top-level page. For low-traffic Greek hotel/villa sites expect origin-level data only, or none.
findings.breaks_when: Treating originLoadingExperience as the page's own data: a fast home page can show 'Poor' because slow booking/forum pages dominate the origin; and sites with no CrUX data have no field verdict at all, so success must then be judged by lab + RUM you add yourself.
findings.how_to_apply: jq: '.loadingExperience.id, .loadingExperience.overall_category, (.loadingExperience.metrics|to_entries[]|{k:.key,p75:.value.percentile,cat:.value.category})' and the same for .originLoadingExperience; compare .loadingExperience.id with the requested URL — if it equals the origin, the page itself had no data. Report both blocks in the plugin's audit output and mark 'no field data' explicitly.
findings.how_to_verify: loadingExperience.id equals the exact tested URL; percentile values change day to day (daily update); LARGEST_CONTENTFUL_PAINT_MS.percentile ≤ 2500, INTERACTION_TO_NEXT_PAINT.percentile ≤ 200, CUMULATIVE_LAYOUT_SHIFT_SCORE.percentile ≤ 10 → overall_category FAST.
findings.correction: Structure confirmed from the get-started sample (percentile, distributions with min/max/proportion, category 'SLOW'; sample still shows legacy FIRST_INPUT_DELAY_MS) and PSI About (origin fallback, daily update, 28-day window). Correction that changes the plugin design: the same get-started page (Last updated 2025-08-28) now says 'We plan to discontinue including real-world data from the Chrome User Experience Report in this API. We recommend the CrUX API or the CrUX History API instead' and its summary calls PSI real-world data 'soon to be discontinued'. Do not build the Field column on loadingExperience/originLoadingExperience; read field data from the CrUX API and keep the PSI block only as a fallback while it exists. Also the PSI release note Aug 8, 2023 confirms the INP key is INTERACTION_TO_NEXT_PAINT (EXPERIMENTAL_ prefix removed).

findings.claim: PSI API quota with a key is 25,000 queries/day per Google Cloud project (resets midnight Pacific) and roughly 240 queries/minute; the API sends no X-RateLimit headers, returns 429 (sometimes 500) when exceeded, and Google's docs do not publish the numbers — only the Cloud Console quota page does.
findings.detail: Unlighthouse rate-limits page: budget alarm at 24,000 of 25,000/day, '~240/min limit: 4 per second is conservative', 'The API doesn't return rate limit headers (X-RateLimit-*). You must track usage client-side', 'Retry-After header tells you how long to wait. If it's missing, default to 60 seconds', exponential backoff on 429/5xx, 'Each project gets its own 25k/day quota', quota increase via Cloud Console. Google's get-started page only says a key is 'recommended for frequent, automated queries' and gives no figures. Observed today: anonymous requests 429 'Queries per day' on the shared project. Lighthouse CI supports collect.method 'psi' with psiApiKey (required) and psiStrategy 'mobile' (default), limited to publicly reachable URLs (staging behind auth cannot use PSI).
findings.breaks_when: A monitoring loop over 10 sites × N pages × several runs/hour can exhaust 25k/day or trip the per-minute limit; staging URLs behind HTTP auth or noindex-only pages still work in PSI, but intranet/localhost do not.
findings.how_to_apply: Pace PSI calls at ≤ 1 per second per project, retry on 429 with Retry-After or 2^n·1 s + jitter backoff, count daily usage client-side, and keep one dedicated GCP project/key per client site set. For CI: lighthouserc.json collect {"method":"psi","psiApiKey":"…","psiStrategy":"mobile","numberOfRuns":3}.
findings.how_to_verify: Google Cloud Console → APIs & Services → PageSpeed Insights API → Quotas shows 'Queries per day' and current usage; a burst of 10 sequential calls at 1/s returns 10× HTTP 200.

findings.claim: Lighthouse 13 removed or renamed most non-scored performance audits; the plugin's lighthouse.sh reads several of them (uses-optimized-images, third-party-summary, largest-contentful-paint-element) and will silently report 0/empty under LH 13 even though today's local runs used LH 12.8.2.
findings.detail: LH 13 blog (Oct 10, 2025) replacement table: layout-shifts → cls-culprits-insight; redirects, server-response-time, uses-text-compression → document-latency-insight; dom-size → dom-size-insight; duplicated-javascript → duplicated-javascript-insight; font-display → font-display-insight; modern-image-formats, uses-optimized-images, efficient-animated-content, uses-responsive-images → image-delivery-insight; work-during-interaction → interaction-to-next-paint-insight; prioritize-lcp-image, lcp-lazy-loaded → lcp-discovery-insight; largest-contentful-paint-element → lcp-phases-insight; legacy-javascript → legacy-javascript-insight; uses-http2 → modern-http-insight; critical-request-chains, uses-rel-preconnect → network-dependency-tree-insight; render-blocking-resources → render-blocking-insight; third-party-summary → third-parties-insight; uses-long-cache-ttl → use-cache-insight; viewport → viewport-insight. Removed with no replacement: first-meaningful-paint, font-size, no-document-write, offscreen-images ('unlikely to have an impact on what Lighthouse measures'), preload-fonts, third-party-facades, uses-passive-event-listeners, uses-rel-preload. Still present: unused-javascript, unused-css-rules, total-byte-weight, network-requests, dom-size-insight, non-composited-animations, unsized-images. Requires Node ≥ 22.19. Local lh/runs/*.json show lighthouseVersion 12.8.2 (npx cache), PSI serves 13.x.
findings.breaks_when: `npx lighthouse` on a fresh machine installs 13.5.0: in lighthouse.sh the jq expressions `.audits["uses-optimized-images"]…//0`, `[.audits["third-party-summary"].details.items[]?.transferSize]|add//0`, and the LCP lazy check on `largest-contentful-paint-element` all evaluate to 0/""/false without error, so the audit would claim 'no image savings, no third-party bytes, LCP not lazy' on every site.
findings.how_to_apply: Pin the version (`npx lighthouse@13` or `npm i lighthouse@13.5.0`) and record .lighthouseVersion in every output line; in lighthouse.sh read the insight ids with fallbacks: image savings from .audits["image-delivery-insight"], third-party bytes from .audits["third-parties-insight"].details.items[].transferSize, LCP discovery flags (lazy-loaded, fetchpriority, preloaded) from .audits["lcp-discovery-insight"].details, LCP phases (TTFB/load delay/load time/render delay) from .audits["lcp-phases-insight"], render-blocking from .audits["render-blocking-insight"], font-display from .audits["font-display-insight"]. Fail loudly (exit non-zero) if an expected audit id is missing instead of defaulting to 0.
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.lighthouseVersion, (.audits|keys|map(select(endswith("-insight")))' on a fresh run shows 13.x and the insight ids; jq '.audits["third-party-summary"]' returns null on 13.x and an object on 12.x.
findings.correction: Removal confirmed: default-config.js on main has no third-party-summary, uses-optimized-images, largest-contentful-paint-element or render-blocking-resources; the LH13 blog table and 'requires Node 22.19 or higher' confirmed. Two corrections to the how_to_apply ids: the blog's names differ from the shipped audit ids. Shipped ids (default-config.js main AND the local 12.8.2 JSON) are lcp-breakdown-insight (not lcp-phases-insight), inp-breakdown-insight (not interaction-to-next-paint-insight) and cache-insight (not use-cache-insight); changelog 12.5.0 'implement use-cache-insight' then 12.7.0 'cache-insight: fix wrong value' shows the rename happened in 12.x. Also forced-reflow-insight exists and is not in the blog table. Second: the local 12.8.2 runs already contain all 17 insight audits alongside the legacy ones, so lighthouse.sh can switch to insight ids today and be correct on both 12.8.2 and 13.x with no version fork. Note PSI skips modern-http-insight and bf-cache (lr configs), so those two are null in PSI JSON.

findings.claim: CLS is the one metric already perfect on these sites (median 0.002) and the cheapest to lose: the staging observation of 0 → 0.107 after enabling LiteSpeed image lazy-load costs ~3 points (metric score 0.88) and would also flip the field CWV verdict (CLS > 0.1 = Poor).
findings.detail: Curve: CLS p10 0.1 (score 0.9), median 0.25 (0.5); by the exact formula 0.107 → ≈0.88 → 25×(1−0.88) ≈ 3 points lost; 0.05 → 0.99 (−0.3). Local runs: 8/10 pages at 0.000–0.005 (0 points lost), limnoupolis.gr at 0.103 (−2.7). Field threshold is identical (Good ≤ 0.1 at p75), and PSI 'About' classifies with the same buckets, so a lab CLS regression above 0.1 predicts a field CWV failure. Lab CLS covers only the load window on a 412×823 viewport without scrolling; field CLS includes the whole session (web.dev lab-vs-field), so lazy-loaded media below the fold that shifts on scroll shows up in the field but not in Lighthouse. LH 13 moved the culprit list to cls-culprits-insight (replacing layout-shifts), with unsized-images and non-composited-animations kept as separate audits.
findings.breaks_when: Any change that removes intrinsic width/height or reserved space from first-viewport images, iframes (maps, booking widgets), cookie banners injected at top, or fonts swapped without size-adjust; a lazy-load plugin that strips/overrides dimensions or injects placeholders of different aspect ratio is the typical cause.
findings.how_to_apply: Before enabling any lazy-load / image-optimisation option (LiteSpeed 'Lazy Load Images', FlyingPress, Perfmatters), run the 5-run median and record CLS; after enabling, re-run; accept only if median CLS stays ≤ 0.02 and cls-culprits-insight lists no new element. Exclude the first-viewport (hero, logo, first row) from lazy-load and keep explicit width/height on every /
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.audits["cumulative-layout-shift"].numericValue, .audits["cls-culprits-insight"].details' before/after; also take Lighthouse's filmstrip screenshots (--save-assets) and click through the page on a 412 px wide device to confirm nothing jumps when images arrive.

findings.claim: PSI runs from one of four Google regions chosen by the tester's location (Oregon, South Carolina, Netherlands, Taiwan), on Google's own hardware, with Lighthouse 13.x; the geo difference matters less than the fixed 150 ms simulated RTT, but the CPU and Chrome version differences are why PSI and a laptop disagree.
findings.detail: DebugBear (third-party; Google does not document it): 'PageSpeed Insights picks the server to run the test from based on your current location. It uses one of four locations: Northwestern US (Oregon), Southeastern US (South Carolina), Northwestern Europe (Netherlands), Asia (Taiwan)'; 'Every time Lighthouse tests a page it runs a very simple CPU benchmark. If a test is run on a faster CPU you'll get higher performance scores'; 'If you run Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools, Chrome extensions can impact your Performance scores. Use Incognito mode or a new Chrome profile'; 'PageSpeed Insights and DebugBear use different timeout settings'; 'The default mobile network latency that's added by PageSpeed Insights… is 150 milliseconds. Compared to that the ping time between the servers isn't that significant.' Lighthouse docs/variability.md lists client hardware and resource contention as High-impact sources and browser extensions/antivirus as contention. A Greek tester is normally routed to the Netherlands region, so a Greek-hosted origin without CDN adds ~30–60 ms RTT per round trip on top of the simulated 150 ms.
findings.breaks_when: Comparing a PSI run made by a US colleague with one made from Greece, or a DevTools run with extensions enabled, and attributing the difference to the site.
findings.how_to_apply: Use PSI (API) as the single reference judge, always from the same place (the API call's region follows the caller's IP — run it from one fixed server), and compare only PSI-vs-PSI over time; use local Lighthouse for fast iteration, in a clean headless Chrome (--chrome-flags='--headless=new --no-sandbox', no extensions). Record .lighthouseResult.environment.benchmarkIndex and .lighthouseVersion from PSI alongside local values.
findings.how_to_verify: Two PSI runs 10 minutes apart from the same caller should agree within ±3 points on a stable page; the Lighthouse HTML report footer shows 'CPU/Memory Power' (benchmarkIndex) and the Lighthouse version for both environments.
findings.correction: Regions confirmed only via DebugBear (article 'Updated on November 29, 2025'): 'one of four locations: Northwestern US (Oregon) Southeastern US (South Carolina) Northwestern Europe (Netherlands) Asia (Taiwan)'; Google does not document this. LH 13 on PSI confirmed by Google's release note (Oct 20, 2025) and changelog 13.5.0 '... PageSpeed Insights within 2 weeks' of 2026-09-17. Correction: the dominant reason PSI and a laptop disagree is not CPU speed per se but the different multiplier applied to it — PSI uses 1.2× on ~benchmarkIndex-280 hardware, a laptop uses 4× on 1500–2000 hardware. By the calculator formula those are meant to be equivalent, so a well-calibrated local run should land near PSI; a discrepancy > ~30% in TBT means the local multiplier is miscalibrated, not that 'PSI is slower'.

findings.claim: For field history and alerting independent of PSI, the CrUX API is a POST to https://chromeuxreport.googleapis.com/v1/records:queryRecord?key=KEY with {origin|url, formFactor PHONE, metrics[…]} returning p75 + 3-bin histograms over a trailing 28-day window; it needs its own API key and returns NOT_FOUND for sites below the popularity threshold.
findings.detail: CrUX API doc: 'Queries are submitted as JSON objects using a POST request to https://chromeuxreport.googleapis.com/v1/records:queryRecord?key=[YOUR_API_KEY]' with body e.g. {"origin":"https://example.com","formFactor":"PHONE","metrics":["largest_contentful_paint","interaction_to_next_paint","cumulative_layout_shift","experimental_time_to_first_byte"]}; identifiers: origin (all pages aggregated) or url (exact page; query strings/fragments stripped); formFactor PHONE | TABLET | DESKTOP (omit for all); response: record.metrics.<name>.histogram [3 bins with density], percentiles.p75, collectionPeriod {firstDate,lastDate} ('will always show 28-days'), plus form_factors fractions; CLS is a string double; floats rounded to 4 decimals; 'Using the CrUX API requires a Google Cloud API key provisioned for Chrome UX Report API usage'. Methodology: eligibility = publicly discoverable + sufficiently popular; data is daily-updated trailing 28 days (PSI) vs monthly origin-only BigQuery.
findings.breaks_when: Low-traffic villa/hotel sites: url-level queries return 404 NOT_FOUND and only origin-level (or nothing) exists, so field success cannot be proven from CrUX alone — a self-hosted web-vitals.js RUM beacon is then the only field source.
findings.how_to_apply: curl -s -X POST "https://chromeuxreport.googleapis.com/v1/records:queryRecord?key=$CRUX_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"origin":"https://pallada.gr","formFactor":"PHONE","metrics":["largest_contentful_paint","interaction_to_next_paint","cumulative_layout_shift"]}' | jq '.record.metrics|map_values(.percentiles.p75)'. Run weekly per origin and per key landing URL; store p75 series; alert when LCP p75 > 2500, INP p75 > 200 or CLS p75 > 0.1.
findings.how_to_verify: HTTP 200 with record.collectionPeriod.lastDate ≈ 2 days ago and p75 values present; 404 means the origin/page is not in CrUX (not an auth error — a wrong key gives 400/403).

findings.claim: Desktop and mobile scores are not comparable: desktop uses its own curves (LCP 1200/2400, FCP 934/1600, SI 1311/2300, TBT 150/350 ms), 40 ms RTT / 10 Mbps / CPU ×1 and a 1350×940 viewport, so a desktop 95 says nothing about mobile; the plugin must default to mobile and label every number with its form factor.
findings.detail: core/audits/metrics/*.js desktop blocks: LCP p10 1200 median 2400 ('25th and 5th percentiles HTTPArchive'), FCP 934/1600, SI 1311/2300, TBT 150/350; CLS shared 0.1/0.25. Lantern desktopDense4G: rttMs 40, throughputKbps 10,240, cpuSlowdownMultiplier 1 ('Dense 4G 25th percentile'). constants.js DESKTOP_EMULATION_METRICS: width 1350, height 940, deviceScaleFactor 1, mobile false; UA 'Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7 … Chrome/136'. PSI API default strategy is DESKTOP if omitted. Scoring doc: 'Prior to Lighthouse v6, all score curves were based on mobile performance data… led to artificially inflated desktop scores.'
findings.breaks_when: A report or client promise built on `--preset=desktop` or an API call without strategy=mobile; the same Elementor page typically scores 20–30 points higher on desktop and nothing has improved for the mobile ranking signal.
findings.how_to_apply: CLI: lighthouse <url> --only-categories=performance --form-factor=mobile (default) for the contract number; add a second line with --preset=desktop only as information. PSI: always strategy=mobile. In the plugin output include formFactor in every row.
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.configSettings.formFactor, .configSettings.screenEmulation.width' → 'mobile', 412 for the contract runs.

findings.claim: TBT is defined as the sum of main-thread task time beyond 50 ms between FCP and TTI and Google's lab target is < 200 ms 'on average mobile hardware'; it is the single heaviest metric (30%) and the one most inflated by host CPU, so TBT verdicts should come from PSI or a calibrated box, while LCP/FCP/CLS verdicts can come from any box.
findings.detail: web.dev/tbt (Last updated October 15, 2025): 'measures the total amount of time after First Contentful Paint (FCP) where the main thread was blocked for long enough to prevent input responsiveness'; 'Lighthouse stops monitoring TBT after Time to Interactive (TTI)'; 'strive to have a Total Blocking Time of less than 200 milliseconds when tested on average mobile hardware'; 'we recommend optimizing for INP over TBT… TBT is a proxy metric for INP in the lab'; measuring TBT in the field is discouraged. Lantern TotalBlockingTime.ts: only CPU nodes ≥ BLOCKING_TIME_THRESHOLD kept, window = FCP→interactive, result = 0.5×optimistic + 0.5×pessimistic (intercept 0). Because the simulator multiplies host task durations by 4, a host task of 60 ms (which is 10 ms blocking after 50 ms) becomes 240 ms → 190 ms blocking: small host noise becomes large TBT noise. Local evidence: TBT ranged 63–615 ms on valid runs with benchmarkIndex swinging 1181–2065 across runs.
findings.breaks_when: Rejecting a fix because local TBT rose 100 ms while LCP improved — on a shared host 100 ms of TBT is within noise; or accepting a page because a fast workstation shows TBT 40 ms that PSI measures at 250 ms.
findings.how_to_apply: Decision rule for the plugin: LCP/FCP/SI/CLS pass/fail from the local 5-run median; TBT pass/fail only from PSI (or from local when benchmarkIndex is within ±15% of the PSI machine's benchmarkIndex observed in .lighthouseResult.environment). Report TBT with the benchmarkIndex next to it.
findings.how_to_verify: Same URL, same day: local median TBT vs PSI TBT differ by < 30% when benchmarkIndex is comparable; if not, mark local TBT as unreliable in the report.
findings.correction: Definition and target confirmed (web.dev/tbt 'Last updated: October 15, 2025': 'less than 200 milliseconds when tested on average mobile hardware', 'Lighthouse stops monitoring TBT after Time to Interactive', 'TBT is a proxy metric for INP in the lab'). Correction to the decision rule: 'benchmarkIndex within ±15% of PSI's' is unattainable (PSI ≈ 280 vs any desktop/server 1000–2000) and unnecessary. Replace with: compute the calibrated multiplier from the local benchmarkIndex via the calculator formula and pass --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=<that>; then local TBT is comparable to PSI's 1.2× result by construction. Keep PSI as the tiebreaker, but also note that Speed Index and FCP are CPU-scaled by Lantern too, so 'LCP/FCP/CLS from any box' should read 'LCP/CLS from any box; FCP/SI/TBT need a calibrated box'.

findings.claim: PSI's mobile lab run is Lighthouse's Lightrider config, not the CLI default: cpuSlowdownMultiplier 1.2, maxWaitForFcp 15 s, maxWaitForLoad 35 s, and the audits modern-http-insight and bf-cache skipped; this has been so since December 2024 and is why a local 4× run and PSI disagree on TBT.
findings.detail: core/config/lr-mobile-config.js (main, 13.5.0): extends lighthouse:default; settings.maxWaitForFcp 15*1000, maxWaitForLoad 35*1000, throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier 1.2 with comment 'Determined using PSI CPU benchmark median and https://lighthouse-cpu-throttling-calculator.vercel.app/', skipAudits ['modern-http-insight' (h2 audit 'so it doesn't lie to us', issue 6539), 'bf-cache' ('always bf-cache failures when testing in headless')]. lr-desktop-config.js: same waits, formFactor desktop, throttling desktopDense4G (CPU ×1), desktop screen/UA. PSI release notes Dec 5, 2024: 'The CPU throttling factor for PageSpeed Insights has been adjusted to account for the low CPU performance benchmarks typical in PageSpeed Insights production environments. In general, this should result in increased lab data TBT scores for sites on mobile. Field data and desktop scores should not be affected.' Lighthouse changelog 12.2.2 (2024-11-14) 'lr: set CPU throttling based on benchmark (#16226)', 12.2.3 (2024-12-02) note. DebugBear (Updated Jan 27, 2026): 'PSI has changed its throttling from 4x to 1.2x in December 2024'. Network simulation (150 ms RTT, 1.6 Mbps) is unchanged.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break a site; it breaks measurement: a plugin that asserts PSI JSON has cpuSlowdownMultiplier 4, or that compares local 4× TBT with PSI TBT without calibrating, will draw wrong accept/reject conclusions.
findings.how_to_apply: In lighthouse.sh compute m from .environment.benchmarkIndex of a first probe run (formula below) and rerun with --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=$m; optionally also --max-wait-for-load=35000 --max-wait-for-fcp=15000 to mirror PSI's timeouts. Record .configSettings.throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier in every result row. When reading PSI JSON, expect 1.2 on mobile and 1 on desktop, and expect audits.modern-http-insight / audits.bf-cache to be absent.
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.configSettings.throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier, .configSettings.maxWaitForLoad' on a PSI lighthouseResult prints 1.2 and 35000; on a default CLI run prints 4 and 45000. Same URL, same day: calibrated local median TBT within ~30% of PSI TBT.

findings.claim: The exact benchmarkIndex → cpuSlowdownMultiplier formula used by the Lighthouse team's calculator is piecewise linear: m = 3 + (bi−1300)/233 for bi ≥ 1300; 2 + (bi−800)/500 for 800 ≤ bi < 1300; 1 + (bi−150)/650 for 150 ≤ bi < 800; below 150 the host is 'too slow to accurately emulate the target Lighthouse device'.
findings.detail: Read from the calculator's bundled pages/index-*.js: if(e>=1300){t=(e-1300)/233; n=3+t; ...} if(e>=800){o=2+(e-800)/500; range ±0.75} if(e>=150){a=1+(e-150)/650; range ±0.25} else message 'This device is too slow to accurately emulate the target Lighthouse device.' It prints 'lighthouse --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=<m> <url>'. Inverting PSI's 1.2 gives a PSI median benchmarkIndex ≈ 280. For today's container: 1181 → 2.8×, 1512 → 3.9×, 1555 → 4.1×, 1674 → 4.6×, 1838 → 5.3×, 2065 → 6.3×, i.e. the default 4× under-throttled the two heaviest pages by ~35–55%, so their already-bad TBT is optimistic. The brackets in docs/throttling.md ('as of Chrome m86') are the coarse version of the same mapping.
findings.breaks_when: Applying the formula to a benchmarkIndex taken while other processes run (the index itself is noisy on shared hosts); always take it from the same run you are calibrating or from a quiet probe.
findings.how_to_apply: bash: bi=$(jq .environment.benchmarkIndex probe.json); m=$(awk -v b=$bi 'BEGIN{ if(b>=1300)m=3+(b-1300)/233; else if(b>=800)m=2+(b-800)/500; else if(b>=150)m=1+(b-150)/650; else m=0; printf "%.1f", m }'); [ "$m" = 0.0 ] && echo 'host too slow' && exit 1; lighthouse $URL --throttling.cpuSlowdownMultiplier=$m ... Store bi and m with every result.
findings.how_to_verify: Enter 1500 on https://lighthouse-cpu-throttling-calculator.vercel.app/ → '3.9x'; enter 280 → '1.2x'. A calibrated run of pallada.gr should bring local TBT within ~30% of PSI's.

findings.claim: Google has announced it will remove CrUX field data from the PSI API response; field reporting must be built on the CrUX API (150 queries/min per project, free) and the CrUX History API (weekly points, 25 periods by default, up to 40 weeks), not on loadingExperience/originLoadingExperience.
findings.detail: PSI get-started (Last updated 2025-08-28): 'The PageSpeed Insights API returns real-world data from the Chrome User Experience Report and lab data from Lighthouse. We plan to discontinue including real-world data from the Chrome User Experience Report in this API. We recommend the CrUX API (guide) or the CrUX History API (guide) instead.' Page summary: 'real-world data (soon to be discontinued)'. CrUX API doc: 'The CrUX API is limited to 150 queries per minute per Google Cloud project, which is offered without charge.' CrUX History API (Published Feb 7, 2023, Last updated Apr 11, 2025): POST https://chromeuxreport.googleapis.com/v1/records:queryHistoryRecord?key=; 'updated each Monday and contains data up until the previous Saturday (as per the standard 2-day lag). It contains the previous 40-weeks worth of data—one collection period per week. By default, 25 collection periods are returned'; 'shares the same limit with the CrUX API for 150 queries per minute'. No removal date is published.
findings.breaks_when: A plugin whose 'Field' column reads PSI's loadingExperience will one day start showing 'no field data' for every site with no code change on your side; CrUX still returns nothing for origins below the popularity threshold (low-traffic villa sites), so a self-hosted web-vitals.js beacon remains the only guaranteed field source.
findings.how_to_apply: Create one GCP project; enable both 'PageSpeed Insights API' and 'Chrome UX Report API'; one key. Field column: POST records:queryRecord with {origin|url, formFactor PHONE, metrics [largest_contentful_paint, interaction_to_next_paint, cumulative_layout_shift]}; trend: records:queryHistoryRecord with the same body and read .record.metrics.*.percentilesTimeseries.p75s. Treat PSI loadingExperience as a bonus field that may be null.
findings.how_to_verify: queryRecord returns 200 with record.collectionPeriod.lastDate about 2 days ago; queryHistoryRecord returns 25 collectionPeriods ascending; Cloud Console quota page shows 150/min for Chrome UX Report API.

findings.claim: The chrome-devtools MCP lighthouse_audit tool cannot be used for the performance score at all: its schema states it 'excludes performance' (accessibility, SEO, best practices, agentic browsing only) and defaults to device 'desktop'; performance in that MCP comes from performance_start_trace, which is a DevTools trace with no Lantern simulation and no score.
findings.detail: Tool schema loaded in this session: description 'Get Lighthouse score and reports for accessibility, SEO, best practices, and agentic browsing. This excludes performance. For performance audits, run performance_start_trace'; parameters device enum [desktop, mobile] default 'desktop', mode [navigation, snapshot] default 'navigation', pageId required. This answers the researcher's open question: do not route the plugin's score measurement through this tool; use the Lighthouse CLI/LHCI (mobile, calibrated) and PSI.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; using it would silently give no performance category and desktop emulation.
findings.how_to_apply: In the plugin, reserve mcp__plugin_ecc_chrome-devtools__lighthouse_audit for a11y/SEO/best-practices spot checks with device='mobile' passed explicitly; use performance_start_trace + performance_analyze_insight only for qualitative LCP/CLS culprit inspection, never for a score.
findings.how_to_verify: Call lighthouse_audit on any page: the returned report has no 'performance' category.

findings.claim: The PSI UI/API resolves 3XX redirects before handing the URL to Lighthouse, while the CLI does not; so the CLI's redirect runWarning (seen on pallada.gr → /en/) and its redirect penalty on every timing metric never appear in PSI for the same URL.
findings.detail: PSI release notes, May 10, 2022: 'PSI will attempt to resolve HTTP redirects before analysis. Before, PSI would send the URL directly to Lighthouse and Lighthouse would handle redirects. Now, PSI will attempt to follow 3XX redirects before handing off that URL to Lighthouse. It is still possible to opt to run with the "original" URL, but this is not usually advised.' Local pallada_gr.json runWarnings: 'The page may not be loading as expected because your test URL (https://pallada.gr/) was redirected to https://pallada.gr/en/. Try testing the second URL directly.' Polylang/WPML sites in this stack redirect / to /el/ or /en/ by browser language, so the CLI will hit this on most of the agency's sites.
findings.breaks_when: Comparing CLI vs PSI for a redirecting URL and attributing the gap to the site; or the plugin testing the root URL of a Polylang site and reporting a redirect-inflated LCP/FCP.
findings.how_to_apply: Before each CLI run: final=$(curl -sIL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' -A 'Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 11; moto g power (2022))' "$URL") and audit $final; for language-redirecting sites audit each language home explicitly (/el/, /en/).
findings.how_to_verify: jq '.runWarnings' is [] and .finalDisplayedUrl == requested URL.

title: Elementor 4.x performance settings, experiments and heavy widgets
summary: On a 4.3.x + Pro site the Elementor-specific floor is ~130 KB gzip of JavaScript on every page (core runtime/frontend ~34 KB, Pro frontend ~24 KB, Pro elements-handlers.min.js ~70 KB monolithic, container chunk ~17 KB) plus one render-blocking post-N.css per Elementor document (page, header, footer, popups, loop items), so the score ceiling is set less by Elementor settings than by what is built on top of it (third-party tags, fonts, hero media, animations) and by how the cache plugin handles Elementor's CSS/JS. The 4.3.5 experiment inventory is small and mostly already optimal: the only front-end levers are e_font_icon_svg, e_optimized_markup, the merged Element Cache (TTL option elementor_element_cache_ttl, per-widget _element_cache) and the Performance-tab options elementor_css_print_method, elementor_optimized_image_loading, elementor_lazy_load_background_images, elementor_optimized_gutenberg_loading, elementor_local_google_fonts and elementor_font_display (still 'auto' by default; 7 of 9 audited homepages fail the font-display audit). e_assets_manager and e_page_audit are hidden editor-side experiments with no front-end effect, and e_optimized_css_files (alpha, off everywhere) is not a byte-saver but the gate for the fix to Elementor's CSS-purge-on-any-update-check problem that leaves cached pages unstyled. The biggest Elementor-specific breakage patterns are documented and reproducible: entrance animations render elements with class elementor-invisible until JS runs (so delaying Elementor JS blanks animated heroes), CSS Print Method 'internal' corrupts REST/AJAX JSON in 4.3.2–4.3.5 (#37468), Element Cache serves stale output for dynamic widgets that do not declare themselves dynamic, double lazy-loading (Elementor + LiteSpeed/WP Rocket) causes CLS or lazy LCP images, and Core/Pro version drift around 4.3.1's hidden nested-elements experiment produces fatal errors. The v4 Atomic editor is the only structural win: the sole controlled comparison found reports −65% DOM and −85% CSS with unchanged JS, and v4 is on by default only for installs created on ≥4.0.0, but it carries open server-side costs (#37016 Cache_Validity bloat up to ~1.1 s per uncached render on large/WPML sites; #36205 editor 508s on cheap hosting). Heavy widgets have measurable prices (Swiper 38 KB, Lottie 60 KB, lightbox 27 KB, Google Maps/YouTube iframes) and all have lazy or static alternatives; the plugin's build mode should treat 'nothing animated or sliding above the fold' and 'one lazy-loader only' as hard rules. Everything below was read from the official source/docs listed; Pro is closed-source so Pro experiment defaults are inferred from live page configs only.
critic_notes: Method: re-opened the WP Rocket, Perfmatters (delay, fetch-priority, lazy-load), LiteSpeed pageopt and FlyingPress Lazy Render docs via the proxy (WebFetch could not resolve those hosts; curl could), read current GitHub main sources for experiments/manager.php, element-cache, document.php, element-base.php, lazyload, image-loading-optimization, gutenberg, interactions (+ frontend handler), google-font.php, frontend.php, files/manager.php, changelog.txt and the Pro changelog page, issues #37468, #35983, #37016, #37443, and re-measured three asset sizes on pallada.gr. Note that 'main' is already 4.4.0-dev; defaults matched the researcher's 4.3.5 clone everywhere I checked. Not re-verified: per-chunk JS sizes other than swiper/handlers/frontend, the 37->23 div help table, the Windows 11 motion-effects article, #36205/#36212/#32226/#37217, Element Manager coverage of Pro template types, and the Reddit 'caching purgatory' thread (two searches found nothing; recommend dropping it). Open question on Greek subsets is now resolved (preserved via unicode-range; subset hint only for locale 'el'); open question on Interactions enqueue is resolved (page-conditional). Skipped: no Novamira calls were made and no site/file was modified. Risk for the user: the Element Caching help page is stale and says the opposite of the code about defaults; the plugin should cite source lines, not that page.

findings.claim: Delaying or deferring Elementor's own JavaScript is the largest mobile TBT lever on these sites, but Elementor renders every element with an entrance animation as class `elementor-invisible` and only reveals it in JS, so delaying core/Pro bundles blanks animated heroes; delay third-party scripts fully, defer (not delay) Elementor + jQuery, and keep the documented exclusion lists.
findings.detail: 4.3.5 source: includes/base/element-base.php:835 adds `elementor-invisible` to the `_wrapper` of any element with an animation; assets/dev/js/frontend/handlers/global.js removes it when the element enters the viewport (also background-video.js). If frontend.min.js/frontend-modules.min.js are delayed until interaction, those elements stay at opacity 0 (LCP never paints in Lighthouse, blank hero for visitors). WP Rocket doc (updated 2026-04-22): Delay JS has one-click Elementor exclusions; 'Load JavaScript deferred' can break Elementor sticky, fix by excluding `\/jquery(-migrate)?-?([0-9.]+)?(.min|.slim|.slim.min)?.js(\?(.*))?( |'|"|>|$)` and `/elementor-pro/assets/lib/sticky/jquery.sticky.min.js` (same list in Delay). Perfmatters doc lists the Elementor exclusions for 'Delay all scripts': jquery.min.js, jquery.smartmenus.min.js, jquery.sticky.min.js, webpack.runtime.min.js, webpack-pro.runtime.min.js, /elementor/assets/js/frontend.min.js, /elementor-pro/assets/js/frontend.min.js, frontend-modules.min.js, elements-handlers.min.js, elementorFrontendConfig, ElementorProFrontendConfig, imagesloaded.min.js, hooks.min.js, i18n.min.js, and notes 'if you're not using a lot of animations, you might not need any exclusions'. LiteSpeed 'Load JS Deferred' offers Deferred vs Delayed modes and recommends testing Delayed. Local Lighthouse: slow sites have TBT 428 ms–1.8 s (limnoupolis 142 s from three.js) with 5 GTM tags + pixel + cookie banner; fast sites (84–86) have few third-party scripts.
findings.breaks_when: Any above-the-fold element has an entrance animation and Elementor frontend JS is delayed -> hero invisible until first tap and LCP measured at interaction; sticky header with deferred jQuery/sticky not excluded -> header not sticky; popup 'On Page Load' trigger, Pro form reCAPTCHA, cookie-consent script delayed -> consent/events not recorded until interaction; GTM/gtag delayed -> page_view fired late or lost (needs marketer sign-off).
findings.how_to_apply: Perfmatters: Assets > JavaScript > Delay JavaScript with 'Delay only specified' (gtm.js, gtag/js, fbevents.js, cookie banner, chat); if 'Delay all' is used paste the Elementor exclusion list above; Defer JavaScript on, and exclude jquery + jquery.sticky if sticky is used. WP Rocket: File Optimization > Delay JavaScript execution > tick Elementor one-click exclusions; Load JavaScript deferred > add the two patterns. LiteSpeed: Page Optimization > JS Settings > Load JS Deferred = Deferred first (Delayed only after testing), JS Delayed Includes = third-party only, Guest Mode JS Excludes for Elementor. Before enabling any delay remove entrance animations from the first viewport (finding on animations).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse mobile before/after: TBT and 'Reduce unused JavaScript'; filmstrip shows hero painted at FCP. Playwright: goto page, wait 5 s with no mouse/keyboard, assert `document.querySelectorAll('.elementor-invisible').length === 0` for elements with top < 800 px, screenshot. Scroll to test sticky header; open a popup; submit a form; in Tag Assistant confirm GTM page_view fires without interaction when that is required.

findings.claim: With Elementor Pro active every Elementor page in 4.3 ships ~130 KB gzip of Elementor JS before any widget (core runtime + frontend-modules ~16 KB, frontend ~18 KB, Pro frontend ~24 KB, Pro elements-handlers.min.js ~70 KB gzip / 292 KB raw and monolithic, container 'shared-frontend-handlers' chunk ~17 KB); only Swiper (~38 KB), lightbox (~27 KB), nested-tabs (~13 KB), counter (~7.5 KB), video (~8 KB) are conditional.
findings.detail: 4.3.5 includes/frontend.php registers elementor-webpack-runtime, elementor-frontend-modules, swiper (assets/lib/swiper/v8/swiper.min.js, 143,709 B raw), flatpickr (50,680 B), elementor-dialog (11,622 B), elementor-frontend; Swiper is only enqueued via widget `get_script_depends()` (image-carousel.php, wordpress.php) or the page-assets loader (`e-swiper`). assets/dev/js/frontend/elements-handlers-manager.js lazy-imports per-widget chunks (accordion, alert, counter, progress, tabs, toggle, video, image-carousel, text-editor, nested-tabs, nested-accordion, contact-buttons, floating-bars) but handlers/container/container.js always imports the 'shared-frontend-handlers' chunk (background-slideshow + background-video), which is why background-video.min.js and background-slideshow.min.js (~8–9 KB each) appear on all 9 audited homepages even with zero slideshows. Measured on pallada.gr (Pro 4.3.x, gzip): elements-handlers.min.js 291,601 B raw / 69,928 B; Pro frontend.min.js 80,170 / 23,895; core frontend.min.js 60,022 / 18,280; swiper 143,709 / 38,152; lottie.min.js 252,588 / 60,581; jquery.smartmenus 24,109 / 6,867; jquery.sticky 3,721 / 1,442; `preloaded-elements-handlers.min.js` returns 404 (Pro 4.x has no non-dynamic bundle). Lighthouse: cretaforums (198 widgets) still loads 67.6 KB Pro handlers; unused JS 82–871 KB across sites. The 2020 developers post describes the dynamic handler/Swiper loading that is now the only mode (the 'Improved Asset Loading' experiment no longer exists in 4.3.5).
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break by itself (informational floor). Dequeuing elementor-pro elements-handlers.min.js breaks every Pro widget's JS (menus, forms, carousels, sticky, popups); dequeuing swiper on a page that has any Swiper consumer breaks that carousel.
findings.how_to_apply: Budget rule for the plugin: expect >= ~130 KB gzip Elementor JS per page with Pro; do not try to split elements-handlers (no chunking in Pro 4.3). Build rules: no Swiper consumer above the fold (Image Carousel, Slides, Loop/Media/Testimonial Carousel, Nested Carousel, container background slideshow); Site Settings > Lightbox > Image Lightbox (`global_image_lightbox`) off unless galleries need it (saves lightbox chunk + dialog); avoid Counter (adds jquery-numerator + chunk). Perfmatters Script Manager (per-page/regex) may unload swiper/smartmenus/flatpickr on pages that do not use them.
findings.how_to_verify: Chrome DevTools Network filtered by 'elementor' on a cached page: list JS files with compressed size and compare to the floor; Lighthouse 'Reduce unused JavaScript' entry for elements-handlers.min.js is expected and acceptable; after any unload, click carousels, open menus/tabs, play videos, open a popup.

findings.claim: Keep `elementor_css_print_method` = external (default) in 4.3.x: 'Internal Embedding' is the subject of the still-open bug #37468 (4.3.2–4.3.5: inline post CSS corrupts REST/admin-ajax JSON, Gutenberg/Yoast/Rank Math saves fail, 300 s hangs on zlib hosts), Elementor's FOUC article says internal 'can create conflicts with site caching mechanisms and degrade overall performance', and each Elementor document (page + header + footer + popups + loop templates) adds one render-blocking post-N.css that the cache plugin, not Elementor, should inline.
findings.detail: includes/settings/settings.php: option `elementor_css_print_method`, values `external` ('External File') | `internal` ('Internal Embedding'), default external; core/files/css/base.php prints `<style id="elementor-post-N">` when internal. Changelog 4.3.5 (2026-10-13): 'Fix: Page editing can fail when Internal CSS Embedding is enabled (#37468)', yet the issue thread reports saves still failing after PR #37643 (REST only) with 4.3.5 affected; workarounds: External File or rollback to 4.2.4. Observed: pallada loads 4 post CSS files (post-4252/4562/4565/4919) among 13 Elementor CSS links, Lighthouse flags post-4252.css render-blocking (150 ms); limnoupolis 4 post files + custom-frontend.min.css + custom-pro-widget-woocommerce-menu-cart.min.css each 240 ms; staging post-37550.css 413 ms; cretaforums (internal + FlyingPress) 0 Elementor CSS requests, score 74. WP Rocket excludes Elementor post CSS from Minify CSS 'to avoid a situation where the cache would be cleared too frequently' and purges when print method is External and Element Caching Default/Active. 'Additional Custom Breakpoints' (active) with a custom breakpoint (e.g. laptop on kand) compiles frontend CSS into uploads/elementor/css/custom-frontend.min.css and custom-pro-widget-*.min.css (seen render-blocking 366 ms).
findings.breaks_when: internal + any REST/AJAX request that applies the_content (Yoast/Rank Math meta save, block editor update, Elementor editor save via admin-ajax) -> 'Updating failed. The response is not a valid JSON response' / 'Server Error'; external + RUCSS/async CSS without exclusion -> FOUC; external + Clear Files & Data while page cache is warm -> cached HTML references deleted CSS (see CSS purge finding).
findings.how_to_apply: Elementor > Settings > Performance > CSS Print Method = External File. Let FlyingPress / LiteSpeed (QUIC.cloud CCSS) / WP Rocket RUCSS generate and inline critical CSS; per Elementor's FOUC doc exclude `/wp-content/plugins/elementor/assets/css/` from async/defer/RUCSS and regenerate critical CSS. Reduce documents per page: one header, one footer, popups only on pages whose conditions need them, avoid per-page popups. Avoid adding custom breakpoints unless the design needs them. If a tiny site insists on internal, test Gutenberg save with Yoast and Elementor editor save, and re-test after every Elementor update.
findings.how_to_verify: `curl -s URL | grep -o 'uploads/elementor/css/post-[0-9]*\.css' | sort -u | wc -l` (target <= 3); Lighthouse 'Eliminate render-blocking resources' lists no uploads/elementor/css/*.css; WebPageTest filmstrip shows no unstyled frame; after any change save a page in Gutenberg with Yoast/Rank Math active and in the Elementor editor without errors; screenshot header/footer/hero on 3 templates.

findings.claim: Entrance animations cost almost no bytes (Elementor 4.3 loads one ~0.4–0.6 KB CSS file per distinct animation, conditionally) but every animated element is output with `elementor-invisible` and only shown after JS + IntersectionObserver fire, so animations on hero/LCP elements delay LCP and make the page blank when JS is delayed; Pro Motion Effects add continuous scroll JS. The audited slow sites have 76–160 entrance animations and 12–38 motion effects; the fast ones 0–12.
findings.detail: core/page-assets/loader.php registers `e-animation-<name>` styles from assets/lib/animations/styles/ and enqueues only those used (marakaki loads fadeIn/fadeInUp/fadeInDown .min.css at 405–548 B each; the full animations.min.css would be 18,468 B). element-base.php:835 adds `elementor-invisible`; global.js removes it on viewport entry. Dev update 3.32: Motion Effects and Animated Headline now respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (no effect on Lighthouse, which does not emulate it). Elementor's FOUC article recommends adding 'Fade In' to hero containers to mask FOUC: this trades a flash for a later LCP; prefer fixing CSS order. Help 'Troubleshooting Motion Effects... Windows 11' (2026-01-08): with OS animations off, Motion Effects, background slideshows and carousels appear frozen (3.33+). Audit: pallada 90 animations still scores 86 (static hero, animations below fold); voreniahorizon 160 animations + 12 motion effects scores 50, LCP 9 s. v4 'Entrance Interactions' (3.34+) depend on assets/lib/motion/motion.min.js (128,346 B raw) plus the interactions bundle.
findings.breaks_when: Hero heading/image/button carries an entrance animation and JS is deferred/delayed -> LCP element paints only when JS runs (or never before interaction); dozens of motion effects -> scroll jank/INP on mid-range phones; visitors with OS animations disabled see static/frozen elements.
findings.how_to_apply: Build rule: never set Advanced > Motion Effects > Entrance Animation on anything in the first viewport (hero container, heading, image, CTA); cap page-wide entrance animations (~10) and Motion Effects to decorative below-fold elements; never use Fade In to hide FOUC; in v4 use Interactions sparingly below the fold. Audit script: parse rendered HTML for `elementor-invisible`, flag any element whose bounding box top < 800 px at 390 px width.
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse 'Largest Contentful Paint element' audit: the element must not have class `elementor-invisible`; Playwright on load: count `.elementor-invisible` above the fold = 0; compare LCP before/after removing hero animation (expect several hundred ms on a 4 s LCP page); filmstrip frame at 1 s shows the hero.
