findings.claim: Greek law sets the banner design floor: prior consent for every non-essential tracker (explicitly including Google Analytics), Reject on the first layer with the same number of clicks and equal button styling, no cookie wall, equal storage period for accept/reject — the HDPA audited 30 sites in 2022 on exactly these points.
findings.detail: HDPA Guidelines 1/2020 (dpa.gr, 25/02/2020): A.1 placing a tracker requires consent regardless of whether personal data is processed; A.2 exemption only for trackers technically necessary for the connection or the service the user requested; A.3 online-advertising trackers are never exempt; A.4 third-party trackers such as Google Analytics only after consent; multi-layer information is allowed if consent is asked after category-level information. IAPP summary (12 March 2020): accept/decline 'with the same number of actions (clicks) and from the same level'; withdrawal as easy as giving; cookie walls prohibited; 'buttons of the same size, tone and color'; same storage period for the choice either way; pre-ticked boxes, scrolling or continued browsing are not consent; repeated nagging after rejection is unlawful. HDPA bulletin 09/05/2022: ex officio audit of 30 high-traffic news sites whose first layer showed 'Συμφωνώ' and 'Περισσότερες επιλογές' but no 'Διαφωνώ/Απορρίπτω', with Accept highlighted; 15-day compliance deadline; all but one complied; the Authority 'calls on all websites, informational or otherwise' to comply with points Γ4 and Γ7. Google's EU user consent policy additionally requires legally valid consent for cookies and personalised ads for EEA/UK/CH users of Google products. Performance consequence: a compliant banner yields real rejections, so the site must be fast with zero marketing JS (basic consent mode), and FAZ/Complianz must be configured with an equal-weight Reject button on layer one.
findings.breaks_when: A Reject-first-layer banner lowers consent rates, so Ads/GA4 report fewer users (expected, lawful); misconfigured 'equal buttons' CSS overrides from the theme restyle Accept as primary → non-compliant; 'Accept all' only + 'Settings' layout (Complianz/CookieYes templates offer it) is exactly the pattern HDPA sanctioned.
findings.how_to_apply: CMP settings: first layer must show Accept and Reject with identical size/colour (FAZ: banner buttons; Complianz: Banner > Buttons > 'Deny' enabled on first layer and same style as Accept); category-level description of trackers (statistics, marketing, functional) with purposes; consent and rejection cookie lifetime identical (e.g. 365 days both); floating 'manage consent' button always available; no cookie wall; Greek + English texts (Polylang/WPML). Google Analytics and Meta in the 'statistics'/'marketing' categories, never 'necessary'. Keep the consent log (FAZ and Complianz both record it).
findings.how_to_verify: Screenshot the first layer on mobile showing Accept and Reject side by side, same size and colour; count clicks to reject (1) vs accept (1); after Reject, Network shows no tracking requests and the site stays fully usable; check the consent cookie expiry for both choices; re-open preferences via the floating button; have the client's legal counsel confirm wording — this finding is technical, not legal advice.

findings.claim: Elementor 4.x sites can now carry a fourth CMP, 'Cookie Consent by Elementor', which blocks scripts before consent and defaults Google Consent Mode v2 to Basic; the plugin's one-CMP rule must detect and reconcile it alongside Complianz/FAZ/Cookie-Script.
findings.detail: Elementor help (Last Update June 22-23, 2026) documents 'Cookie Consent by Elementor': a setup wizard with 'Opt-in (GDPR-style): Cookies and scripts are blocked until the user explicitly consents. Users can Accept, Reject, or Customize', an initial website scan categorising cookies into Necessary/Functional/Analytics/Advertisement, consent logs, geo-targeting, 'How to block scripts before consent', and a GCM v2 toggle with 'Basic Mode (Default): Google tracking scripts are completely blocked from loading until the visitor explicitly clicks Accept' vs 'Advanced Mode: Google tracking scripts load immediately ... in a restricted, cookieless state'. Removing the Elementor logo from the banner requires a paid subscription. Its banner script weight, hosting origin (first-party vs Elementor CDN) and whether it ships a GTM template were not measurable from the docs; test on staging before adopting.
findings.breaks_when: Enabled next to Complianz/FAZ: two banners, two consent 'default' pushes (last one wins), split consent logs; its Basic default silently blocks GA4/Ads on a site whose marketer expects advanced-mode modelling.
findings.how_to_apply: Inventory: WP admin > Plugins and the Elementor dashboard for 'Cookie Consent'; grep rendered HTML for its banner container and its JS. Decide one CMP per site (criteria: first-party asset hosting, GCM v2 with all 7 signals, equal Accept/Reject on layer 1, consent log). If Elementor's CMP is chosen, deactivate Complianz/FAZ/Cookie-Script and re-point the GTM consent-initialisation tag; if not, keep it uninstalled.
findings.how_to_verify: Network shows exactly one CMP origin; dataLayer has one consent 'default' and one 'update'; gcs=G100 before, G111 after Accept; Lighthouse network-requests shows the banner CSS/JS within the first second and the LCP element is not the banner.

findings.claim: Elementor Pro Forms' reCAPTCHA v3 field is a site-level third-party script (google.com/recaptcha/api.js + recaptcha__xx.js) on every page where a form renders (hotel sites: footer/popup forms = every page); prefer the built-in Honeypot field or delay grecaptcha until interaction.
findings.detail: Elementor help 'Add reCAPTCHA to prevent spam' (Last Update: November 19, 2024): 'We recommend v3 as it is the new more secure, less intrusive method'; v3 'operates discreetly in the background, generating a score based on user behavior'; keys and the 0.5 score threshold live in Elementor > Settings > Integrations (settings page, Last Update May 29, 2024). Google's reCAPTCHA loading doc: 'reCAPTCHA can be loaded asynchronously without impacting its ability to detect suspicious traffic and is generally recommended for performance benefits'. FlyingPress lists 'grecaptcha.execute' among 'Common Third-party Scripts to Delay'. Elementor's form field list (developers.elementor.com, seen via search result) includes 'Honeypot (honeypot)' and no Cloudflare Turnstile; Turnstile for Elementor forms needs a third-party plugin (several on wordpress.org). The recaptcha bundle's CPU cost on these 10 sites was not measured; treat the gain as 'remove one third-party entity', typically tens to a few hundred ms TBT on mobile.
findings.breaks_when: Removing reCAPTCHA v3 without another anti-spam measure lets booking/contact forms get spammed; delaying api.js with a delay-JS plugin that also delays Elementor Pro's form handler can break submission if the delayed order is wrong (test a real submit); v3 token is generated on submit so delay-until-interaction is normally safe, but verify on staging.
findings.how_to_apply: Audit: count pages where a Form widget renders (footer templates, popups) and check Network for www.google.com/recaptcha/api.js. Options in order of preference: (1) swap the reCAPTCHA field for Elementor's Honeypot field on low-value forms; (2) keep v3 but add 'recaptcha' / 'grecaptcha' to Perfmatters/FlyingPress delay lists so it loads on first interaction; (3) Turnstile via a third-party plugin if the client insists on a challenge (adds challenges.cloudflare.com instead).
findings.how_to_verify: Mobile Lighthouse third-party-summary no longer lists 'Google reCAPTCHA' before interaction; a real test submission on each form type (contact, booking enquiry, popup) succeeds and arrives by email; spam volume monitored for 2 weeks.

findings.claim: Elementor's Facebook widgets (Like Button, Comments, Embed, Page) pull the Facebook JS SDK via the 'Facebook SDK' App ID integration; a Facebook Page/Like widget in a site-wide footer adds a connect.facebook.net SDK download and execution to every page before consent.
findings.detail: Elementor settings help (Last Update May 29, 2024) lists under Integrations: 'Facebook SDK: Facebook SDK lets you connect to your dedicated application so you can track the Facebook Widgets analytics on your site. Enter your APP ID here'. The SDK is a different asset from the Meta pixel (fbevents.js) so consent-gating the pixel in GTM does not remove it; CMP script blockers must block it separately (Complianz/FAZ 'social media' category). Not observed on the 10 audited home pages; check audit-summary.json widget counts for facebook_* widgets on inner pages and footers.
findings.breaks_when: Removing the widget removes the live like-count/comments; blocking the SDK via CMP without a placeholder leaves an empty box until consent.
findings.how_to_apply: Search Elementor templates for Facebook widgets (Theme Builder footers especially). Replace Facebook Page/Like widgets with a static image + link; if Comments are needed, load the widget only on single posts and let the CMP block connect.facebook.net until the 'social media/marketing' category is accepted (Complianz placeholder or FAZ blocked-resource placeholder).
findings.how_to_verify: Pre-consent Network has no connect.facebook.net/*/sdk.js or xfbml requests; after Accept the widget renders; Lighthouse third-party-summary 'Facebook' entity absent before consent.

findings.claim: For hotel/villa brochure sites with no Ads or Meta spend, replace GTM + gtag entirely with Perfmatters 'Local Analytics' using the 'Google Analytics 4 Minimal' script (2.2 KB vs 104 KB gtagv4.js, both first-party), still consent-gated by the CMP.
findings.detail: Perfmatters Local Analytics doc (opened): 'gtagv4.js is 104 KB and is the standard Google Analytics script with all features included ... hosted locally'; 'Minimal v4 analytics (analytics-minimal-v4.js) is a smaller and optimized open source script that is only 2.2 KB. Reporting for page views, users, locations, devices, traffic sources, and real-time will all work fine. However, it doesn't have all of the features of gtagv4.js, such as engagement time'; 'Both script types will generate a request to https://www.google-analytics.com/collect ... it happens after the page loads'; option 'Use MonsterInsights' exists; the doc mentions no Google Consent Mode support, so legal gating must come from the CMP's script blocker. Compared with the observed GTM stack (GTM 171 KB + G- 190 KB + ~1.1 s blocking on limnoupolis) this removes the entire 'Google Tag Manager' entity from the lab run.
findings.breaks_when: The client runs Google Ads/Meta or needs GA4 events, ecommerce, engagement time or conversions: Minimal cannot send them; a local copy of gtagv4.js falls behind Google's version until Perfmatters refreshes it; without CMP blocking the local script fires before consent (HDPA 1/2020 A.4 violation).
findings.how_to_apply: Perfmatters > Google Analytics: 'Enable Local Analytics', enter the G- measurement ID, Script type = 'Google Analytics 4 Minimal' (or gtagv4.js if engagement metrics matter), leave 'Track logged-in admins' off. Remove GTM and all inline gtag. In Complianz/FAZ add the Perfmatters analytics script to the 'statistics' category so it is blocked until consent (verify the blocker catches it; otherwise keep GTM with basic consent mode instead).
findings.how_to_verify: Incognito, no interaction: no request to googletagmanager.com or google-analytics.com/collect; after Accept: one /collect request with tid=G-...; GA4 Realtime shows the visit; Lighthouse third-party-summary has no 'Google Tag Manager' entity; compare 7-day users/sessions with the previous GTM period (expect parity on pageviews, loss of engagement time with Minimal).

findings.claim: Google's certified-CMP requirement applies only to publisher products (AdSense, Ad Manager, AdMob), not to Google Ads/GA4 advertisers, so none of the agency's sites needs a Google-certified CMP; pick the CMP on performance and HDPA criteria.
findings.detail: Google Ad Manager help (opened): 'This help center article is for publishers ... If you are an advertiser or CMP for advertisers, please find more information here for advertisers'; 'partners using our publisher products—Google AdSense, Ad Manager, or AdMob—are required to use a consent management platform (CMP) that has been certified by Google and integrates with the IAB's Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF)': EEA/UK as of 16 January 2024, Switzerland as of 31 July 2024; non-certified CMP traffic 'may be eligible for non-personalized ads or limited ads'. No Google page found that requires certification for advertisers; the EU user consent policy only requires legally valid consent. Relevance: vendor marketing (Cookie-Script, CookieYes) pushes 'Google-certified' as a reason to use a third-party CDN banner; for sites that do not serve AdSense/Ad Manager ads this is not a constraint, so a first-party plugin (FAZ, Complianz, Elementor's) is acceptable.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; only if a site later adds AdSense/Ad Manager display ads for EEA users would a certified, TCF-integrated CMP become mandatory (FAZ lists IAB TCF v2.3 support but requires the site's own registered IAB Europe CMP ID).
findings.how_to_apply: In the CMP selection checklist record 'serves AdSense/Ad Manager ads? no' and skip the certification criterion; weight first-party hosting, deferred loading, GCM v2 signals and HDPA layer-1 Reject instead.
findings.how_to_verify: Google Ads/GA4 keep receiving data after Accept with any CMP (gcs=G111); if display ads exist, check the Ad Manager/AdSense policy centre for CMP warnings.

title: Hosting, TTFB, caching layers and dynamic pages
summary: On these ten sites the server side is binary: a full-page cache HIT returns the HTML in 0.15-0.6 s (Lighthouse server-response-time passes), while any request that reaches PHP costs 1.7-13 s (dev6 sites with no cache 2.3-4.2 s in Lighthouse; staging.limnoupolis cache MISS 12.9 s; limnoupolis /cart/ 3.1 s, /my-account/ 2.7 s, ?wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments 1.7 s, all measured today with curl). Lighthouse fails the audit above 600 ms and web.dev's good TTFB is 0.8 s, so nothing but a cache hit (or an edge cache) gets a 95+ mobile score, and every purge, language redirect or bypass cookie that drops a visitor onto PHP costs the whole budget. The origins are the agency's own Plesk servers (Hetzner DE with LiteSpeed+HTTP/3+Brotli, LeaseWeb NL with nginx and no HTTP/3) plus one Greek reseller on Hetzner; four sites sit behind Cloudflare but with cf-cache-status DYNAMIC, so Greek visitors still round-trip to Germany for HTML. Because the agency controls the servers it can do what Greek shared hosting cannot (Redis, LiteSpeed crawler, ESI, QUIC, OPcache), and the hosting.gr 2025 benchmark shows Greek shared plans are mostly Apache/nginx in Belgium/Germany with 0.9-2.8 s TTFB anyway. WooCommerce is safe to cache if Cart/Checkout/My Account and the woocommerce_* / wp_woocommerce_session_ cookies bypass (LiteSpeed, WP Rocket, FlyingPress and Cloudflare APO all do this by default and limnoupolis already shows the right no-cache headers); booking calendars stay cacheable when availability loads via Ajax (YITH "Update non-available dates on loading (AJAX)"). The two biggest avoidable losses found are pallada.gr's PHP language redirect (302 with no-store, 0.65-1.0 s before the real page) and cache plugins installed with caching effectively off (kand/W3TC 4.2 s). Object cache, PHP/OPcache tuning and database cleanup matter only for the uncached paths (checkout, bookings, logged-in forum users) and move the mobile score of the home page very little.
critic_notes: Method: WebFetch could not resolve DNS in this sandbox, so every source was fetched with curl through the session proxy using the existing scratchpad helper (text copies in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-everything-claude/bcd5434c-e674-5a25-baaa-faec7a068a29/scratchpad/critic_hosting/). Pages opened and quoted: docs.litespeedtech.com cache (Sep 29 2026), crawler, general (Aug 14 2026), admin, thirdparty (Jul 27 2026), api, troubleshoot; LSCWP readme changelog (7.9.1 Sep 1 2026, 8.0 'coming soon'); Cloudflare APO about/faq/plugin-compatibility (Sep 16 / Oct 1 2026); cloudflare.com/network; FlyingPress Cloudflare integration (Jun 2 2026), APO note, role cache, changelog; Polylang detection doc; WPML redirect doc; WooCommerce MaxMind, caching-plugins, Bookings troubleshooting, cart-fragments blog; php.net OPcache; Elementor requirements and element-caching help (Sep 15 2026); Memberium; Perfmatters LiteSpeed guide; Google PSI about; Lighthouse SRT doc and Lighthouse 13 blog; WordPress nonces and cron handbook pages; local audit-summary.json and lh/runs/*.json. Not independently re-opened: hosting.gr and Greek provider pages, talk.plesk.com, WP Rocket user-cache and WooCommerce-compat pages, web.dev TTFB, LiteSpeed QUIC/Cloudflare compression pages, WP core autoload sources, the YITH booking-form doc (returned navigation only) and the wordpress.org YITH thread. Open-question updates: (a) Cloudflare does have Athens and Thessaloniki PoPs; (b) the FlyingPress '4.22.1' version string is impossible per the changelog and should be re-read on the sites; (c) e_element_cache is ON (24h) on 8/10 sites though Elementor ships it inactive - test MISS timing on staging with it on/off as the researcher proposed, and disable it per element wherever dynamic tags/user data appear; (d) WPML's wp-wpml_current_language cookie is reportedly only set when 'Language filtering for AJAX operations' is enabled (hosting KB summaries from search, pages not opened) - verify before relying on APO for WPML sites; (e) the docs.wp-rocket.me 'cache lifespan' article could not be located (1186 and 1510 resolve to unrelated articles), so WP Rocket's default lifespan rationale is unsourced here. Skipped: hosting.gr table re-check and Elementor Pro Menu Cart source inspection (help pages redirect to marketing). Risk to the plugin: any audit script keyed on Lighthouse <=12 audit ids will fail on current PSI output.

findings.claim: A full-page cache hit is the only way these Elementor pages pass Lighthouse's 600 ms server-response audit; every PHP-rendered request on the agency's servers costs 1.7-13 s TTFB.
findings.detail: Lighthouse (developer.chrome.com) fails 'Reduce initial server response time' above 600 ms; web.dev (updated Nov 2025) calls TTFB good at <=0.8 s and poor >1.8 s and notes it is a floor for FCP/LCP. Measured today: Lighthouse server-response-time was 145 ms (onar, LiteSpeed hit), 147 ms (staging), 408 ms (cretaforums, FlyingPress), 518-572 ms (voreniahorizon, limnoupolis, marakaki) but 2,264 ms (fagitiotiszois, no cache), 2,322 ms (platonos, no cache), 4,246 ms (kand, W3TC installed but no cache headers) and 1,626 ms (pallada, includes an 891 ms redirect). curl today: staging.limnoupolis.gr first request x-litespeed-cache: miss = 12.9 s TTFB, second request hit = 0.47 s; limnoupolis.gr /cart/ 3.1 s, /my-account/ 2.7 s, /?wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments 1.7 s (all no-cache by design). Evidence files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-everything-claude/bcd5434c-e674-5a25-baaa-faec7a068a29/scratchpad/hosting-research/hdr/sites.txt and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-everything-claude/bcd5434c-e674-5a25-baaa-faec7a068a29/scratchpad/lh/runs/*.json.
findings.breaks_when: Dynamic pages (cart, checkout, my-account, booking Ajax, logged-in users) are cached by mistake, or a sitewide cookie/query string makes every request bypass the cache (see the LiteSpeed 'Do Not Cache Cookies' pitfall).
findings.how_to_apply: LiteSpeed hosts (server1.inglelandi.com, pallada's server): LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > [1] Cache: Enable Cache ON; TTL tab: Default Public Cache TTL 604800 (plugin default, one week) or 2592000 as Perfmatters recommends, Default Front Page TTL same. Replace W3 Total Cache/WP Rocket with LiteSpeed Cache on LiteSpeed servers (pallada.gr runs WP Rocket 3.23.2.1 on a LiteSpeed server and serves HTML with cache-control: public, max-age=0 from PHP/.htaccess instead of the server cache). nginx hosts (dev6): FlyingPress or WP Rocket with preload. Never ship a cache plugin with caching off (kand: W3TC present, 4.2 s TTFB).
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI -A 'Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 10) Chrome/129 Mobile' https://site/ twice and read x-litespeed-cache: hit (LiteSpeed), x-flying-press-cache: HIT, or WP Rocket's cache file; curl -w '%{time_starttransfer}' must be <0.6 s from Europe on the second request; Lighthouse 'server-response-time' numericValue < 600; repeat for the home page, one inner page and the booking page.
findings.correction: Verify with audits['document-latency-insight'] (score 1 = passes redirects, >=600 ms server time and text compression) on Lighthouse 13+/PSI, and fall back to audits['server-response-time'].numericValue only on Lighthouse <=12. Rest of the claim stands.

findings.claim: After every purge (Elementor save, product stock change, plugin update) the next visitor pays the full 2-13 s render unless the cache is re-warmed; on LiteSpeed enable the Crawler and Serve Stale, on FlyingPress/WP Rocket rely on preload.
findings.detail: LiteSpeed Cache v7 crawler: most knobs are now fixed or wp-config constants: Delay 500 µs (define('LITESPEED_CRAWLER_USLEEP', $us)), Run Duration fixed 900 s, Interval Between Runs 600 s (LITESPEED_CRAWLER_RUN_INTERVAL), Threads 3 (LITESPEED_CRAWLER_THREADS), Timeout 30 s (LITESPEED_CRAWLER_TIMEOUT), Server Load Limit (0 disables; doc suggests 1 for a two-core server, 2 for four cores), Role Simulation now limited to the Server IP, Cookie Simulation (used for WPML/WCML language or currency cookies), Custom Sitemap. 'Serve Stale' (Cache > Purge) serves the purged copy while a new one is generated instead of hammering PHP. WP Rocket preloads per language with WPML/Polylang; FlyingPress purges and preloads the product page plus its category/archive pages on product updates and offers Auto-Refresh Cache every 2/6/12/24 h (default off). Evidence: staging.limnoupolis.gr MISS 12.9 s vs HIT 0.47 s today.
findings.breaks_when: The host disabled the crawler at the vhost (CacheEngine without 'crawler'), Server Load Limit is too low so it never completes, or Guest Mode / Cache Mobile / Vary for Mini Cart multiply the number of crawler varies and the run never reaches the end of the sitemap; Serve Stale can show a stale price/stock for one request.
findings.how_to_apply: LiteSpeed Cache > Crawler > General Settings: Crawler ON, Server Load Limit = number of cores / 2, Sitemap = the Yoast/Rank Math sitemap index; Crawler > Simulation: add the language cookie only if the language is cookie-driven; Cache > Purge: Serve Stale ON; keep Purge All On Upgrade OFF so plugin updates do not wipe the cache. FlyingPress: Caching > Preload after purge (automatic) and optionally Auto-Refresh Cache 24 h. WP Rocket: Preload > Activate Preloading with the sitemap.
findings.how_to_verify: LiteSpeed Cache > Crawler > Summary shows Size, Position and 'Status: completed'; immediately after a purge, curl -sI the home page and expect x-litespeed-cache: hit (or 'stale' header value) within one crawler interval; compare curl TTFB on the first request after an Elementor save before/after.
findings.correction: Keep Purge All on Upgrade ON (LiteSpeed's recommendation) and rely on Serve Stale + crawler to absorb it; simulate _icl_current_language (WPML) or the WCML currency checkbox, not an arbitrary cookie; Server Load Limit default is 1 and may be overridden at server level.

findings.claim: Safe WooCommerce caching = page cache for everything except Cart, Checkout, My Account plus a bypass on the WooCommerce cookies; LiteSpeed, WP Rocket, FlyingPress and Cloudflare APO all do this automatically, and limnoupolis.gr already returns the right headers.
findings.detail: WooCommerce's official doc: exclude Cart, My Account, Checkout; cookies woocommerce_cart_hash, woocommerce_items_in_cart (session), wp_woocommerce_session_ (2 days), woocommerce_recently_viewed, store_notice[id]; W3TC: add 'mfunc' to Minify 'Ignored comment stems'; Varnish: pass /cart|/my-account|/checkout|/addons, ?add-to-cart=, ?wc-api=; a cached My Account causes the password-reset loop. LiteSpeed: 'By default, the My Account, Checkout, and Cart pages are excluded from caching'; its thirdparty/woocommerce.cls.php adds woocommerce_cart_hash to litespeed_vary_cookies and purges products on stock/sale changes; the WooCommerce tab has 'Product Update Interval' and 'Vary for Mini Cart' (OFF; only for themes that print the cart count in PHP; it edits .htaccess). WP Rocket: automatically excludes Cart/Checkout/My Account; for PHP-rendered cart widgets add woocommerce_items_in_cart under Advanced Rules > Never Cache Cookies. FlyingPress: same auto-exclusion; Caching > Bypass Cache for Cookies: woocommerce_items_in_cart only if the cart count does not update (it lowers hit ratio). Cloudflare APO bypasses on cookie prefixes wp-, wordpress, comment_, woocommerce_, yith_wcwl_session_, yith_wrvp_, bookly, edd_, and on any query string outside its marketing allowlist. Measured today on limnoupolis.gr (LiteSpeed + Cloudflare): /cart/, /my-account/, /checkout/ (302 to cart), /?wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments all return x-litespeed-cache-control: no-cache and cache-control: no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0, private; the home page is still a HIT with Cookie: woocommerce_items_in_cart=1, which is correct because the Elementor Pro Menu Cart updates via wc-cart-fragments-js (present in the HTML).
findings.breaks_when: WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced page assignments point to the wrong pages or the Greek slugs were changed after the fact (LiteSpeed: 'Misconfigured page associations ... may cause pages to be classified incorrectly'); a custom checkout URL (FunnelKit-style) is not recognised; the theme prints cart totals in PHP; a sitewide cookie is added to 'Do Not Cache Cookies' (that disables caching for the whole site).
findings.how_to_apply: Leave the automatic exclusions; add manual ones only for custom URLs: LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > Excludes > Do Not Cache URIs (REQUEST_URI partial match; ^ anchors start, $ exact), FlyingPress > Caching > Exclude Pages from Cache (plain keyword, no regex, never '/'), WP Rocket > Advanced Rules > Never Cache URL(s). Keep 'Vary for Mini Cart' OFF with Elementor Pro Menu Cart. Behind Cloudflare, keep the DNS record proxied and let APO/FlyingPress honour the same cookies.
findings.how_to_verify: For each of /cart/, /checkout/, /my-account/, a booking product and the thank-you page: curl -sI -A mobile-UA URL | grep -i -E 'x-litespeed-cache|cache-control|cf-cache-status' and expect no-cache (LiteSpeed shows X-LiteSpeed-Cache-Control: no-cache); then in a browser add an item, open the home page in a new tab and check the header cart count updates; test the WooCommerce password reset; curl with -H 'Cookie: woocommerce_items_in_cart=1' must not return a HIT if the theme prints the cart in PHP.

findings.claim: Booking product pages (YITH Booking, WooCommerce Bookings) can stay fully cached as long as availability is loaded by Ajax, the WooCommerce session cookie is never cached, and the Ajax endpoints are not blocked or JS-delayed.
findings.detail: WooCommerce Bookings troubleshooting: with page caching 'the booking product page's calendar keeps loading indefinitely ... a 403 error in the browser console' because the wp_woocommerce_session_ token (2-day expiry) gets cached; fix is to exclude all WooCommerce cookies from caching and to disable Cloudflare Rocket Loader. YITH's documented workaround (quoted by the plugin contributor on wordpress.org): Booking Form settings > 'Update non-available dates on loading (AJAX)' so non-available dates load via Ajax when the product is viewed, plus exclude YITH JS from minification (W3TC Performance > Minify > Advanced > 'Never minify the following JS files', relative paths). limnoupolis.gr home page carries 34 yith-wcbk-booking-form elements and is served as a LiteSpeed HIT, so the form itself is cache-safe; the live data comes from wc-ajax, which is no-cache (1.7 s TTFB today, so object cache/PHP speed decides calendar snappiness). Cloudflare APO lists bookly cookies and YITH Wishlist in its bypass/compat lists; YITH Booking is not on either list.
findings.breaks_when: A security plugin, firewall or CDN rule returns 403/404 for /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php or ?wc-ajax= (calendar spins forever); 'Delay JS' (Perfmatters, LiteSpeed, FlyingPress) delays the booking form scripts until interaction; the page cache TTL exceeds the 2-day session cookie and a cached page carries another visitor's session; the thank-you/order-received or custom booking confirmation URL is cached.
findings.how_to_apply: YITH > Booking > Settings > Booking forms: enable 'Update non-available dates on loading (AJAX)'; keep /cart/, /checkout/, /my-account/ and the confirmation page excluded; add the booking plugin's JS handles to the Delay-JS exclusion list; Cloudflare: Speed > Optimization > Rocket Loader OFF; make sure admin-ajax.php and ?wc-ajax= are reachable (no WAF block); do not add wp_woocommerce_session_ to any 'cache cookies' allowlist (Plesk nginx) because the name is unique per visitor.
findings.how_to_verify: In Chrome DevTools (mobile emulation, incognito) open a booking product twice: the document must be a cache HIT, the calendar must render, and the Network tab must show the wc-ajax/admin-ajax availability request returning 200 (not 403/404); pick a date already booked on staging and confirm it is greyed out after a hard reload; run the same with Delay JS on.
findings.correction: Before trusting a long TTL on a booking page, grep the cached HTML for 'nonce' / '_wpnonce' / 'security'. If present and ESI is unavailable, cap that page's TTL at <=43200 s (LiteSpeed per-URI TTL in Force Cache URIs, e.g. '/product/x 43200') or exclude it; with ESI, add the action to Cache > ESI > ESI Nonces. YITH's AJAX option remains plausible but unverified here. Risk stays medium.

findings.claim: A PHP language redirect at the root (Polylang 'detect browser language' / WPML 'Browser language redirect') adds 0.65-1.0 s of uncacheable TTFB before the real page; serve the default language at '/' with no redirect and let the switcher do the rest.
findings.detail: pallada.gr (Polylang: connect-polylang-elementor in the HTML) answers https://pallada.gr/ with HTTP 302 -> /en/ and cache-control: no-cache, no-store; curl TTFB today 0.65 s and 1.03 s, Lighthouse 'redirects' audit wastedMs 891 on the LCP path. WP Rocket's doc: with Polylang browser detection 'the first visit for each user will be uncached so that the language can be accurately detected' (cookie pll_language), and for 'redirect to default language' you must add '/' to Advanced Rules > Never Cache URL(s); Polylang's own doc: 'If you don't want any redirection to occur, you must deactivate the browser preferred language detection and hide the default language code in URLs'. WPML: Settings > URLs and SEO > Browser language redirect defaults to 'not redirect'; the redirect runs once per 24 h and the doc warns Google follows it. LiteSpeed stores a separate copy per language page (thirdparty doc) and both LiteSpeed Cache (tested Jan 2 2025) and WP Rocket (June 2026) are WPML-recommended; WCML currency/geo needs cookie varies (WP Rocket: wcml_client_currency, wcml_client_currency_language, wcml_client_country). platonos (Polylang) sets pll_language on every uncached response, confirming the cookie is server-set when PHP runs. LiteSpeed Guest Mode is also risky on multilingual sites: 'the wrong language, incorrect pricing ... may be momentarily displayed'.
findings.breaks_when: The client requires auto-language landing for SEO/marketing; URL-parameter language mode (?lang=) which caches poorly; Guest Mode ON; a redirect plugin (Yoast/Redirection) handles old URLs in PHP (limnoupolis /shop/ -> /tickets/ 301 was no-cache and took 1.78 s).
findings.how_to_apply: Polylang > Languages > Settings: 'Detect browser language' OFF and URL modifications > 'Hide URL language information for default language' ON so '/' is the Greek (or English) home; WPML > Settings > Browser language redirect: 'Don't redirect'. If a redirect is a hard requirement, do it client-side (the JS approach WP Rocket documents for Weglot) or at the edge, never in PHP, and set the cache plugin's '/' exclusion as documented. Move permanent URL redirects into .htaccess/LiteSpeed/nginx rules or Cloudflare Redirect Rules so they return without PHP.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI https://domain/ must return 200 with a cache HIT header, not 302 no-store; Lighthouse 'redirects' audit numericValue 0; curl with -H 'Accept-Language: en' and 'el' both HIT; test that the language switcher still works and that pll_language is set by JS (check document.cookie after load on a cached page).

findings.claim: The four Cloudflare-proxied sites serve HTML as cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC, so every Greek visitor still round-trips to Germany; caching HTML at the edge (Cloudflare APO, FlyingPress 5.1+ Cloudflare full-page cache, or QUIC.cloud) is the only remaining TTFB lever once the origin cache hits.
findings.detail: limnoupolis.gr, cretaforums.gr, www.marakaki.com and voreniahorizon.gr resolve to Cloudflare (AS13335) and return cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC on HTML today; origins are Hetzner Nuremberg (195.201.92.155, server1.inglelandi.com) and LeaseWeb Amsterdam (85.17.67.5). Cloudflare APO (docs updated Sep/Oct 2026): caches HTML for 30 days and invalidates within 30 s via the Cloudflare WordPress plugin; caches only GET/HEAD 200 text/html with cf-edge-cache: cache,platform=wordpress and no bypass cookies (wp-, wordpress, comment_, woocommerce_, yith_wcwl_session_, bookly ...), no query strings outside the UTM/gclid/fbclid allowlist, excluded paths (checkout, wp-cron.php, feeds); optional 'cache by device type' sends CF-Device-Type; compatible-plugin list includes WooCommerce, WPML, FlyingPress, WP Rocket >= 3.8.6, Perfmatters, Redis Object Cache, YITH Wishlist; no multisite. FlyingPress (doc June 2 2026): built-in Cloudflare page caching on all plans incl. free, syncs excluded pages, ignored query strings, bypass cookies and mobile cache, purges with FlyingPress purges, 'Disable Cloudflare APO before enabling this integration', logged-in users always bypass. Perfmatters notes LiteSpeed Cache does not talk to APO, so you run two cache layers and purge both. QUIC.cloud (LiteSpeed's CDN): Free plan = 6 floating PoPs (US E/C/W, Europe E/C/W), Standard = 80+ PoPs including Athens at $0.02/GB for Europe; billing changes 10 Nov 2026. hosting.gr measured 39-61 ms network RTT from Greece to German/Belgian hosts vs 3-15 ms inside Greece, which is the latency an Athens PoP removes per round trip.
findings.breaks_when: 'Cache Everything' is used without cookie bypass (WP Rocket doc: admin bar shown to all visitors); the theme prints cart state in HTML; purge chains break (LiteSpeed purge does not purge APO); WPML language cookie varies content on the same URL; APO is combined with FlyingPress's own Cloudflare integration (they conflict); Page Rules with Cache Level: Bypass override APO.
findings.how_to_apply: Option A: Cloudflare dashboard > Speed > Optimization > APO ON + Cloudflare WordPress plugin (automatic purge), optionally 'Cache by device type' if any content differs per UA. Option B (FlyingPress sites): FlyingPress > CDN/Cloudflare > enable page caching with Zone ID + API key, APO off. Option C (LiteSpeed sites): LiteSpeed Cache > General > Online Services > Enable QUIC.cloud services and the QUIC.cloud CDN Standard plan for the Athens PoP. In all cases keep the DNS record proxied (orange cloud).
findings.how_to_verify: curl -svo /dev/null -A CF https://domain/ -H 'accept: text/html' 2>&1 | grep -i 'cf-cache-status\|cf-edge\|cf-apo-via' should show cf-cache-status: HIT, cf-apo-via: tcache, cf-edge-cache: cache,platform=wordpress (APO) or cf-cache-status: HIT (FlyingPress integration); run PageSpeed Insights twice and compare 'server-response-time'; test cart, checkout, login and the language switcher with a non-empty cart.
findings.correction: Edge HTML caching mostly improves field TTFB for Greek visitors (Athens/Thessaloniki PoPs exist) and improves PSI lab TTFB only to the extent the European Google datacenter is closer to a Cloudflare PoP than to Nuremberg; expect a modest lab gain. On LiteSpeed sites APO is incompatible with Guest Mode. FlyingPress Option B requires 5.1+; confirm the real installed version.

findings.claim: LiteSpeed Cache baseline for Elementor + WooCommerce + Greek multilingual sites: cache ON with the defaults, Guest Mode OFF, Cache Mobile OFF, no cookies in 'Do Not Cache Cookies', Browser Cache ON, and let the WooCommerce auto-rules stand.
findings.detail: From the LiteSpeed Cache docs (page dated Sep 29 2026): Cache tab defaults Cache Logged-in Users ON (private cache per IP + session), Cache Commenters ON, Cache Login Page OFF since 7.9, Cache favicon removed in 6.2 (404s cached via 'Default HTTP Status Code Page TTL', 3600 s), Cache Mobile OFF ('primarily used for non-responsive themes'; Elementor is responsive via CSS so leave OFF; 'List of Mobile User Agents' must be filled if ON); Private Cached URIs / Force Cache URIs / Force Public Cache URIs with optional per-URI TTL ('/mypath/mypage 300'); Drop Query String list. TTL: Default Public 604800, Private 60-3600, Front Page, Feed, REST, 404/403/500 TTL. Excludes: Do Not Cache URIs (REQUEST_URI partial match, ^ and $ anchors), Query Strings, Categories, Tags, Cookies ('If you exclude a cookie that appears on every page of your site, you effectively exclude your entire site from caching'), User Agents, Roles. WooCommerce tab: 'We highly recommend ESI with WooCommerce'; Product Update Interval; Vary for Mini Cart OFF. Browser tab: Browser Cache ON, Browser Cache TTL 31557600. General: Guest Mode serves a default copy on the first request with no varies and no ESI and may flash the wrong language/price; Guest Optimization requires Guest Mode; Perfmatters recommends both OFF and all Page Optimization OFF when Perfmatters handles front-end optimisation (Guest Mode 'will interfere with Perfmatters'). Advanced: Login Cookie, Vary Cookies, Instant Click. Observed: limnoupolis.gr 404 pages cached public,max-age=3600 as documented; staging header 'x-litespeed-cache-control: public,max-age=604800' confirms default TTL; no 'esi=on' so ESI is off.
findings.breaks_when: A consent-banner (Complianz/Cookie-Script) or analytics cookie is added to Do Not Cache Cookies (whole site uncached); Cache Mobile ON without the UA list (save fails) or with it (double cache size, crawler time); Vary for Mini Cart ON rewrites .htaccess and doubles cache; Cache Logged-in Users ON on a forum (cretaforums) with per-user content creates a private copy per IP+session and can fill disk; Instant Click doubles server load.
findings.how_to_apply: LiteSpeed Cache > Cache: Enable Cache ON, Cache Mobile OFF, Cache Login Page OFF; TTL: Default Public Cache TTL 604800 (or 2592000), Default Front Page TTL 604800, Default HTTP Status Code Page TTL '404 3600'; Excludes: leave Do Not Cache Cookies empty, Do Not Cache Roles: administrator while testing only; WooCommerce tab: Product Update Interval 'Purge product on changes to the quantity or stock status. Purge categories only when stock status changes', Vary for Mini Cart OFF; Browser: Browser Cache ON, TTL 31557600; General: Guest Mode OFF, Guest Optimization OFF (with Perfmatters) ; Page Optimization: leave to Perfmatters/FlyingPress, except HTML minify if pages are very large.
findings.how_to_verify: Non-logged-in browser, DevTools Network, first resource: x-litespeed-cache: hit on repeat views of home/inner pages; X-LiteSpeed-Cache-Control: no-cache plus cache-control: no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0 and expires: Wed, 11 Jan 1984 on cart/checkout/my-account; after enabling Browser Cache, static assets show cache-control max-age=31557600; LiteSpeed Cache > Toolbox > Debug Log 'Admin IP' to read why a page was not cached.

findings.claim: The agency's sites are not on Greek shared hosting but on its own Plesk servers at Hetzner (LiteSpeed) and LeaseWeb (nginx), so it can do what Greek shared plans cannot: Redis, LiteSpeed crawler/ESI, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, OPcache tuning; Greek shared hosting is mostly Apache/nginx in Belgium or Germany with 0.9-2.8 s TTFB.
findings.detail: DNS/ASN lookups today: onar-seaside-lounge.gr and staging.limnoupolis.gr -> 195.201.92.155 Hetzner Nuremberg (rDNS server1.inglelandi.com, server: LiteSpeed, Plesk, PHP 8.3.35, alt-svc h3 + h3-29, content-encoding br); dev6.inglelandi.com -> 85.17.67.5 LeaseWeb Amsterdam (rDNS server8.inglelandi.com, server: nginx, Plesk, no alt-svc, br yes); pallada.gr -> 157.90.95.105 Hetzner Falkenstein (rDNS server20.serversmarket.gr, a Greek reseller; LiteSpeed-style alt-svc). hosting.gr 2025 'Mega Συγκριτικό' of Greek shared plans: web server LiteSpeed only at DnHost Scale (Athens, Plesk), IP.GR Business Premium (Germany, cPanel) and Polar55 (Germany); Papaki Professional and TopHost Tera = Apache + nginx reverse proxy in Belgium (Papaki's plan page advertises Varnish and Redis), Pointer Unlimited = nginx in Thessaloniki, IpHost = Apache+nginx Athens, Fastpath = nginx Athens, CretaForce = nginx Germany; network response time 3-15 ms from Greek DCs vs 39-61 ms for Germany/Belgium; measured TTFB 0.89 s (CretaForce) to 2.76 s (TopHost). LiteSpeed docs: ESI needs LiteSpeed Enterprise/ADC/QUIC.cloud and 'In a shared hosting environment, your system administrator controls whether a specific virtual host account has CacheEngine on/off; esi on/off'; the crawler can likewise be disabled per vhost; object cache needs Redis/Memcached plus the PHP extension installed by the host. Evidence: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-everything-claude/bcd5434c-e674-5a25-baaa-faec7a068a29/scratchpad/hosting-research/hdr/origins.txt.
findings.breaks_when: A site is moved to a Greek shared plan for latency reasons and loses LiteSpeed/Redis/ESI/crawler, ending up with higher TTFB than Hetzner+edge cache; a LiteSpeed Enterprise license tier on the Plesk server without the cache module (check with the admin).
findings.how_to_apply: Keep the Hetzner LiteSpeed server as the standard origin; move dev6/LeaseWeb production sites either to the LiteSpeed server or give that server a page cache (FlyingPress/WP Rocket) and HTTP/3; on the Plesk servers install redis-server and enable the 'redis' PHP extension per PHP version (Plesk > PHP Settings), open UDP 443, and confirm the LiteSpeed license includes LSCache with ESI (ask LiteSpeed support or check 'esi=on' in headers after enabling). For client-owned shared hosting, prefer the LiteSpeed Greek plans (DnHost/IP.GR) and accept no ESI/crawler.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI shows server: LiteSpeed (or x-turbo-charged-by: LiteSpeed behind Cloudflare), alt-svc: h3, content-encoding: br; LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > ESI shows no 'disabled' warning and x-litespeed-cache-control includes esi=on; `redis-cli ping` and Site Health > Info > Server list the redis extension; hosting.gr table for client plans.
findings.correction: Same recommendation (keep the LiteSpeed Hetzner origin), but the Greek-shared-hosting figures are unverified by this review and the latency argument should cite the Cloudflare Greek PoPs rather than raw RTT to Germany.

findings.claim: A Redis object cache does nothing for cached home pages but is the main lever for the uncached paths that still cost 1.7-3.1 s here (cart, checkout, my-account, wc-ajax fragments, booking availability, logged-in forum users, cache misses).
findings.detail: LiteSpeed docs: 'If LSCWP fully caches a site, object caching may not be used often. Object caching is needed when WordPress builds a page through PHP'; FlyingPress Redis doc: useful for 'WooCommerce cart, checkout, and account pages' and logged-in pages, requires a Redis server plus the phpredis extension, only one object-cache.php drop-in may be active. LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > Object tab fields: Object Cache ON, Method Redis, Host (localhost or /path/to/redis.sock with Port 0), Port, Default Object Lifetime 360 s, Username/Password, Redis Database ID, Global Groups, Do Not Cache Groups (default 'comment counts plugins'), Persistent Connection ON, Cache WP Admin ON (may serve stale admin data), Store Transients deprecated in 7.8 (transients always stored now); per-site key prefix via wp-config to isolate sites on one server; status line '<!-- Object Cache [total] ... [hit] ... [miss] -->' appears in page source with Debug Log ON. Redis Object Cache plugin (Till Krüss) is WPML- and APO-listed. Measured today: limnoupolis /cart/ 3.1 s, /my-account/ 2.7 s, ?wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments 1.7 s TTFB; no independent 2025 benchmark for the gain was found, so treat the size of the win as site-specific.
findings.breaks_when: Two sites share one Redis without a prefix (cross-site key reads); stale options after plugin updates when Cache WP Admin is ON; LSMCD with SASL fatal error (meta.php:588) if Memcached is chosen instead of Redis; another object-cache.php drop-in (W3TC's) is already present; Redis memory full with no eviction policy.
findings.how_to_apply: Plesk server: install redis-server, enable the 'redis' extension for the site's PHP 8.3 handler, then either LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > Object (Method Redis, Host 127.0.0.1 or socket, Port 6379/0, Default Object Lifetime 360, Persistent Connection ON) or the Redis Object Cache plugin with WP_REDIS_HOST/WP_REDIS_PORT/WP_REDIS_PREFIX in wp-config.php; remove W3TC's object cache first.
findings.how_to_verify: LiteSpeed: enable Toolbox > Debug Log (Admin IP) and read the Object Cache hit/miss comment in page source; Redis plugin: Settings > Redis shows 'Connected'; measure curl -w '%{time_starttransfer}' on /cart/ and a booking product with an item in the cart before and after, and `redis-cli info stats` keyspace_hits rising; rerun Lighthouse on /checkout/.

findings.claim: Logged-in users (the cretaforums.gr forum, hotel My Account) only get fast pages via ESI (LiteSpeed Enterprise with esi on), role-based cache (FlyingPress) or per-user cache (WP Rocket User Cache, LiteSpeed private cache); each has a leak or cost trade-off, so decide per site rather than globally.
findings.detail: LiteSpeed: ESI 'allows pages to be served from cache to logged-in users' by punching holes (default blocks: Admin Bar, Comment Form; WooCommerce cart as a private ESI block; 'ESI widgets do not work with WordPress v5.8 and later' without Classic Widgets; 'ESI has a cost'); without ESI, 'Cache Logged-in Users' stores a private copy per IP + session ID. FlyingPress 'Cache for Logged-In Users by Role' creates one file per role (index-logged-in-subscriber.html.gz), served without front-end optimisations, with 'Exclude specific user roles' as the safety valve, and warns against it for per-user dashboards. WP Rocket's User Cache add-on makes one cache set per user; Preload, Remove Unused CSS and lazy background images do not apply to it; Query Monitor sets DONOTCACHEPAGE; Cloudflare 'Cache Everything' cannot distinguish logged-in users. Cloudflare APO always bypasses on wp-/wordpress cookies, so edge caching never helps logged-in traffic. Today no agency server shows 'esi=on' in x-litespeed-cache-control.
findings.breaks_when: Role-based cache on pages with user-specific content (order history, private messages) shows one user's data to another with the same role; ESI not enabled at the vhost (page silently uncached) or on OpenLiteSpeed/QUIC.cloud-less setups; nonces inside ESI blocks expire (LiteSpeed ships an esi_nonce list); private per-user caches balloon disk on a busy forum.
findings.how_to_apply: Forum (cretaforums, FlyingPress): try Caching > Cache for Logged-In Users by Role for 'subscriber'/'participant' only on listing pages, exclude roles that see private content, test two accounts side by side. LiteSpeed sites: ask the server admin to set 'CacheEngine on esi' for the vhost, then LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > ESI > Enable ESI ON, Cache Admin Bar ON, Cache Comment Form ON; keep My Account excluded. WP Rocket: Add-ons > User Cache only on membership-style sites with the no-store htaccess helper.
findings.how_to_verify: Log in as two different non-admin users in two browsers, load the same pages and diff the HTML for names, carts, unread counts; check x-litespeed-cache-control contains esi=on and the page source has <esi:include> markers when ESI is on; confirm the admin bar never appears to a logged-out curl; run Lighthouse logged in via a Puppeteer script with the cookie.

findings.claim: Set WooCommerce 'Default customer location' to 'Shop base address' or 'No location by default' on these Greek stores; 'Geolocate (with page caching support)' appends ?v=<hash> to URLs, forcing per-location cache copies, an extra Ajax call and a self-redirect per page, and defeats Cloudflare APO entirely.
findings.detail: WooCommerce dev blog (the feature's design): on each page an Ajax call geolocates the visitor and, if the location is new or changed, 'the page redirects back to itself with an extra querystring e.g. v=12345 ... The hash causes cache invalidation'. WooCommerce MaxMind doc: 'you will see ?v=$hash query strings added to your site's URLs ... If you'd like to prevent these query strings from being added, select the Geolocate option instead'. Plain 'Geolocate' is PHP and never runs on a cached page, so the first cached visitor's location is what everyone sees; irrelevant when all customers are taxed the same. Cloudflare APO bypasses cache for any query parameter outside its UTM/gclid allowlist, so ?v= makes every page DYNAMIC. LiteSpeed's WooCommerce integration explicitly removes the geolocation redirect on ESI pages, confirming the interaction is known. WP Rocket handles WCML geolocation only via mandatory cookies (wcml_client_country) that block caching until set.
findings.breaks_when: The shop legitimately charges location-dependent tax or shipping to customers outside Greece on the product page (water park e-shop sells to tourists but prices are the same, so not here); WCML multi-currency by client location is enabled.
findings.how_to_apply: WooCommerce > Settings > General > Default customer location = 'Shop base address' (or 'No location by default'); if geolocated prices are required, use 'Geolocate' plus a price-by-country plugin that loads prices in the background, never the 'page caching support' variant; add 'v' to LiteSpeed Cache > Excludes > Do Not Cache Query Strings only as a last resort.
findings.how_to_verify: Browse the shop in incognito and confirm no URL gains ?v=; curl -sI a product URL and expect a cache HIT without query string; Cloudflare: cf-cache-status HIT (not DYNAMIC) on product pages; Lighthouse 'redirects' audit 0 ms.

findings.claim: Plesk's 'Enable nginx caching' is a second, half-working page cache on the nginx servers (cretaforums shows x-cache-status: MISS under FlyingPress); either configure it deliberately or turn it off, never stack it blindly over a WordPress cache plugin.
findings.detail: cretaforums.gr today: x-flying-press-cache: HIT, x-flying-press-source: Web Server, cache-control: no-cache, must-revalidate, and x-cache-status: MISS (Plesk nginx caching enabled on the vhost but never storing because FlyingPress' response says no-cache and requests carry cookies). Plesk forum (staff and senior members): the option lives in the domain's Apache & nginx Settings ('Enable nginx caching', with 'Bypass cache when' options and a 'Cache requests with cookies' allowlist); 'by default, requests with cookies are not cached'; 'the average WP site is fully bloated with cookies and that can be a problem, causing Nginx cache being bypassed'; wildcards are not supported so wp_woocommerce_session_* cannot be allowlisted; 'the optimal results can only be achieved by customizing the default Nginx templates'. The official docs.plesk.com page for this feature returned 404 today, so the forum is the best source available. Third-party cookies set server-side (official-facebook-pixel sets _fbp on limnoupolis responses) and consent cookies make most requests cookie-bearing.
findings.breaks_when: Both caches store HTML: a FlyingPress/WP Rocket purge does not purge the nginx cache so edits and stock changes appear late; nginx serves a cached page with another visitor's Set-Cookie or logged-in state when 'Bypass cache when' is loosened; cookie allowlists include session cookies.
findings.how_to_apply: For sites already on FlyingPress/WP Rocket: Plesk > Websites & Domains > domain > Apache & nginx Settings > untick 'Enable nginx caching' (keep 'Serve static files directly by nginx' and PHP-FPM served by nginx). Only for a plain WordPress site with no cache plugin: enable it with all three 'Bypass cache when' options ON and no cookie allowlist, accepting that cookie-bearing visitors bypass.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI the home page three times: x-cache-status should be absent (feature off) or HIT with no FlyingPress/WP Rocket cache headers (feature deliberately on); after editing a page in WordPress, reload within 5 s and confirm the change is live; with Cookie: wordpress_logged_in_x=1 expect BYPASS.
findings.correction: Same recommendation; treat the Plesk-side facts as practitioner-sourced (forum + KB summary), not official docs. Add 'PHP-FPM served by nginx' as the Plesk-recommended prerequisite if the feature is ever used deliberately.

findings.claim: HTTP/3 and Brotli are already on for the LiteSpeed origins and Cloudflare, but the LeaseWeb nginx server has no HTTP/3 and limnoupolis ships a 129 KB .glb uncompressed; the fixes are a firewall port, a Cloudflare toggle and a MIME type, with small lab gains but real mobile field gains.
findings.detail: Headers today: LiteSpeed origins send alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=2592000, h3-29=":443" and content-encoding: br; Cloudflare sites send alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 and br; dev6.inglelandi.com (nginx) sends br but no alt-svc. LiteSpeed docs: 'QUIC is on by default, and HTTP/3 connections will automatically be made ... Simply open UDP port 443' (CSF: add 443 to UDP_IN and UDP_OUT; `netstat -lupn | grep 443` shows litespeed on udp 443). Cloudflare: HTTP/3 available on all plans, Speed > Settings > Protocol Optimization > HTTP/3 ON, 'HTTP/3 connection to the origin is not yet supported'. Cloudflare compression: supports Gzip/Brotli/Zstandard to visitors, keeps the origin's br/gzip if the response carries content-encoding, compresses only 200/403/404 responses above 48-50 bytes, and 'cache-control: no-transform' stops recompression; LSWS editions table lists 'GZIP and Brotli compression' and 'HTTP/3'. Lighthouse flagged https://limnoupolis.gr/wp-content/uploads/lmn-3d/buoy.glb (129,232 bytes, 17,316 bytes wasted) as uncompressed because model/gltf-binary is not in the default compressible types. Lighthouse's mobile throttling does not reward HTTP/3 much; CrUX field TTFB on lossy mobile does.
findings.breaks_when: UDP 443 blocked by the datacenter firewall makes browsers silently fall back to HTTP/2 (looks 'enabled' but is not); Brotli added for already-compressed types wastes CPU; no-transform set by a plugin stops Cloudflare from compressing.
findings.how_to_apply: server8 (nginx/Plesk): open UDP 443 and enable HTTP/3 in the nginx build/Plesk, or simply put the site behind Cloudflare with HTTP/3 ON; server1 (LiteSpeed): confirm UDP 443 is open in the firewall; add model/gltf-binary (and .glb) to the compression types in LiteSpeed (Server > Tuning > Compressible Types) or via a Cloudflare Compression Rule; keep Brotli on for text/*, application/javascript, application/json, image/svg+xml, font/* as already observed.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI shows alt-svc with h3; Chrome DevTools Network 'Protocol' column shows h3 on the second load; `curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' URL.glb | grep content-encoding` returns br; Lighthouse 'uses-text-compression' overallSavingsBytes 0.

findings.claim: PHP 8.3/8.4 settings that matter: WP memory 512 MB (Elementor's recommendation with WooCommerce), OPcache sized above its defaults (memory_consumption 128, interned_strings_buffer 8, max_accelerated_files 10000), and leave JIT at its default (disabled since 8.4); none of this moves a cached home page, all of it shortens the 1.7-3 s uncached requests.
findings.detail: Elementor System Requirements (fetched today): PHP 7.4+ with 8.x recommended, MySQL 5.6+/MariaDB 10.5+, 'WP Memory limit of 256 MB (Elementor and Elementor Pro only), 512 MB recommended, 768 MB for best performance ... if you are using additional plugins such as WooCommerce, you may need to increase your memory to 512 MB'. php.net OPcache defaults: opcache.enable=1, opcache.memory_consumption=128, opcache.interned_strings_buffer=8, opcache.max_accelerated_files=10000, opcache.validate_timestamps=1, opcache.revalidate_freq=2, opcache.jit='disable' as of PHP 8.4 (was 'tracing' with jit_buffer_size 0, i.e. effectively off, on 8.3), opcache.jit_buffer_size 64M default since 8.4; a php.net note explains the interned-strings buffer is carved out of memory_consumption. Lighthouse's own SRT guidance recommends OPcache and Redis/Memcached. The agency servers run PHP 8.3.35 (x-powered-by header). An Elementor+Pro+WooCommerce+addons install exceeds 10,000 PHP files, so the default max_accelerated_files thrashes.
findings.breaks_when: opcache.validate_timestamps=0 on a server where plugins auto-update (new code not loaded until PHP restart); memory_consumption too small for several sites in one PHP pool (hit rate drops, 'cache full' restarts); JIT enabled with buggy extensions; WP_MEMORY_LIMIT above the PHP memory_limit (ignored).
findings.how_to_apply: wp-config.php: define('WP_MEMORY_LIMIT','512M'); Plesk > PHP Settings for the site: memory_limit 512M; php.ini/opcache.ini for the PHP 8.3 handler: opcache.memory_consumption=256, opcache.interned_strings_buffer=32, opcache.max_accelerated_files=20000 (count with `find /var/www -name '*.php' | wc -l` and stay above it), opcache.validate_timestamps=1 with opcache.revalidate_freq=60, opcache.jit left at default; restart PHP-FPM/lsphp.
findings.how_to_verify: WP Admin > Tools > Site Health > Info > Server shows PHP memory limit 512M and OPcache enabled; `php -r 'print_r(opcache_get_status(false));'` (or a one-line admin-only PHP file) shows hit rate >95% and cache_full false; compare curl TTFB of /cart/ and an Elementor editor load before/after.

findings.claim: Database bloat barely touches TTFB once pages are cached; the measurable parts are autoloaded options (Site Health flags >800,000 bytes; WP 6.6 stops autoloading new options >150,000 bytes), never-expiring transients (autoloaded) and Elementor revisions that slow saves and backups, not front-end rendering.
findings.detail: WordPress core: WP_Site_Health uses apply_filters('site_status_autoloaded_options_size_limit', 800000) and reports 'Autoloaded options could affect performance'; the 6.6 dev note explains all autoloaded options are fetched with one query on every request and adds wp_max_autoloaded_option_size (150,000 bytes default) plus autoload values on/off/auto/auto-on/auto-off with no upgrade routine for old 'yes'/'no' rows. set_transient(): 'transients that never expire are autoloaded, whereas transients with an expiration time are not'; delete_expired_transients() removes expired ones. WordPress revisions doc: WP_POST_REVISIONS (false/0 disables, int keeps that many; old ones deleted on next update); Elementor only caps revisions at 25 on Elementor-hosted sites, self-hosted is unlimited. Audit numbers: autoload 43-720 KB (pallada 720 KB is close to the 800 KB flag; all others well under), transients 6-6,938 (marakaki), revisions 0-1,872 (onar) with Elementor meta 1-71 MB (pallada 71 MB, onar 64 MB because each revision duplicates _elementor_data). Lighthouse server-response-time on the cached sites (145-572 ms) shows no correlation with these numbers today.
findings.breaks_when: Revision deletion is irreversible (restore history lost); deleting non-expired transients of booking/filter plugins forces expensive rebuilds; setting autoload=off on an option a plugin reads on every page adds a query per request instead of removing one.
findings.how_to_apply: wp-config.php: define('WP_POST_REVISIONS', 10); prune: wp post delete $(wp post list --post_type=revision --format=ids --posts_per_page=-1) on a backup-verified copy, or the audit script's revisions_prune with confirmation; wp transient delete --expired (scheduled daily by core anyway); for autoload: SELECT option_name, LENGTH(option_value) FROM wp_options WHERE autoload IN ('yes','on','auto','auto-on') ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 20 and set autoload='off' on logs/caches of removed plugins; recheck Site Health.
findings.how_to_verify: Site Health > Status no longer lists 'Autoloaded options could affect performance' and Info > Database shows the autoloaded size; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM wp_posts WHERE post_type='revision'; Elementor editor save time and WP export size drop; curl TTFB on an uncached page (e.g. /my-account/) before and after, expecting only tens of ms difference.

findings.claim: Elementor Pro's Menu Cart loads wc-cart-fragments on every page, which fires an uncacheable ?wc-ajax=get_refreshed_fragments request (1.7 s TTFB on limnoupolis) after each page view; WooCommerce 7.8+ only enqueues it where a mini-cart is present, so remove the header cart from brochure pages or use the Mini-Cart block to cut server load without breaking caching.
findings.detail: WooCommerce dev blog: since 7.8 the cart fragments script 'will now only be enqueued if using the Mini Cart widget', when a third party registers it as a dependency, or when enqueued in code; 'If you expose the mini-cart widget on every page of your site and also have server/page caching enabled ... it's likely the mini-cart widget will not update' without fragments; the Mini-Cart block 'does not use the cart fragments API'. limnoupolis.gr home HTML today contains wc-cart-fragments-js and woocommerce-menu-cart markup (Elementor Pro Menu Cart), and the fragments endpoint answered in 1.7 s with x-litespeed-cache-control: no-cache. This is server load and main-thread work after load rather than LCP, so the PageSpeed effect is small; it matters for the uncached-request budget and for hosts counting PHP workers.
findings.breaks_when: Removing cart fragments while the header cart is PHP-rendered leaves stale cart counts on cached pages (then the only safe options are 'Vary for Mini Cart'/woocommerce_items_in_cart bypass, which cost cache hit ratio); the cart page itself relies on fragments to update the header.
findings.how_to_apply: Show the Elementor Pro Menu Cart only in the shop/booking header template (Theme Builder display conditions) and not on hotel/villa brochure pages; where a live cart is needed, prefer the WooCommerce Mini-Cart block; keep ?wc-ajax= uncached (already automatic); never disable fragments globally on pages that still render the cart in PHP.
findings.how_to_verify: View source of a brochure page: no wc-cart-fragments-js; DevTools Network on a shop page: one get_refreshed_fragments request, status 200, cache-control no-cache; add an item and confirm the header count updates on a cached page; server logs show fewer wc-ajax hits.

findings.claim: Lighthouse 13 (in PSI and Chrome 143) removed the server-response-time, redirects and uses-text-compression audits from the JSON; the plugin's verification must read document-latency-insight instead, or it will report 'audit missing' on every current PSI run.
findings.detail: developer.chrome.com blog 'Lighthouse 13.0': 'in Lighthouse 13 we are removing the old audits from both the report and the underlying JSON'; table maps server-response-time -> document-latency-insight (alongside cls-culprits-insight, dom-size-insight, font-display-insight, image-delivery-insight, lcp-discovery-insight, lcp-phases-insight, legacy-javascript-insight, network-dependency-tree-insight, modern-http-insight ...). 'Lighthouse 13 is available immediately ... and will be available in PageSpeed Insights within the next week. It will land in Chrome stable in Chrome 143.' The SRT doc page now says 'This audit has moved into the Document request latency insight as of Lighthouse 13'. The agency's local runs are Lighthouse 12.8.2 and still contain both ids (checked in scratchpad/lh/runs/*.json: all 10 have server-response-time and document-latency-insight).
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break a site; it breaks the plugin's own measurement scripts if they key on the old audit ids.
findings.how_to_apply: In the plugin's Lighthouse/PSI parser: prefer audits['document-latency-insight'] (score 1/0, details list redirect, server time and compression sub-checks), fall back to audits['server-response-time'].numericValue, audits['redirects'] and audits['uses-text-compression'] only when lighthouseVersion < 13. Record lighthouseVersion in every result row.
findings.how_to_verify: Run the PSI API on one site and assert that audits['document-latency-insight'] exists and that audits['server-response-time'] is absent when lighthouseVersion >= 13; compare the 600 ms pass/fail with a curl TTFB measurement.

findings.claim: Long page-cache TTLs (604800-2592000 s) silently break anything that prints a WordPress nonce into cached HTML (filters, booking/add-on forms, REST calls) after 12-24 hours; LiteSpeed only protects nonces when ESI is on, so either enable ESI + ESI Nonces or cap TTL on those pages at 12 hours.
findings.detail: developer.wordpress.org: 'By default, a nonce has a lifetime of one day' and WordPress validates 'nonces from the current tick and the last tick' (12 h ticks). LiteSpeed API doc: 'Default WordPress nonces are already treated as ESI blocks automatically. They are cached for 12 hours independently of the surrounding page's TTL. Register custom nonces with litespeed_nonce' and 'If ESI is disabled for the request, LSCWP falls back to a normal wp_create_nonce() call'. Cache doc, ESI Nonces: 'Nonces often expire before the site TTL, which can cause problems on pages that use them. Converting a nonce to an ESI block allows it to expire independently of the rest of the page'. LSCWP 7.9 changelog shows this is live breakage: 'DIVI 5 - Disable Rest API cache to fix the invalid_nonce issue', 'Added Gravity Forms ESI nonce detection', 'Fixed ESI nonce generation for actions with custom nonce lifetimes'. No agency server shows esi=on today, so right now every nonce on a cached page is frozen for the full TTL.
findings.breaks_when: ESI is not enabled at the vhost (nonce ESI silently falls back to a static nonce); a plugin uses a custom nonce action not in LiteSpeed's list; the 12 h LiteSpeed nonce TTL is combined with a plugin that shortens nonce_life.
findings.how_to_apply: After purge, save the cached HTML of the home page, a booking product, a JetSmartFilters archive and the checkout: grep -i -E 'nonce|_wpnonce|"security"' . For each page with hits: LiteSpeed with ESI available -> Cache > ESI > Enable ESI ON and add the nonce action names to ESI Nonces; without ESI -> Cache > Cache > Force Cache URIs '/path 43200' (per-URI TTL) or set Default Public Cache TTL 43200 site-wide; FlyingPress/WP Rocket -> keep their shorter default lifespans on those pages instead of 'never expire'.
findings.how_to_verify: Purge, load the page, wait >24 h (or temporarily set add_filter('nonce_life', fn() => 300) on staging and wait 10 min), then submit the filter/booking/add-to-cart: must return 200, not 403/'invalid nonce'/-1. With ESI on, x-litespeed-cache-control must include esi=on and the page source must show the esi nonce block comment.

findings.claim: Elementor's Element Caching (e_element_cache) is active with a 24 h expiry on 8 of the 10 audited sites although Elementor ships it inactive and experimental; it shortens uncached renders but must be set Inactive on any element with dynamic tags/shortcodes/user data (forum, My Account, booking widgets) because it has caused one user's data to be shown to another.
findings.detail: elementor.com/help 'Speed up page loading with Element Caching' (Last Update: September 15, 2026): 'when widgets are rendered on the server the HTML output is stored in the database ... reduces the Time To First Byte (TTFB)'; 'Element Caching cannot be used on elements that contain dynamic tags or any other type of dynamic information, such as shortcodes ... the feature is inactive by default'; 'Element Caching is an experimental feature'; Settings > Performance > 'Element Cache Expiration' dropdown and 'Element Cache' dropdown > Disable; per-element Advanced > Cache Settings Active/Inactive. Memberium: 'If your users are seeing incorrect or other users' data, the first step is to disable Elementor's Element Caching feature' (Elementor > Settings > Features > Element Caching = Inactive). Local audit-summary.json: element_cache '24h' on cretaforums, fagitiotiszois, kand, marakaki, platonos, voreniahorizon; 'default' on limnoupolis/staging/onar; 'disabled' on pallada. This answers the researcher's open question about Element Cache only partially: it does reduce PHP render time on misses, but the size is untested here.
findings.breaks_when: Any cached widget contains a dynamic tag, shortcode, nonce, logged-in-user data, cart count, or booking availability; the Expiration is longer than the content's change frequency; a plugin (Memberium-style membership, bbPress/forum widgets) renders per-user HTML inside an Elementor widget.
findings.how_to_apply: Elementor > Settings > Features: keep Element Caching Active only on brochure sites; Elementor > Settings > Performance > Element Cache Expiration: 1 day or less on sites with prices/stock; for every widget with dynamic tags, shortcodes, forms, cart or booking output: Advanced > Cache Settings > Inactive. On cretaforums.gr (forum) and on any My Account/booking template set the feature Inactive site-wide. Measure a LiteSpeed MISS with it on vs off on staging before relying on it.
findings.how_to_verify: Log in as two different users in two browsers and compare pages containing dynamic widgets (names, cart counts, booking dates) - must differ; curl -w '%{time_starttransfer}' on a purged (MISS) page with Element Cache on vs off; check that price/stock changes appear on the front end within the configured expiration after a WooCommerce stock update.

findings.claim: Cloudflare already has Athens and Thessaloniki PoPs, so for the four proxied sites static assets and TLS terminate in Greece today; only the DYNAMIC HTML goes to Nuremberg/Amsterdam, and PSI lab TTFB is measured from a Google datacenter in Europe, not from Greece.
findings.detail: cloudflare.com/network (opened today) lists 'Athens, GR' and 'Thessaloniki, GR' among European locations. Google PSI 'About' page: 'PageSpeed also runs in a Google datacenter that can vary based on network conditions ... PageSpeed will report running in one of: North America, Europe, or Asia'. Consequence: the hosting.gr 39-61 ms Greece->Germany RTT quoted by the researcher is the cost of the HTML fetch only, and an Athens edge PoP improves Greek CrUX field TTFB but changes the PSI lab number only by the difference between a Cloudflare European PoP and Hetzner as seen from Google's European region. Cloudflare APO docs also state 'cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC' with a 'cf-apo-via' reason header when any criterion fails, which is the quick way to see why HTML is not cached.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; the lab gain is overestimated if one expects PSI to run from Greece.
findings.how_to_apply: When deciding on APO / FlyingPress Cloudflare page cache / QUIC.cloud, set the expectation per metric: CrUX p75 TTFB for Greek users (field) is the KPI; for the PSI lab score the origin cache HIT is what gets the page under 600 ms. Check the serving colo with curl -s https://<domain>/cdn-cgi/trace | grep colo= from a Greek network (expect ATH or SKG) and read cf-apo-via on HTML to learn why it is DYNAMIC.
findings.how_to_verify: Before/after enabling edge HTML caching: PSI lab 'document-latency-insight' server time, and CrUX field TTFB p75 from the PSI API 'loadingExperience' after 28 days; cf-cache-status: HIT on HTML with -H 'accept: text/html'.

findings.claim: The recorded 'FlyingPress 4.22.1' version does not exist in FlyingPress' changelog; the sites are either on a 4.x build from before May 2025 or the version was misread, and everything the researcher relies on (Cloudflare page caching, Redis object cache, the new background queue) requires FlyingPress 5.1-5.6.
findings.detail: flyingpress.com/changelog (opened today): 5.6.5 - 20 August 2026 (latest), 5.6.0 - 24 June 2026 'New: Object Caching with Redis', 5.5.0 - 02 June 2026 own queue replacing Action Scheduler + 'Enhanced Cloudflare integration with automatic zone detection, API token support', 5.2.x fixes for Cloudflare page cache purge and bypass-cookie sync (Oct 2025-Jan 2026), 5.1.0 - 12 August 2025 'New: Cloudflare Integration for full page caching and faster global TTFB', 5.0.0 - 28 May 2025, then 4.16.4 - 15 February 2025; there are no 4.17-4.22 releases. FlyingPress APO doc: 'Starting from FlyingPress 5.1, we also offer a built-in Cloudflare Full Page Caching integration without using APO'. Also relevant: 5.2.1 'Properly cleanup .htaccess and advanced-cache.php contents after deactivation, when Cloudflare integration was enabled' and 5.2.4 'Add Super Page Cache to the incompatible plugins list'.
findings.breaks_when: A major upgrade from 4.x to 5.x changes defaults (queue, cache structure); test on staging. Running two Cloudflare HTML caches (APO plus FlyingPress integration, or Super Page Cache) conflicts.
findings.how_to_apply: Read the real version from the plugin header (wp plugin list --name=flying-press or Plugins screen) on cretaforums.gr and voreniahorizon.gr; if < 5.6.5, update on staging first, then production; only then configure CDN > Cloudflare (Zone ID auto-detected, API token) and Object Cache (Redis) in FlyingPress.
findings.how_to_verify: Plugins screen shows FlyingPress 5.6.x; FlyingPress > CDN shows the Cloudflare page-caching toggle; curl -sI with -H 'accept: text/html' returns cf-cache-status: HIT on the second request; no APO plugin active at the same time.

findings.claim: WP-Cron must move to a system cron on fully cached sites: the cache keeps PHP from running so scheduled purges/posts/booking expirations fire late, and when PHP does run on an uncached request it pays for the cron spawn too.
findings.detail: LiteSpeed troubleshooting doc: 'Normally, WordPress triggers the cron job each time a request hits the backend. The backend is rarely hit, however, when using a cache, and this causes scheduled posts to publish late. LSCWP will correctly purge the cache when a scheduled post is published in the cron job. All you need to do is make sure that you can reliably hit the backend' with the example '*/15 * * * * wget http://your_wp_site/wp-cron.php' and 'define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true);'. WordPress Plugin Handbook: 'WordPress will continue to run WP-Cron on each page load. This is no longer necessary and will contribute to extra resource usage on your server. WP-Cron can be disabled in the wp-config.php file ... define( 'DISABLE_WP_CRON', true );'. LSCWP's own crawler, QUIC.cloud queue and 7.9 async Health service all 'resume through WP cron', so a reliable cron is a prerequisite for the crawler finding in this dimension. The htaccess 'noconntimeout' rule for long wp-cron runs is also in the LiteSpeed doc.
findings.breaks_when: The system cron is created with the wrong URL (http vs https, www vs non-www, redirect) and silently never runs; DISABLE_WP_CRON is set without a working system cron (crawler, Action Scheduler, booking reminders stop); a Plesk 'Scheduled Tasks' entry runs under a user that cannot reach the site.
findings.how_to_apply: Plesk > Websites & Domains > Scheduled Tasks (or crontab): every 5-15 min run `curl -sS -o /dev/null https://<domain>/wp-cron.php?doing_wp_cron` or `wp cron event run --due-now --path=...`; then add define('DISABLE_WP_CRON', true); to wp-config.php. Do this per language domain if WPML uses separate domains.
findings.how_to_verify: wp cron event list --due-now shows nothing overdue 10 minutes after a scheduled post time; Site Health no longer warns about scheduled events; LiteSpeed Cache > Crawler > Summary advances between runs without manual 'Run' clicks.

findings.claim: LiteSpeed's 'Cache REST API' defaults ON, which is fine for public JSON but has already caused invalid_nonce failures for builders using the REST API; if JetSmartFilters, Elementor Pro forms or the WooCommerce Store API misbehave on a LiteSpeed site, exclude their routes or turn REST caching off before blaming the plugins.
findings.detail: Cache doc (Sep 29 2026): 'Cache REST API ON - This option allows requests made through WordPress REST API calls to be cached.' LSCWP 7.9 changelog: '3rd DIVI 5 - Disable Rest API cache to fix the invalid_nonce issue (PR#1004)'; 7.9.1: 'Do Not Cache, Private Cached, Force Cache, Optimization and Lazy Load URI rules now compare the same query string against both spellings of a REST route' (i.e. /wp-json/x and ?rest_route=/x), confirming REST exclusion rules are a supported path. Elementor's own LiteSpeed guidance (thirdparty doc, July 27 2026) only covers Performance/Features settings (CSS Print Method unchanged, Optimized Image Loading Disable, Optimized Gutenberg Loading Enable, Inline Font Icons Active, Additional Custom Breakpoints Inactive, Lazy Load Background Images Inactive) and says nothing about REST, so the REST caching interaction with Elementor 4.x atomic widgets/filters is untested by the vendors.
findings.breaks_when: A REST response that embeds a nonce or per-user data is cached for the Default Public TTL; filter results for one query string are served for another when the plugin posts filters in the body rather than the URL.
findings.how_to_apply: Default: leave ON. If a REST-driven feature returns stale or 403 results only on cache HITs: LiteSpeed Cache > Cache > Excludes > Do Not Cache URIs add '^/wp-json/jet-smart-filters' (or the plugin's namespace), or Cache > Cache > Cache REST API OFF; purge all.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI 'https://site/wp-json/<namespace>/...' twice: x-litespeed-cache: hit only for routes you intend to cache; filter/forms work on a 25-hour-old cached page; no invalid_nonce in the browser console.

title: A safety harness: proving nothing broke after each change
summary: The harness is a gate chain that runs after every single optimisation step, on the same machine and network, in this order (cheapest and most decisive first): purge caches → console/pageerror/failed-request diff → interaction smoke tests (menu, form, add-to-cart, booking calendar, popup, language) → CLS via PerformanceObserver at mobile width with a scroll pass → Playwright screenshot diff at 390px and 1366px with animations disabled, carousels masked and a saved consent state → Elementor editor load check → tracking-request check → median-of-5 Lighthouse mobile compared against the before-median with a non-overlap rule. Any red stops the run and triggers the undo for that one step, which is only possible if every step recorded its before-value first (wp option get --format=json, wp litespeed-option export, wp w3-total-cache export, Perfmatters JSON export, wp db export before non-reversible actions).
