So the Design System > Defaults rule 'div padding 0' is needed for Div Blocks too, and the Div-vs-Flexbox choice is about layout semantics, not bytes. Hello theme settings page (Last Update Sep 25, 2026) confirmed: tabs 'SEO and accessibility' (Disable description meta tag, Disable skip link — the researcher omitted the skip-link toggle, which should stay ON for accessibility), 'Structure and layout' (Disable theme header & footer, Hide page title), 'CSS and styling control' (Deregister Hello reset.css, Deregister Hello theme.css); Hello stable 3.5.1 (2026-08-25). 'Disable Default Colors/Fonts' at Elementor > Settings > General confirmed (Jun 15, 2025 page). Hedrick's mapping not re-verified.

findings.claim: Figma data access is tiered: file/node/style/image REST endpoints work with a personal access token on any plan, the Variables API is Enterprise-only, and the Figma MCP is useless on Starter/View seats (20 calls per month); the connector in this environment is not authenticated.
findings.detail: developers.figma.com Variables page: 'To use this API, you must have a Full seat in an Enterprise org'; scopes `file_variables:read|write`. OpenAPI spec (figma/rest-api-spec main): `GET /v1/files/{file_key}`, `/v1/files/{file_key}/nodes`, `/v1/files/{file_key}/styles`, `/v1/styles/{key}` and `/v1/images/{file_key}` need only `files:read` / `file_content:read`; `/v1/files/{file_key}/variables/local` is marked 'available to full members of Enterprise orgs'. Images endpoint: `ids` (comma list), `scale` 0.01–4, `format` jpg|png|svg|pdf (default png), `use_absolute_bounds`, `svg_outline_text` — no WebP/AVIF, so convert locally. Figma MCP rate limits (official): View/Collab seats and Starter plan 20 tool calls/month; Dev/Full seats 200/day at 10/min (Professional), 200/day at 15/min (Organization), 600/day at 20/min (Enterprise); remote server `https://mcp.figma.com/mcp` recommended, desktop server needs Dev/Full seat on a paid plan; `whoami` is exempt. Tools include get_design_context, get_variable_defs, get_screenshot, get_metadata. This session lists `plugin:design:figma` as requiring OAuth, so no Figma call is possible until the user authorises it.
findings.breaks_when: Agency on Figma Starter or with Viewer seats burns the 20 monthly MCP calls on one page; a token without `file_content:read` returns 403 on nodes; Variables call returns 403 outside Enterprise; files over the limit of the images endpoint time out when many ids are requested at scale 4.
findings.how_to_apply: Plugin fallback chain: (1) Figma MCP `get_variable_defs` + `get_design_context` on the frame if a Dev/Full seat is available; (2) else REST: `GET /v1/files/{key}?depth=2` for page/frame list, `GET /v1/files/{key}/nodes?ids=…` to read `fills`, `strokes`, `style.fontFamily/fontSize/fontWeight/lineHeightPx/letterSpacing`, `cornerRadius`, `itemSpacing`, `padding*`, and `GET /v1/files/{key}/styles` for published colour/text styles; (3) export raster nodes with `GET /v1/images/{key}?ids=…&format=png&scale=2` and vectors with `format=svg`, then convert to WebP/AVIF locally; (4) if the designer has Tokens Studio, accept its JSON. Ask the user to authorise the Figma connector in claude.ai connector settings before relying on (1).
findings.how_to_verify: `GET /v1/me` returns the account; `/v1/files/{key}` returns `document.children`; the `/variables/local` call returns 403 on non-Enterprise (expected); MCP `whoami` prints the seat type and plan before any design call.

findings.claim: Export and upload images by rule: largest edge ≤ 2560 px (WordPress scales anything bigger to a '-scaled' copy), AVIF or WebP generated outside Figma, explicit width/height, Elementor image size set to a custom size matching the box, lazy-load off and fetchpriority high only on the hero.
findings.detail: WordPress 5.3+: uploads with width or height above `big_image_size_threshold` (default 2560 px) are scaled and the scaled copy becomes the largest size; disable with `add_filter('big_image_size_threshold','__return_false')`. WordPress 6.5 added AVIF upload and sub-size generation when Imagick/GD supports it (check Tools → Site Health → Info → Media Handling); quality per mime via `add_filter('wp_editor_set_quality', fn($q,$mime)=> 'image/avif'===$mime ? 75 : $q, 10, 2)`. WordPress 6.3 automatically adds `fetchpriority="high"` to the first large in-viewport image, never combines it with `loading="lazy"`, default `wp_omit_loading_attr_threshold` is 3 images, and preset attributes are respected. Elementor's 'Optimized Image Loading' (Elementor → Settings → Performance) does the same prioritisation and skips lazy-load above the fold. Elementor's Image Size group control offers thumbnail/medium/medium_large/large/full or `custom` (`image_custom_dimension` {width,height}). Lighthouse 13 'Improve image delivery' flags only ≥ 4 KiB savings, judges oversizing against rendered size × DPR, and recommends AVIF/WebP; Figma's own export is png/jpg/svg/pdf only (REST and UI), so WebP/AVIF conversion is a local step (sharp/cwebp/avifenc).
findings.breaks_when: Hosting without AVIF in Imagick/GD rejects AVIF uploads or creates no sub-sizes; iOS < 16 cannot decode AVIF/WebP (Chrome note) — serve WebP+JPEG fallback through the optimiser if that audience matters; a hero set to `image_size: full` on a 2560 px upload ships ~1 MB on a 390 px phone; LiteSpeed/FlyingPress lazy-load applied to the hero raised CLS to 0.107 on staging.
findings.how_to_apply: Export from Figma at 2× (REST `scale=2` or UI 2x PNG/JPG), then generate: hero 1920/1280/768 px wide in AVIF (q≈50–60) with WebP fallback, cards 2× their box width, logos/icons as SVG. Register sizes in the child theme (`add_image_size('hero-mobile', 768, 0)` etc.). In the e-image/Image widget pick that custom size, set Lazy Load = No only for the hero, keep WordPress' automatic `fetchpriority`, and keep the cache plugin's lazy-load excluded for the first image (LiteSpeed: exclude by class/URL; FlyingPress 'Exclude above-fold images' count). Reject uploads > 2560 px and > 300 KB in the build lint.
findings.how_to_verify: View-source of the home page: hero `` has `fetchpriority="high"`, no `loading="lazy"`, `width`/`height` and a `srcset` whose chosen candidate ≈ rendered width × DPR; Lighthouse 'Improve image delivery' shows 0 KiB for the hero; 'LCP request discovery' shows the image discoverable in HTML; CLS stays ≤ 0.04 after enabling the cache plugin's lazy-load.
findings.correction: WP 6.3 fetchpriority behaviour confirmed (make.wordpress.org dev note, 'typically improves LCP by 5-10%'). But on Elementor sites WordPress core's logic is not what runs: Elementor's 'Optimized Image Loading' (Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance, option `elementor_optimized_image_loading`, default Enable, label text 'applying fetchpriority="high" on LCP image and loading="lazy" on images below the fold') adds `wp_lazy_loading_enabled => false`, stops core's fetchpriority flag, buffers output from `get_header` and rewrites every `` via `wp_content_img_tag` — so `wp_omit_loading_attr_threshold` and other core filters do not apply; tune Elementor's module instead. Second correction: the atomic `e-image` template (`atomic-image.html.twig` + `Image_Transformer`) outputs `src`, `width`, `height`, `srcset`, `alt` (and, as written, the attachment `id` as an HTML attribute) but no `sizes` attribute, so the browser evaluates the srcset as if the image were 100vw and WP 6.7's `sizes="auto"` cannot be added (it needs an existing sizes attr). Pick the Resolution/custom size so the chosen file is about the rendered width × DPR, or add `sizes` through a filter, and verify in DevTools which candidate loaded. Also note Performance tab 'Lazy Load Background Images' (default Enable) hides every CSS background-image except the first via `background-image:none !important` until JS runs.

findings.claim: Use UiChemy (the only maintained Figma→Elementor converter with a V4-classes mode) for structure and token import only, then audit its output; the other converters output desktop-only v3 trees, and Elementor has no official Figma plugin.
findings.detail: UiChemy on wordpress.org: version 5.3.0, 8,000+ installs, requires WP 6.9+, changelog 7 Oct 2026 'Fixed: Global classes sync with Elementor Atomic'; builders: 'Elementor, including v4 with Atomic Elements and global classes'. Product page: default export uses free Container/Heading/Image widgets; 'Or Convert Into Elementor V4 Atomic … your styles become reusable classes rather than settings on each element'; Global Style Sync pushes Figma colours, font styles and container widths (e.g. 1140 px) into Elementor globals; Classic Mode (tag layers → widgets, free) vs AI Express (credits, needs Auto Layout, also builds header/footer); 'Almost always the Figma file rather than the conversion' causes bad output: missing Auto Layout, wrong nesting, negative gaps, unflattened masks. Red flags for a lean build: the new 'UiChemy Composer' stores raw HTML/CSS/JS in one widget and its 'Add library' catalogue injects pinned cdn.jsdelivr.net scripts and fonts.googleapis.com stylesheets per widget. Competitor comparison (Figmentor, Jan 2026, biased): UiChemy 80% of auto-layout frames convert cleanly, 15% of multi-level nested frames need fixes, images auto-converted to WebP; Fignel: no Auto Layout support, desktop-only output. Hedrick (Aug 2026): 85–94% fidelity, 15–45 min QA per page, export one section at a time, name layers (a 'Frame 47' becomes a container called Frame_47), bind every colour/size to Figma Variables before export. Elementor's own route is indirect: Elementor AI 'Reference a website' (URL → three containers; cannot do nested elements, carousels, repeating elements or site parts), Angie (screenshot → Variables and Classes), and the Elementor MCP which lets an AI tool that can read Figma build native elements.
findings.breaks_when: Composer sections are HTML widgets with inline CSS/JS (fail the plugin's 'no scripts in HTML widgets' rule and bypass Classes); AI Express adds motion/hover effects and extra Google Fonts; absolute-positioned Figma frames produce fixed-pixel containers that break at 390 px; converted pages often carry per-element inline styles and 5+ nesting levels.
findings.how_to_apply: Prepare the Figma file: Auto Layout on every frame, semantic layer names, all fills/text bound to Variables, images flattened. Run UiChemy Classic Mode → 'Elementor V4 Atomic' → Live Import to staging, one section at a time. Then run the plugin's audit: reject Composer widgets, strip per-element `styles` in favour of the imported Global Classes, cap depth at 4, remove any `fonts.googleapis.com`/`cdn.jsdelivr.net` asset, re-export images per finding 7. Treat the result as a starting tree for `elementor-set-content`, not a finished page.
findings.how_to_verify: Saved JSON contains only whitelisted `widgetType`s (no `uichemy-composer`, no `html`); Design System panel shows the synced classes/variables; Lighthouse requests list has no jsdelivr/googleapis hosts; screenshot diff at 390/768/1440 against the Figma frame within the agency's tolerance.
findings.correction: Facts confirmed: wordpress.org shows Version 5.3.0, 'Last updated 3 days ago', 'Active installations 8,000+', trunk readme 'Requires at least: 6.9', changelog 5.2.5 (7 October 2026) 'Fixed: Global classes sync with Elementor Atomic', 5.3.0 dated 12 October 2026; builders line 'Elementor, including v4 with Atomic Elements and global classes'. Correction: the DEFAULT output is now the Composer HTML widget, not atomic elements — the readme opens with 'UiChemy converts your design into WordPress using a single UiChemy Composer widget, an AI first visual editor that holds real HTML, CSS and JavaScript' and 'rebuilds the page inside your builder as a UiChemy Composer section holding real HTML, CSS and JavaScript'; the jsDelivr 'Add library' catalogue is confirmed in the readme. So the plugin must force Classic Mode → Elementor V4 Atomic and reject any `uichemy` Composer widgetType in the saved JSON; the V4 path itself was not tested by me (open question stands). 'Only maintained converter' and competitor claims (Figmentor, Fignel, Hedrick) were not re-verified.

findings.claim: Enforce container structure rules in the builder: one atomic container per visual block, Div Block by default, Flexbox only where flex is needed, Grid for repeated cards, depth ≤ 4, and never rely on removed v3 wrapper classes in CSS.
findings.detail: Elementor help 'Optimized DOM Output': wrappers `.elementor-inner`, `.elementor-row`, `.elementor-column-wrap` (3.0), `.elementor-image`, `.elementor-text-editor` (3.2), `elementor-section-wrap` (3.6) were removed and 'Starting with Elementor 3.19, these DOM improvements were fully incorporated into the Elementor Core meaning they are not longer optional'; the `e_optimized_markup` feature seen on the agency sites is the later widget-inner-wrapper removal (off on onar-seaside-lounge.gr, which also has the deepest nesting). V4 FAQ: atomic markup 'is based on pure HTML tags that render without additional wrapper layers'. Default Styles help: a Flexbox is a `<div>` with a 10 px default padding; setting the `div` tag default to 0 px in Design System → Defaults overrides it site-wide. Lighthouse DOM thresholds: warn > ~800 body nodes, fail > ~1,400 (moved to the 'Optimize DOM size' insight in Lighthouse 13). audit-summary.json shows current agency nesting depth 4–9 and 96–854 containers per site; Snapelement measured 65% of a V3 homepage DOM as Elementor structural overhead.
findings.breaks_when: Kit custom CSS targeting removed wrappers silently stops applying when optimized markup is turned on (screenshot pages with custom CSS first); a `div` Default Style of 0 padding also strips padding from every Flexbox that relied on the default; nesting below 768 px changes when Flexbox direction is per-breakpoint.
findings.how_to_apply: Builder rules: section = e-div-block (full-bleed background) containing at most one inner e-flexbox/e-grid (boxed content width via a `section-boxed` class); cards = e-grid children as e-div-block; no empty spacer containers (use gap/padding on the parent); max depth 4 counted from `content[]`; set Design System → Defaults → div padding 0 and define `section-boxed`/`section-full` classes once. Lint the JSON tree for depth and for containers with a single child that only adds padding (merge them).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse 'Optimize DOM size' insight: body nodes < 800, max depth lower than before, max children < 60; `document.querySelectorAll('.e-div-block, .e-flexbox, .e-grid').length` roughly equals the number of visual blocks × 2; no `.elementor-widget-container` wrappers in view-source.
findings.correction: Optimized DOM page confirmed (Last Update Feb 1, 2024; wrappers removed in 3.0/3.2/3.6, mandatory since 3.19). Two corrections: (1) Div Block carries the same 10 px base padding as Flexbox plus `min-width:30px` (`div-block.php` `get_base_padding`/`get_base_min_width`), so 'Div Block by default' does not save padding or bytes; set Defaults → div padding 0 once and pick Div vs Flexbox by layout need. (2) The '800 warn / 1,400 fail body nodes' thresholds belong to the old `dom-size` audit, which Lighthouse 13 removed; the replacement `dom-size-insight` (core/audits/insights/dom-size-insight.js) reports 'Total elements', 'DOM depth', 'Max children' and only fires from the DevTools DOMSize model when a layout/style-recalc event is longer than 40 ms with more than 100 dirty layout objects or 300 style-recalc elements (DOMSize.ts constants). It is non-scored, so gate on TBT/INP and use the three statistics as trend numbers, not pass/fail. Also `e_optimized_markup` is `default => STATE_INACTIVE` in core's experiments manager, so new sites must enable it explicitly for v3 widgets.

findings.claim: Fonts for Greek sites: ship two families, self-hosted WOFF2 subset to Latin + Greek (U+0370-03FF) and only add Greek Extended (U+1F00-1FFF) when polytonic text exists; Elementor Pro Custom Fonts has no unicode-range field, so subsetting happens before upload.
findings.detail: Google Fonts' own CSS for Roboto splits subsets as `greek` = U+0370-0377, U+037A-037F, U+0384-038A, U+038C, U+038E-03A1, U+03A3-03FF and `greek-ext` = U+1F00-1FFF (plus latin, latin-ext). Elementor Pro Custom Fonts: WP Admin → Elementor → Editor → Custom Elements → Add New Font → Add Static Font per weight/style (every weight is a separate file), formats WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, SVG, EOT; uploaded fonts are stored under wp-content/uploads; the UI exposes only Weight and Style, not unicode-range. Elementor → Settings → General → 'Disable Default Fonts' / 'Disable Default Colors' stops Elementor's own defaults from competing with the kit. Audit evidence: the two fast agency sites use 2 families; slow ones carry 5–7 families plus per-widget families (e.g. Inter, Comfortaa, Roboto, Lato in widgets on limnoupolis.gr).
findings.breaks_when: A Latin-only subset makes Greek text fall back to the system font (visible FOUT and metric shift); dropping Greek Extended breaks polytonic/ancient-Greek content; a Google-Fonts `<link>` added by a converter or add-on (UiChemy Composer, Premium Addons) reintroduces third-party requests; uploading .ttf instead of .woff2 doubles bytes.
findings.how_to_apply: For each family keep 2–3 weights; build `family-400.woff2` etc. with `pyftsubset Font.ttf --flavor=woff2 --layout-features='*' --unicodes='U+0000-00FF,U+0131,U+0152-0153,U+02BB-02BC,U+02C6,U+02DA,U+02DC,U+2000-206F,U+20AC,U+2122,U+2191,U+2193,U+2212,U+2215,U+FEFF,U+FFFD,U+0370-03FF' (add `,U+1F00-1FFF` if polytonic); upload each weight in Elementor Pro Custom Fonts; set family/weights only in the kit or in V4 Font Variables; turn on 'Disable Default Fonts'; set Elementor's Google Fonts loading off once self-hosted. Alternative for finer control: declare `@font-face` with `unicode-range` blocks in the child theme and type the family name into the Variable/kit.
findings.how_to_verify: DevTools Network: ≤ 6 font files, all `.woff2`, each < 40 KB, none from fonts.gstatic.com; a Greek paragraph renders in the brand font (glyph check for ά, ώ, ς); Lighthouse 'Font display' insight is empty and CLS ≤ 0.04.
findings.correction: Custom Fonts help (Last Update Jan 20, 2026) confirms path Elementor > Editor > Custom Elements > Add New Font > Add Static Font, per-variation Weight and Style only, formats WOFF/WOFF2/TTF/SVG/EOT, files stored in wp-content/uploads — no unicode-range and no font-display control. Correction/addition: Elementor core now has 'Load Google Fonts Locally' (Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance, option `elementor_local_google_fonts`, default Disable) which downloads Google's CSS and font files to the server (`core/files/fonts/google-font.php` `download_fonts`), keeping Google's own unicode-range split (latin, latin-ext, greek, greek-ext as separate @font-face blocks) with zero manual subsetting; and General tab 'Google Fonts Load' (`font_display`, options Default/Blocking/Swap/Fallback/Optional, 'Recommended: Swap') applies only to Google-served fonts. So the plugin has two valid routes: (a) Pro Custom Fonts with pyftsubset WOFF2 as described, or (b) Local Google Fonts = Enable + Google Fonts Load = Swap when the brand fonts are Google families; set General > 'Google Fonts' = Disable only for route (a). The Greek unicode ranges quoted from Google's CSS were not re-opened by me.

findings.claim: Adobe XD is a dead end as a source format but a readable one: it is in maintenance mode with no official XD→Figma migration, and an `.xd` file is a ZIP of JSON artboards that can be parsed for colours, text styles and artboard sizes.
findings.detail: Adobe Community thread (posts through Nov 2025): XD 'in maintenance mode', Adobe has made no significant improvement in years, users migrated to Figma; no official migration tool. File format (Gergely Vándor, confirmed by xd2svg/xd-file READMEs): a ZIP container, MIME `application/vnd.adobe.sparkler.project+dcxucf`, with `mimetype` (must be the first, uncompressed entry or XD throws error 86), `manifest`, `interactions.json`, `artwork/artboard-{uuid}/graphics/graphicsContent.ags` (JSON per artboard), `resources/graphics/graphicsContent.ags` (shared resources, colours, text styles), PNG assets. npm `xd-file` `readXDFile(path)` returns `{document, interactions, metadata, resources, artboards[]}`; `xd2svg` (archived) converts artboards to SVG. XD's native export covers PNG/JPG/SVG/PDF only, so image conversion is the same local step as for Figma.
findings.breaks_when: Repacking an `.xd` after edits with the mimetype compressed or not first corrupts the file (error 86); Adobe staff have said the JSON schema may change, so parsers are best-effort; designs built with XD's repeat grids and component states have no Elementor equivalent and must be rebuilt.
findings.how_to_apply: Plugin step 'xd-tokens': `unzip -o design.xd -d xd/`; parse `xd/resources/graphics/graphicsContent.ags` and each `artwork/*/graphics/graphicsContent.ags` with `python3 -I` for `fill.color.value` (r,g,b → hex), `style.font.family/style/size`, `style.textAttributes.lineHeight/letterSpacing`, artboard `width/height`; dedupe into the token sheet of finding 2; export rasters/vectors from XD itself (Export → Batch, 2x PNG and SVG) and convert with sharp. Recommend converting the XD file to Figma (Convertify or manual rebuild) only if the client will iterate on the design.
findings.how_to_verify: `unzip -l design.xd | head` lists `mimetype` first; parsed colour count matches the designer's palette; parsed font families are the ones the kit will carry (max 2); a side-by-side of the hero artboard PNG and the built page at the artboard width.
findings.correction: Not independently re-verified in this pass (sources not re-opened), and the claim is low-stakes. Correction to confidence only: mark 'low' until the plugin parses one real agency .xd fixture; the JSON schema is undocumented and the npm parsers cited are archived/unmaintained, so the 'xd-tokens' step must fail soft (report what it found, never block the build) and the practical path is still 'export PNG/SVG from XD, rebuild tokens by hand'.

findings.claim: For reference-screenshot inputs, let Angie generate the first Variables/Classes draft from the screenshot, then prune it to the two-family, small-palette budget before building.
findings.detail: Elementor help: paste or upload the page screenshot into the Angie prompt box with 'Create reusable classes and variables based on the attached image'; 'the AI analyzes the visual style, creates color and typography variables, and configures primary class tokens instantly'; results appear in the Design System panel. Angie is a free plugin and adds abilities to the Elementor MCP (custom widgets, admin customisation, bulk actions). Elementor AI's 'Reference a website' creates up to three containers from a URL but cannot reproduce nested elements, carousels, repeating elements or site parts, and reproduces Elementor-built pages more exactly than others. The Elementor MCP launch post explicitly positions 'a design from Figma … turned into real Elementor content' through the AI tool's own Figma connector rather than an Elementor-side importer.
findings.breaks_when: AI-generated tokens typically over-produce (many colour stops, several type scales) and may name fonts that are not licensed/self-hosted; Angie/Elementor AI consume credits and create drafts that carry inline styles unless the prompt insists on classes; Pro widgets appear in AI containers even without Pro.
findings.how_to_apply: Workflow: 1) Angie → screenshot → variables/classes; 2) open Design System → Variables and delete down to ≤ 8 colours, 2 font families, 1 size scale; rename to semantic names; 3) Class Manager → delete one-off classes; 4) build sections with the MCP or `elementor-set-content` referencing those classes only; 5) export the resulting design system ZIP as the client's blueprint.
findings.how_to_verify: Variables Manager shows ≤ 8 colours and 2 fonts; every e-heading/e-button on the first page has a green (global) class and no pink local overrides for colour/font; Lighthouse font requests ≤ 6.

findings.claim: After the build, run Element Manager → Scan Element Usage → Deactivate Unused Elements so unused core/Pro/add-on widgets disappear from the editor, and record the kept list in the handover.
findings.detail: Help centre: WP Admin → Elementor → Editor → Home → System → Element Manager; 'Scan Element Usage' then 'Show' buttons list where/how often each element is used; toggle off, or 'Deactivate Unused Elements' (applies to ALL unused elements regardless of filter); filters by All Plugins / Elementor / WordPress widgets / Elementor Pro / third-party; warning: disabling elements that are in use 'could even break your site'. The documented benefit is editor speed and clutter; front-end CSS/JS savings depend on how each add-on enqueues assets (not documented on this page).
findings.breaks_when: An element used only inside a popup, Theme Builder template, or a draft is reported unused by the scan and disabled, then breaks when that template renders; add-on packs that enqueue globally keep loading assets anyway.
findings.how_to_apply: Finish all pages, templates and popups first; Element Manager → Scan Element Usage → review the third-party filter → Deactivate Unused Elements → Save Changes; export the enabled list into `references/checklist.md`; re-scan after each new page type.
findings.how_to_verify: Editor panel shows only the kept elements; front-end pages, popups, 404 and Woo templates render unchanged (screenshot diff); `scripts/audit.php` widget counts match the scan.

findings.claim: The local skills on this machine cover migration parity, generic frontend taste and token extraction from live sites, but none covers V4 tokens, Elementor JSON generation or image export; the Figma connector exists but is unauthenticated.
findings.detail: Found: /root/.claude/skills/synced/…/adobe-xd/SKILL.md (30 lines of generic 'use XD' bullets; nothing on parsing .xd, tokens or Elementor); …/kallyas-to-elementor/SKILL.md (strong 1:1 migration method: Playwright capture at 1920/1440/1024/390, kit CSS rules, Polylang `general/pll_language_<slug>` conditions, Woo CSS porting, verification loop ≤ 5 px, mu-plugin theme preview, Inglelandi = white-labelled Hello — but v3 containers only, no Classes/Variables, no performance rules); …/extract-design-system/SKILL.md (npm `extract-design-system <url>` → `.extract-design-system/normalized.json`, `design-system/tokens.css|json`; works only on public live sites, no Figma/XD input, no Elementor output); …/design-taste-frontend/SKILL.md (87 KB React/Tailwind anti-slop playbook with a 'Design Read' step and dials; not WordPress); /root/.claude/plugins/synced/…/taste-skill/skills/image-to-code-skill/SKILL.md (36 KB Codex image-first workflow; no component mapping or export rules); design plugin skill design-handoff (handoff spec with a token table from a Figma URL; depends on the Figma MCP). No SKILL.md named figma exists; the session lists `plugin:design:figma` among servers that 'require authentication'. The draft plugin's elementor-build skill already states 2 fonts / static hero / ≤ 4 depth / core widgets, but targets ≥ 85 and knows nothing about V4 elements, Variables/Classes, JSON fixtures or image export.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; the risk is duplication: re-implementing capture/verification that kallyas-to-elementor already specifies, or copying React-oriented rules from design-taste-frontend into a WordPress context.
findings.how_to_apply: Reuse: kallyas-to-elementor §2 and §8 for the screenshot-parity loop and §5 for Polylang/Mega Menu patterns; extract-design-system for 'reference = live site' inputs; design-taste-frontend §0 'Design Read' as the brief-reading step. Add to elementor-lean: `references/tokens.md` (Figma/XD/screenshot → Variables/Classes mapping, finding 2), `references/elements.md` (component → atomic element table, finding 5), `references/images.md` (finding 7), JSON fixtures (finding 4), and new targets (finding 3). Ask the user to authorise the Figma connector; until then route Figma reads through REST with a personal access token.
findings.how_to_verify: `grep -ril 'e-div-block\|global class\|variables' /home/user/everything-claude/plugins/elementor-lean` returns the new references; the builder agent's checklist cites the finding-3 numbers; a dry run on a staging site produces a page whose JSON passes the lint and whose Lighthouse mobile score is ≥ 95.

findings.claim: Page-by-page build checklist with gates: site setup once, then per page a static hero, atomic-only first screen, ≤ 4 depth, images per rule, and a Lighthouse gate at the 95/100 numbers before the next page starts.
findings.detail: Combines the sourced facts above into the order the builder agent should follow. Site setup: Atomic Editor on; Design System imported (finding 2) and Defaults set (h1–h6, p, a, button, div padding 0); Hello/Inglelandi settings (header/footer off, page title off); 'Disable Default Colors/Fonts'; custom fonts uploaded (finding 10); Elementor → Settings → Performance → Optimized Image Loading = Enable; one cache plugin with the hero excluded from lazy-load. Per page (home, one inner, booking/checkout): hero = e-div-block + e-image (custom size, lazy off) + e-heading + e-paragraph + e-button; nothing animated, no video/3D/carousel/counter above the fold (slow agency sites: three.js or autoplay video heroes, 76–160 entrance animations); containers ≤ 4 deep; only whitelisted elements; videos click-to-play with poster; maps as static image except contact page. Gate: Lighthouse mobile median of 3 runs ≥ 95 with LCP ≤ 1.6 s, TBT ≤ 70 ms, CLS ≤ 0.04, FCP ≤ 1.1 s, SI ≤ 2.0 s, DOM < 800 nodes, ≤ 60 requests, ≤ 1.5 MB; then Element Manager cleanup and design-system export at handover.
findings.breaks_when: Design briefs that insist on a video/3D hero: build the static version first and offer the heavy version below the fold with the measured score cost (the agency's video/3D heroes correlate with scores 27–50 in results.jsonl); booking/Woo pages will not reach 100 while YITH/WooCommerce Bookings/JetSmartFilters scripts load — gate those at ≥ 90 and document why.
findings.how_to_apply: Encode as `references/checklist.md` sections 'Site setup', 'Per page', 'Gate', 'Handover' with the exact menu paths from findings 1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13 and the numbers from finding 3; have the builder agent refuse to start page N+1 until page N passes the gate or the user accepts a documented exception.
findings.how_to_verify: Each page has a saved Lighthouse JSON under the plugin's run folder with the five metric values and DOM count; `scripts/audit.php` flags are zero for animations, videos without lazy-load, HTML scripts and FA4 shim; the handover lists the design-system ZIP, enabled elements, font files and image sizes.
findings.correction: Keep the structure, fix four items from the corrections above: (1) 'Optimized Image Loading = Enable' is already the default; the actionable settings are to keep it on, decide 'Lazy Load Background Images' (default Enable) per hero type, and never add a second lazy-loader (the staging CLS 0.107 case); (2) Design System → Defaults: set padding 0 on `div` — this covers Div Block and Flexbox, both of which ship 10 px base padding; (3) the per-page gate must inspect `interactions: []` on every element (V4 animations) and reject `elType:'container'` at the top level of an atomic page; (4) drop 'DOM < 800 nodes' as a hard gate (Lighthouse 13 has no node threshold; use the dom-size-insight 'Total elements / DOM depth / Max children' as trend metrics and TBT as the gate). Also require Elementor ≥ 4.3.4 and CSS Print Method = External File before building through MCP (4.3.4 fixed settings loss via MCP; 4.3.5 fixed editing failures with Internal Embedding).

findings.claim: Atomic `e-image` renders `srcset` without a `sizes` attribute, so phones download the ~100vw candidate for small images unless the Resolution is pinned per element.
findings.detail: Elementor main `modules/atomic-widgets/props-resolver/transformers/image-transformer.php` returns `id, src, width, height, srcset (wp_get_attachment_image_srcset), alt` for an attachment; `atomic-image.html.twig` loops over those keys and prints each as an HTML attribute on `` (so the attachment id is also emitted as `id="123"`, which can collide with `_cssid` ids). No `sizes` is produced and the `wp-image-{id}` class is absent, so WordPress's `wp_img_tag_add_srcset_and_sizes_attr` does not add one and WP 6.7's `sizes="auto"` (only appended to an existing sizes attr on lazy images) never applies. A browser without `sizes` assumes 100vw: on a 390 px / DPR 3 phone a 300 px card image picks the ~1170 px candidate. Default `size` is `full` (`define_props_schema` -> `->default_size('full')`).
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; pinning a too-small Resolution makes retina images soft. A filter that injects `sizes` must match the element's real rendered width per breakpoint or it reintroduces oversizing.
findings.how_to_apply: In the builder: for every `e-image`, set `settings.image.value.size` to a registered size whose width ≈ max rendered width × 2 (register `add_image_size('card-2x', 800, 0)`, `('hero-mobile', 780, 0)` in the child theme), never leave `full`; for the hero use a size matching the mobile breakpoint and rely on Elementor's Optimized Image Loading for fetchpriority. Optionally hook `wp_content_img_tag` in the child theme to add `sizes="(max-width: 767px) 100vw, <box>px"` on `img.e-image-base` only after measuring. Lint: reject any `e-image` with `size: 'full'` unless it is the hero.
findings.how_to_verify: View-source of a built page: each `` shows `srcset` and `width/height`; DevTools Network column 'Size' at 390 px shows the chosen candidate ≤ 2× rendered width; Lighthouse 13 'Improve image delivery' insight shows 0 KiB for cards; confirm whether `id=""` appears and does not duplicate another element id (Lighthouse 'Best practices' / HTML validator).

findings.claim: Elementor's 'Optimized Image Loading' replaces WordPress core's lazy-load/fetchpriority logic for the whole page (header included), so core filters are inert and stacking a cache-plugin lazy loader double-processes the hero.
findings.detail: `modules/image-loading-optimization/module.php` (Elementor main): `add_filter('wp_lazy_loading_enabled','__return_false')`, `stop_core_fetchpriority_high_logic` on init, `set_buffer` on `get_header` and `flush_header_buffer` on `the_content` priority 0, and `wp_content_img_tag` → `loading_optimization_image` which injects `fetchpriority="high"` on the LCP candidate and `loading="lazy"` on later images. Setting: Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance > 'Optimized Image Loading' (option `elementor_optimized_image_loading`, `std => '1'` = Enable). Help page (Sep 25, 2026): 'lazy loading is not applied to above the fold images'. Elementor's `the_content` priority is 9 (`Frontend::THE_CONTENT_FILTER_PRIORITY`), so WP's `wp_filter_content_tags` (priority 12) still runs but with core lazy-loading disabled.
findings.breaks_when: LiteSpeed Cache / FlyingPress / Perfmatters lazy-load on top of it adds `loading=lazy` or a placeholder to the hero after Elementor already set `fetchpriority=high` — the staging test showed CLS 0 → 0.107. Disabling Elementor's option and relying on the cache plugin is the alternative, not both.
findings.how_to_apply: Keep Elementor 'Optimized Image Loading' = Enable; in the cache plugin turn image lazy-load OFF (LiteSpeed: Page Optimization > Media > Lazy Load Images = OFF; FlyingPress: Images > Lazy load = off or exclude the first N images; Perfmatters: Lazy Loading > Images = off). Do not use `wp_omit_loading_attr_threshold` or `wp_get_loading_optimization_attributes` filters expecting core behaviour. Document in checklist 'exactly one image lazy-loader: Elementor'.
findings.how_to_verify: View-source: hero `` has `fetchpriority="high"`, no `loading="lazy"`, no `data-src`/placeholder; below-fold images have `loading="lazy"`; Lighthouse 'LCP request discovery' insight passes (discoverable, not lazy, fetchpriority applied); CLS unchanged after enabling the cache plugin.

findings.claim: 'Lazy Load Background Images' (Performance tab, default Enable) hides every CSS background-image except the first with `background-image:none !important` until JavaScript runs — a hero that is not the first background container gets a delayed LCP.
findings.detail: Elementor main `includes/settings/settings.php`: field `lazy_load_background_images`, label 'Lazy Load Background Images', `std => '1'`, description 'lazy loading all background images except the first one'. `modules/lazyload/module.php` prints CSS in `wp_head` setting `background-image: none !important` on lazy-marked elements and swaps them in from `wp_footer` JS. If the header template or a top banner uses a background image, the hero container is the second background and becomes lazy, pushing LCP past JS execution; Lighthouse then reports the LCP element as lazy/late-discovered.
findings.breaks_when: Disabling it on long pages re-downloads every decorative background up front (more bytes, same LCP). Using an `e-image` (an ``) for the hero instead of a container background sidesteps the issue entirely.
findings.how_to_apply: Builder rule: hero = `e-image` inside the hero `e-div-block`, never a container background image; allow the setting to stay Enable. If a design insists on a background hero, confirm it is the first background-image in DOM order (no header background) or set Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance > Lazy Load Background Images = Disable for that site and re-measure.
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse 'LCP by phase' / 'LCP request discovery' insight: the LCP resource is discoverable in HTML and not marked lazy; view-source shows no `background-image: none !important` rule applied to the hero's class; WebPageTest filmstrip shows hero painted before first JS.

findings.claim: Elementor core can self-host Google Fonts with Google's own unicode-range subsets (incl. greek/greek-ext) via 'Load Google Fonts Locally', avoiding Pro Custom Fonts uploads for Google families.
findings.detail: `includes/settings/settings.php` Performance tab field `local_google_fonts`, label 'Load Google Fonts Locally', `std => '0'` (Disable), description 'Fonts will be served from your own server instead of Google's. Only the very first load (in the editor and on the front end) may take slightly longer.' `core/files/fonts/google-font.php` reads `elementor_local_google_fonts`, fetches Google's CSS, `download_fonts()` saves each font URL locally and stores the map in `_elementor_local_google_fonts`; the generated CSS keeps Google's per-subset `@font-face` blocks, so Greek glyphs load only from the greek subset file. General tab 'Google Fonts Load' (`font_display`: Default/Blocking/Swap/Fallback/Optional, 'Recommended: Swap') controls font-display for these fonts. Pro Custom Fonts (help Jan 20, 2026) has no font-display or unicode-range fields.
findings.breaks_when: Non-Google brand fonts still need Pro Custom Fonts or child-theme @font-face; the first page load after a cache flush is slower while files download; cache plugins that already localise Google fonts (LiteSpeed 'Localize Resources', Perfmatters 'Local Google Fonts', FlyingPress) must be turned off to avoid double hosting.
findings.how_to_apply: For Google families: Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance > 'Load Google Fonts Locally' = Enable; General > 'Google Fonts Load' = Swap; keep General > 'Google Fonts' = Enable; set the families only in the kit / Font Variables; disable the cache plugin's font localisation. For non-Google families: keep the pyftsubset + Pro Custom Fonts route and set General > 'Google Fonts' = Disable.
findings.how_to_verify: DevTools Network: font files served from the site's own uploads path, none from fonts.gstatic.com; stylesheet shows `font-display: swap` and separate `unicode-range` blocks for greek; Lighthouse 'Font display' insight empty; a Greek paragraph renders in the brand font.

findings.claim: V4 animations live in each element's `interactions` array and are JavaScript-driven; the build lint and the 'nothing animated above the fold' rule must target that field, not v3 `_animation`.
findings.detail: Interactions help (Last Update Jun 19, 2026): 'The Interactions tab is home to Javascript functions that affect widgets. These include entrance and scrolling animations'; triggers Page load, Scroll into view, While scrolling, On hover, On click; effects Fade/Slide/Scale, In/Out, Direction, Duration, Delay; 'Interactions apply to all devices, you cannot customize interactions for different screen sizes' (Core). 4.0 blog (Apr 15, 2026) adds Pro 'Custom effect' and per-breakpoint interactions. Data structure docs: every atomic element/widget object has `interactions: []`. Page-load interactions on first-screen elements start them hidden/offset until JS runs, which inflates LCP and can register as layout shift.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; stripping `interactions` from imported templates removes designer-intended motion, so report rather than silently delete.
findings.how_to_apply: Lint rule: fail when any element in the first-screen section has non-empty `interactions`; warn when more than 2 elements per page have `interactions`; on the frontend, Lighthouse must show no 'Avoid non-composited animations' items. Add `interactions` to the `elementor-audit` counters next to `_animation`/`motion_fx`.
findings.how_to_verify: `jq '[.. | objects | select(.interactions? | length > 0)] | length' page.json` returns 0 for the hero section; Lighthouse mobile LCP unchanged with Interactions removed vs present on one test page.

findings.claim: Pin Elementor ≥ 4.3.4 and CSS Print Method = External File before any MCP/Novamira build: 4.3.3–4.3.5 fixed MCP style/settings loss and an Internal-Embedding editing failure.
findings.detail: Elementor main readme changelog: 4.3.3 (2026-09-30) 'Fix: Certain MCP style values are not applied correctly in Atomic elements'; 4.3.4 (2026-10-05) 'Fix: Element settings may lost when updating pages through MCP', 'Fix: Editor can freeze when editing settings or styles in large nested elements'; 4.3.5 (2026-10-13) 'Fix: Page editing can fail when Internal CSS Embedding is enabled (#37468)'. Settings: Elementor > Editor > Settings > Performance > 'CSS Print Method' options 'External File' (default, 'better performance (recommended)') / 'Internal Embedding'. audit-summary.json shows cretaforums.gr on `css_method: internal` and sites on 4.3.3–4.3.4.
findings.breaks_when: Not known to break; External File relies on writable wp-content/uploads/elementor/css and needs 'Regenerate CSS & Data' after switching.
findings.how_to_apply: Pre-build check in the builder agent: read Elementor version (Novamira `elementor-check-setup`) and refuse MCP/`elementor-set-content` writes below 4.3.4; set CSS Print Method = External File, then Elementor > Tools > Regenerate CSS & Data; add both to 'Site setup' in references/checklist.md.
findings.how_to_verify: check-setup JSON reports version ≥ 4.3.4; view-source links `/wp-content/uploads/elementor/css/post-<id>.css` instead of an inline `<style id="elementor-post-...">` block; a page written through MCP re-opens in the editor with all settings intact.

title: Case studies: Elementor sites at 95-100 and what they did; cross-check with our audit
summary: Documented 95-100 mobile cases exist but are few and mostly 3.x-era: WP Rocket's own mobile test (Elementor Pro 3.21.1, Twenty Twenty-Three) went 74->99 with Remove Unused CSS + deferred/delayed JS + Imagify; Justin Ferriman's GapScout (Rocket.net + Perfmatters delay-all + RUCSS + self-hosted preloaded fonts) went 50->94-99; a Feb-2025 Substack test site reached 100 only after delaying GTM to interaction, removing motion effects above the fold and loading elementor frontend.min.js last; a May-2026 ThemeZhub post claims 100/100 on WP Engine with sub-200ms TTFB, hero 'Loading: Eager', Font Awesome disabled and a lean plugin stack. None of these is a verified Elementor 4.x case, and the only large field study (PageSpeed Matters, CrUX May 2026, ~2.1M WordPress origins) shows Elementor passing CWV on just 30.0% of mobile sites, failing almost entirely on LCP (44.8% good) while CLS (92.3%) and INP (92.6%) are fine. The agency's own Lighthouse data mirrors this exactly: every slow site fails on LCP (7.7-16.4s) and the fast ones have LCP 2.2-2.5s. What separates pallada (86) and platonos (84) from limnoupolis (27), onar (44) and vorenia (50) in the data is: zero third-party KB in the lab run vs 471-1423KB (GTM/GA4/Ads/FB), a text/static LCP vs a 3D three.js hero (142s TBT), autoplay hero MP4 (255-352KB on mobile) and a lazy-loaded LCP image (CLS 0.103), 2 self-hosted WOFF2 font files (77KB) vs 11 files (382KB) or a 272KB .woff, no icon fonts vs Font Awesome + FA4 shim, and 62-64 requests/0.7-1.6MB vs 127-147 requests/2.4-4.0MB. Entrance animations above the fold plus FlyingPress 'delay all' produce 3.6-7.8s LCP render delay on vorenia and cretaforums. The fast sites' own ceiling is TTFB: pallada loses 891ms to a / -> /en/ redirect plus 1.6s server response, platonos 2.3s on an uncached dev server; both would need sub-600ms TTFB to pass 95. Practices with no support in the data: theme choice (Hello child vs custom Inglelandi child both fast), plugin count (pallada has 41 plugins and is fastest), DOM size (pallada 2024 nodes), DB bloat/revisions, Element Caching (disabled on the fastest site).
critic_notes: Method: elementor.com, perfmatters.io, docs.flyingpress.com, docs.litespeedtech.com and web.dev were unreachable through WebFetch (DNS), so every page was fetched with curl and text-extracted; corewebvitals.io returned HTTP 500 and GitHub issue #37452 returned 403, so neither is cited. Pages opened and dated: Elementor performance features (Jun 19 2026), Element Caching (Sep 15 2026), FOUC (Aug 27 2026), atomic Background Video (Sep 18 2026), legacy background video options (Oct 26 2025), Google Fonts Load (Jan 20 2026), Load Google Fonts Locally (Jan 20 2026), Image Loading Optimization (Sep 25 2026), Image widget (Sep 15 2026), Lazy loading (Dec 17 2024), Core+Pro changelog (Core 4.3.5 2026-10-13, Pro 4.3.2 2026-10-13), Perfmatters delay JS, FlyingPress delay-all/third-party/specific/RUCSS, LiteSpeed pageopt, web.dev lcp-lazy-loading (2022-03-31) and tag-best-practices, Chrome Lighthouse 13 blog (Oct 10 2025), PageSpeed Matters (CrUX May 2026), Plus Addons 4.3 (Sep 29 2026), ThemeZhub (May 13 2026), Savvy (Jun 17 2026), WP Rocket, FacetWP, Elementor 3.24 dev post, Polylang URL modifications, and Elementor source on GitHub main (core/experiments/manager.php, core/files/manager.php). Answers to the researcher's open questions: (2) e_optimized_css_files identified from source, alpha, CSS-purge hygiene not CSS size; (3) the MP4s are Elementor's own container background video with Play On Mobile on (background-video.min.js precedes the Media request on both sites), not a third-party widget; (4) not separable from the lab JSON alone, but limnoupolis TBT attribution is 135,289 ms to the document itself and 28,902 ms to frontend.min.js vs 743 ms to the largest GTM script, so three.js dominates by two orders of magnitude; (1) still no Elementor 4.x 95-100 case with published JSON found. Not checked: Inglelandi theme assets, Dynamic.ooo device-visibility feature, Complianz settings names, CrUX for the 10 origins, and no page or site was modified. Risk for the user: several researcher verify steps and any plugin script keyed on Lighthouse 12 audit ids will silently pass on PSI/Lighthouse 13; fix that before trusting any 'done' gate.

findings.claim: Delaying all marketing tags (GTM, GA4, Google Ads, Facebook pixel) until first interaction is the single largest separator between the agency's fast and slow home pages and is a precondition in every documented 100-score case.
findings.detail: Local Lighthouse (12.8.2, mobile, simulated): pallada (86) and platonos (84) report 0 KB third-party and 0 ms third-party blocking; limnoupolis (27) loads 1260 KB third-party with 1625 ms blocking (GTM 849 KB/1105 ms: gtm.js + GA4 + 2x AW gtag + FB fbevents 114 KB + FB config 159 KB), staging 1423 KB/1966 ms, onar 471 KB/323 ms. pallada's HTML still contains googletagmanager (3 refs) but Perfmatters delay keeps it out of the lab run. The Feb-2025 Substack test reached 100 only with the caveat 'Google Tag Manager is delayed and will load on user interaction (or after 6 seconds)'. Ongage gained ~5 mobile points just by loading a chatbot after scroll. web.dev's tag guidance: LCP is 'vulnerable to bandwidth contention' and tag managers should never deliver cookie notices or hero assets. Perfmatters doc (updated 2026-10-01) gives exact delay strings: /gtm.js, /gtm-, /gtm., google-analytics.com/analytics.js, and a 'Delay timeout' (default 15 s, filter perfmatters_delay_js_timeout). FlyingPress: 'Load third-party scripts on interaction' + 'Delay specific scripts on interaction'.
findings.breaks_when: Consent Mode / cookie-banner scripts are delayed together with the tags (banner appears late or consent signal is lost); GA4 pageviews drop for bouncing visitors who never interact; Google Ads conversion tags fire late on landing pages; a 15 s timeout fires in Lighthouse's window on slow runs and the gain vanishes.
findings.how_to_apply: Perfmatters > Assets > JavaScript: Delay JavaScript ON, Delay behavior 'Only delay specified scripts' with /gtm.js, /gtm-, /gtm., fbevents.js, connect.facebook.net, googleads, doubleclick; Delay timeout ON (10 s per OMM, or keep 15 s). FlyingPress: JavaScript > 'Load third-party scripts on interaction' ON and add googletagmanager.com, connect.facebook.net, googleads.g.doubleclick.net under 'Delay specific scripts'. LiteSpeed Cache: Page Optimization > JS Settings > Load JS Deferred = 'Delayed'. Keep the consent banner (Complianz/FAZ/Cookie-Script) and Elementor core scripts excluded from delay. Consolidate 5 tags to GTM with GA4 only; move Ads/FB to server-side or consent-gated triggers.
findings.how_to_verify: Re-run Lighthouse mobile: audit 'third-party-summary' shows 0 ms blocking and <50 KB before interaction; TBT drops (limnoupolis 142 s -> target <200 ms once the 3D hero is also removed). Then tap the page and confirm in DevTools Network that gtm.js and fbevents.js load, GA4 Realtime shows the hit, and the cookie banner still appears without interaction. Screenshot PSI 'Reduce the impact of third-party code' before/after.
findings.correction: Keep the lever and the Perfmatters/FlyingPress/LiteSpeed settings, but state the timeout is off by default (15 s when enabled), name FlyingPress's two distinct options, drop the 'every 100-score case' wording, and read 'third-parties-insight' (not 'third-party-summary') when verifying with PSI/Lighthouse 13. Risk stays medium: FlyingPress's auto third-party delay will also delay cdn.cookie-script.com (onar, limnoupolis) and GTM-injected consent unless excluded by domain.

findings.claim: A static hero (text or one Image widget) on mobile, with no 3D canvas, no GSAP timeline and no autoplay MP4, is what the fast sites share; a JS-driven hero is what the slow sites share.
findings.detail:
limnoupolis: three.module.min.js (170 KB) + GLTFLoader for a 3D hero -> frontend.min.js bootup 28.9 s, main-thread 171 s, TBT 142 017 ms, LCP 7.7 s. onar: onar-seaside-lounge.mp4 352 KB and vorenia Main-Video-Final.mp4 255 KB are downloaded in the mobile lab run (bgvideo markers=2 in HTML of both); onar LCP 16.4 s, vorenia 9.0 s. platonos (84) has no Elementor animations but ships gsap.min.js + ScrollTrigger + SplitText = 1.78 s bootup, its TBT 358 ms is its largest remaining front-end cost. pallada (86) and platonos LCP element is a

text node at 2.2-2.5 s with Load Delay 0 and Load Time 0. PageSpeed Matters (CrUX, May 2026): Elementor is 'good on LCP for only 44.8%'; the authors name 'large hero images placed without much loading discipline'. wptraining.at (Aug 2026): 'in nine out of ten Elementor projects... the large image at the very top is the reason for a poor LCP'; embed video via preview image and load on click. Elementor's own bg-video tutorial (element.how) notes Elementor disables background video on mobile and shows the fallback image, so an MP4 reaching the phone means a widget (Dynamic.ooo/Premium Addons video, Elementor Video widget autoplay) is bypassing that.
findings.breaks_when: Brand/UX insists on motion in the hero; a static poster is used but the Video widget is only hidden with Elementor responsive visibility (display:none), so the MP4 and swiper assets still download on mobile; Elementor 4.3's new atomic 'Background Video' element (Sept 2026) is dropped in with Autoplay on.
findings.how_to_apply: Build rule: hero = one Container with an Image widget (Loading: Eager / fetchpriority high) + heading + button. Video only on desktop and only via a widget whose mobile output is empty (not display:none); for self-hosted video use Elementor's Video widget with 'Image Overlay' + 'Lazy Load' so it loads on click. Remove three.js/GSAP heroes or ship them only above lg breakpoint via a server-side check, never via CSS hiding. Keep swiper/background-slideshow out of the hero (pallada loads background-slideshow.min.js and swiper.min.js on mobile for its 8 slideshows).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse mobile: 'largest-contentful-paint-element' is the hero img/h1 with Render Delay < 300 ms; no .mp4/.webm, three*, gsap* in network-requests on a 390px emulated phone; TBT < 200 ms; bootup-time has no entry > 100 ms other than jQuery/frontend. Screenshot the filmstrip to show hero painted by ~1.5 s.
findings.correction: Hero rule stands. Replace 'Elementor disables bg video on mobile' with: check every hero container's Background > Video > 'Play On Mobile' and set it to No (fallback image shows instead); treat chunks/background-video.min.js in the mobile waterfall as the audit signal. Server-side device gating needs a third-party condition (e.g. the installed Dynamic.ooo visibility extension, unverified here) or PHP; Elementor Pro Display Conditions cannot do it.

findings.claim: Entrance animations or motion effects on any above-the-fold element, combined with a cache plugin that delays Elementor's frontend JS, hide the LCP element and add 3.6-7.8 s of render delay; the fast site keeps its LCP element un-animated.
findings.detail:
vorenia (FlyingPress, 160 entrance animations site-wide): LCP element is the hero

, LCP 8.95 s of which Render Delay = 7 831 ms; its HTML has 33 'elementor-invisible' wrappers and 10 delay-JS markers. cretaforums (FlyingPress, 76 animations): LCP

4.4 s with Render Delay 3 620 ms. pallada (Perfmatters, 90 animations, 14 elementor-invisible in HTML) still gets LCP 2.47 s with Render Delay -344 ms because the LCP paragraph itself is not animated and Perfmatters is not delaying Elementor's frontend bundle. Savvy (Mar 2026, updated Jun 2026): 'Chrome does not count an element with opacity: 0 as an LCP candidate'; hero entrance animation pushed LCP from <2 s to 5.3 s, fixed to 2.4 s by starting at opacity 0.1 and triggering the class from an inline script. Substack (Feb 2025): had to remove motion effects above the fold and load elementor/assets/js/frontend.min.js last for delayed JS to work. Elementor 3.24 dev update: animations CSS is now split per animation (18.4 KB -> 0.077-0.835 KB), so the cost is no longer CSS weight but the opacity:0 wait. Elementor's FOUC article (updated 2026-08-27) ironically recommends Fade In on hero containers to hide flicker; that is the anti-pattern for LCP.
findings.breaks_when: A designer relies on entrance animation to mask FOUC caused by async CSS (fix the CSS exclusion instead); page uses Elementor Pro scroll Motion Effects on the hero (same opacity/transform wait); FlyingPress 'Load after interaction' is active so elementor-invisible never flips until the user scrolls.
findings.how_to_apply: Build checklist: Advanced > Motion Effects > Entrance Animation = None and Scrolling/Mouse Effects off for the hero container, h1, hero image, first CTA and header. Audit script: count 'elementor-invisible' and '_animation' in the first viewport's HTML (vorenia 33/27, onar 3/3, pallada 14/11, limnoupolis 0). Never add elementor/assets/js/frontend.min.js, webpack.runtime.min.js, frontend-modules or elementor-pro frontend to delay lists; with FlyingPress use 'Load when idle' not 'Load after interaction' on animated pages. For mobile, set entrance animations to 'None' via the Mobile responsive control (_animation_mobile).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse 'largest-contentful-paint-element' phases: Render Delay < 300 ms (vorenia today 7 831 ms). DevTools Rendering > Paint flashing or filmstrip shows h1 visible in first frame. Grep rendered mobile HTML of the hero for elementor-invisible = 0. Confirm below-fold animations still play on scroll.

findings.claim: Never lazy-load the LCP image, and if LiteSpeed Cache lazy-load is used it must run with Responsive Placeholder + VPI (or explicit excludes), otherwise it costs both LCP and CLS, as the staging test (CLS 0 -> 0.107) and limnoupolis production (CLS 0.103) show.
findings.detail: limnoupolis LCP element is ' Images + 'Add Missing Image Dimensions' + logo excluded. OMM FlyingPress guide: FlyingPress excludes above-the-fold images automatically; if PSI still flags it, add them under Exclusions or switch to Perfmatters lazy load.
findings.breaks_when: Two lazy-loaders run at once (WordPress core + LiteSpeed/FlyingPress/ShortPixel; ShortPixel's post lists this as problem #14); the hero image lives in a Loop/Carousel whose markup lacks width/height, so placeholders cannot be sized; images excluded by class need the class on the , not on the widget wrapper (element.how: a compound selector makes the image wait for JS).
findings.how_to_apply: LiteSpeed: Page Optimization > Media Settings: Lazy Load Images ON only together with Responsive Placeholder ON, Add Missing Sizes ON, and either VPI ON (QUIC.cloud) or the hero/logo filenames in 'Lazy Load Image Excludes'. Or leave LiteSpeed lazy load OFF and rely on WordPress core (loading=lazy + fetchpriority=high on the first image). Elementor Image widget: set the hero's Loading to Eager (Elementor exposes this per widget) and keep WordPress core fetchpriority (Perfmatters 'Disable Core Fetch' only when core picks the wrong image). FlyingPress: Images > Lazy load ON, exclude hero by keyword. Check the 'Optimized Image Loading' feature is active (Elementor Performance tab).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse: 'lcp-lazy-loaded' passes, 'prioritize-lcp-image' passes, LCP Load Delay < 200 ms; CLS < 0.02 with 'layout-shifts' not naming the hero; hero has fetchpriority="high" and no loading="lazy" in view-source; below-fold images still have loading="lazy". Re-run the staging A/B that produced 0.107.
findings.correction: Keep the rule. Replace 'Elementor Image widget Loading: Eager' with 'enable Image Loading Optimization (Performance tab) and make sure no second lazy-loader (LiteSpeed/FlyingPress/Perfmatters) re-adds loading=lazy to the hero'; use the 2022 web.dev article only for the mechanism, not for current WordPress behaviour; verify with lcp-discovery-insight / lcp-phases-insight on Lighthouse 13.

findings.claim: The fast sites are now capped by TTFB, not by the front end: pallada pays 891 ms for a / -> /en/ language redirect plus 1.6 s server response, platonos 2.3 s uncached; sub-600 ms TTFB with no redirect is what every 100-score write-up has in common.
findings.detail: Local Lighthouse: pallada requestedUrl https://pallada.gr/ -> finalDisplayedUrl https://pallada.gr/en/, 'redirects' audit 891 ms, server-response-time 1 626 ms, LCP TTFB phase 2 817 ms of a 2 473 ms LCP (render delay negative, i.e. the page paints as soon as HTML arrives). platonos server-response-time 2 322 ms (dev, 'none' cache). By contrast LiteSpeed sites onar/staging show 144-146 ms TTFB, proving the server stack can do it when the page cache hits. ThemeZhub (May 2026, claims 100/100): 'TTFB under 200ms... before any WordPress-level optimization', LCP target 'Under 1.2 seconds (Excellent / 100 score)', remove competing cache plugins. OMM (updated Oct 2026): TTFB 'is 40% of LCP'. web.dev LCP guidance splits LCP into TTFB/load delay/load time/render delay and recommends ~40% budget for TTFB. Ongage's host upgrade cut TTFB 2.0 -> 1.3 s. Justin: 'use a host that doesn't suck' (Rocket.net) was step 1.
findings.breaks_when: Default-language-at-root is enabled in Polylang/WPML but old /en/ URLs are not 301'd (duplicate content), or the browser-language detection redirect is kept and so the root never caches; W3 Total Cache page cache is bypassed by cookies set by the consent plugin (FAZ/Complianz) or by WooCommerce/YITH session cookies; a WAF/CDN (Cloudflare) sits in front without caching HTML.
findings.how_to_apply: Polylang: Languages > Settings > URL modifications: 'Hide URL language information for default language' ON and 'Detect browser language' OFF (WPML: Languages > Language URL format 'Different languages in directories', default language at root, Browser language redirect OFF). Make / return 200 with the default language. Ensure a full-page cache HIT for anonymous mobile: LiteSpeed (x-litespeed-cache: hit) with Cache Mobile only if the markup differs; W3TC Page Cache enabled with 'Cache 404/feeds' off and consent cookies not in the reject list; FlyingPress with Cloudflare APO or FlyingCDN. PHP 8.3 + OPcache + Redis object cache for uncached pages. Target server-response-time < 400 ms from EU test locations.
findings.how_to_verify: curl -sI https://site/ shows 200 (no 301) and a cache HIT header on the second request; Lighthouse 'redirects' = 0 ms, 'server-response-time' < 600 ms (audit passes), LCP TTFB phase < 800 ms. For pallada this alone should move LCP from 2.47 s toward ~1.3 s; re-check score.

findings.claim: Two font families, at most ~4 self-hosted WOFF2 files (Greek+Latin subset kept), served from the site's own origin with font-display swap, is the font profile of the fast sites; the slow ones ship 11 files, a 272 KB legacy .woff, or a live fonts.gstatic.com request.
findings.detail: pallada: 2 Font requests, 77 KB total (inter-*.woff2 47 KB + arima-*.woff2 30 KB) from /wp-content/uploads/elementor/google-fonts/fonts/ (Elementor's local Google Fonts), no font-display failures. platonos: 3 families but 6 files, 269 KB (Noto Serif Display + Noto Serif + Inter), the one front-end cost it could still cut. onar: 11 Font requests, 382 KB (Noto Serif Display x2, Inter x3, Inter Tight x2, Open Sans, Baskervville, fa-solid-900.woff2 76 KB, kritiagro_icons). limnoupolis: Modak-Regular.woff 272 KB + Poppins-Regular.woff 72 KB (WOFF, not WOFF2) flagged by 'font-display', plus Open Sans from fonts.gstatic.com (third-party). web.dev font best practices: 'Use only WOFF2' ('compresses 30% better than WOFF'), subset with unicode-range, preload only fonts used above the fold, preconnect if a third-party host is unavoidable. Justin's 94-99 setup: custom fonts uploaded to Elementor, preloaded in Perfmatters with CrossOrigin, and the filter add_filter('elementor_pro/custom_fonts/font_display', fn() => 'swap') then Elementor > Tools > Regenerate Files. OMM: host locally as woff2, preload above-the-fold fonts, 'preloading unused fonts decreases performance'. ThemeZhub: Google Fonts render-blocking cost '200-400 ms of LCP' until swap/self-hosting.
findings.breaks_when: Subsetting is done with a Latin-only range and Greek text falls back to a system font or tofu (all 10 sites are Greek); font-display swap on a display face with very different metrics causes a visible CLS jump (use size-adjust/fallback tuning or 'optional'); a preload points to a font file name that Elementor regenerates (hash changes) so the preload 404s; Perfmatters 'Disable Google Fonts' is switched on while the design still references Google families.
findings.how_to_apply: Elementor > Settings > Advanced (or Performance in 4.x): Google Fonts Load = Swap and keep Elementor's local Google Fonts (files under uploads/elementor/google-fonts/). Limit the Site Settings Global Fonts to 2 families, 2-3 weights each; do not pick per-widget fonts (audit shows +4 widget-level families on limnoupolis and marakaki). For custom fonts: convert to WOFF2 with a Greek+Latin subset (unicode-range U+0370-03FF, U+1F00-1FFF plus Latin), upload under Elementor > Custom Fonts, apply the font_display filter above, regenerate. Preload only the 1-2 files used in the hero (Perfmatters > Preloading, type Font, CrossOrigin; FlyingPress > Fonts > Preload fonts). Perfmatters > Fonts: Display Swap ON, Local Google Fonts ON if Google fonts remain.
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse network-requests: Font count <= 4, total < 120 KB, all from the site origin, 'font-display' audit passes; CLS < 0.02 with no layout-shift attributed to text; load a Greek page and screenshot headings/body in the brand font (no fallback); Console shows no 'preloaded but not used' warnings.
findings.correction: Settings path: Google Fonts Load = Elementor > Editor > Settings > Advanced; Load Google Fonts Locally = Performance tab, off by default since 3.32.1, must be re-enabled after some updates. Add an audit check for font requests whose host differs from the page origin (vorenia -> villavorenia.gr). Risk stays medium because of the Greek-subset requirement.

findings.claim: Icon fonts are a slow-site marker: onar and vorenia still load Font Awesome plus the FA4 shim and custom icon fonts, while the two fast sites load none; Elementor's stable 'Inline Font Icons' feature plus dropping the FA4 shim removes them.
findings.detail: onar: fa-solid-900.woff2 76 KB, 10 'font-awesome' refs and kritiagro_icons.woff2 (font-display fail), audit 'fa4_shim: yes', optimized_markup OFF, 56 stylesheet requests/197 KB. vorenia: elementor/assets/lib/font-awesome/js/v4-shims.min.js + 7 font-awesome refs, fa4_shim yes. pallada/platonos: 0 Font Awesome/eicons requests. Elementor help 'Improve performance features' (updated 2026-06-19) lists 'Inline Font Icons: Renders icons as inline SVG without loading the Font-Awesome and the eicons libraries and their related CSS files and fonts' as a stable feature in the Features tab (observed flag e_font_icon_svg). Element.how 90+ guide: 'Disable Font Awesome 4 Support. If you have font awesome 4 icons on your website though, you will need to replace them'. Crocoblock: upload only needed icons under Elementor > Custom Icons, then deactivate Font Awesome; dequeue 'elementor-icons' if eicons unused. ThemeZhub: 'Disable Font Awesome if your design uses a different icon library'. Elementor's older asset-loading post explains the Icons library loads 'a Font file and a CSS file containing all the classes'.
findings.breaks_when: Legacy widgets still store FA4 class names (fa fa-*) and the shim is turned off -> blank icons; third-party addons (Premium Addons, Dynamic.ooo, JetMenu) enqueue their own Font Awesome regardless of Elementor's setting; custom icon sets (kritiagro_icons) uploaded as fonts are not covered by Inline Font Icons and still need a font file.
findings.how_to_apply: Elementor > Settings > Features: Inline Font Icons = Active (stable). Elementor > Settings > Advanced: 'Load Font Awesome 4 Support' = No after migrating FA4 icons (Elementor offers the FA5 migration in the editor). Replace custom icon fonts with SVG uploads (Elementor > Custom Icons accepts SVG sets). Use Perfmatters Script Manager or Elementor's Element Manager to disable addon widgets that enqueue font-awesome on pages that don't use them. Confirm no 'Font Awesome' standalone plugin is active (staging.limnoupolis has one).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse network-requests: no URL matching font-awesome, fa-*.woff2, eicons, elementor-icons; stylesheet count down (onar 56 -> target < 20); visually check every icon widget, menu icon and social icon on 3 templates; Console shows no missing-glyph CSS 404.

findings.claim: Remove Unused CSS plus defer/delay JavaScript in the cache plugin, with Elementor's CSS and frontend JS excluded, is the lever every published 95-100 case used; the audit confirms the slow sites carry 310-871 KB unused JS and 83-158 KB unused CSS versus 82-122 KB / 0-23 KB on the fast sites.
findings.detail: WP Rocket's mobile test (page updated 2025-12-16, Elementor Pro 3.21.1, Twenty Twenty-Three, Paris servers): 74 -> 99 after Remove Unused CSS, Minify/Load JS deferred/Delay JS execution and Imagify. Justin Ferriman (2023): Perfmatters Defer JavaScript + Include jQuery + Delay JavaScript (Delay All Scripts) + Delay Timeout + Remove Unused CSS -> 50 -> 94-99. Andreas Stricker: WP Rocket minify/combine + Delay JavaScript Execution took mobile from 44 to a claimed 100, but Remove Unused CSS broke popups and was disabled. Local data: render-blocking savings 631-1391 ms on slow sites vs 126-615 ms fast; unused-js 689-871 KB (limnoupolis/staging) vs 82-122 KB. Elementor's FOUC article (updated 2026-08-27): exclude /wp-content/plugins/elementor/assets/css/ from Defer CSS / Load CSS Asynchronously / Remove Unused CSS, regenerate Critical CSS, turn Cloudflare Rocket Loader off, and do NOT switch CSS Print Method to Internal Embedding. FlyingPress RUCSS doc (2025-05-23): used CSS is inlined in <style id="flying-press-css">, safelist selectors (not file names) for popups/menus/tabs. FlyingPress Delay doc (2025-06-25): 'Load after interaction... not suitable if your site has sliders, animations, menus... above the fold'; exclusions are partial case-insensitive keywords, no wildcards. Perfmatters: 'Delay all' is the only mode that can delay jQuery; exclude jquery.min.js when a script depends on it. LiteSpeed: UCSS via QUIC.cloud, 'UCSS Allowlist' for selectors missing after generation, 'Load JS Deferred = Delayed'.
findings.breaks_when: Elementor Pro popups, Off-Canvas, mega-menu, JetSmartFilters, YITH/WooCommerce Bookings calendars or Dynamic.ooo widgets lose styles (RUCSS misses interaction-only selectors) or stop responding on first tap (delayed handlers); CSS Print Method set to 'internal' interacts badly with cache (Elementor says so); two tools do RUCSS at once (Perfmatters + FlyingPress/LiteSpeed) producing duplicate inlined CSS; delayed jQuery breaks inline scripts from booking plugins.
findings.how_to_apply: Pick ONE tool per job (OMM 'duplicate settings' rule): FlyingPress sites -> FlyingPress RUCSS + 'Load when idle' + Perfmatters common exclusions; LiteSpeed sites -> Page Optimization > CSS: Generate UCSS ON (QUIC.cloud), UCSS Inline ON, JS: Load JS Deferred = Delayed, JS Excludes for elementor frontend if any widget misbehaves; W3TC + Perfmatters sites -> Perfmatters Remove Unused CSS (Used CSS Method 'file', Stylesheet Behavior 'delay' before trying 'remove'), Defer + Delay JS. Everywhere: exclude /wp-content/plugins/elementor/assets/css/ from async/RUCSS per Elementor; keep elementor frontend.min.js, webpack.runtime, jquery.min.js, consent banner and booking scripts out of delay; add RUCSS safelist for .elementor-popup-modal, .elementor-menu-toggle, .e-off-canvas, jet-smart-filters, cmplz-, faz-. Elementor: CSS Print Method stays External File; after changes Elementor > Tools > Regenerate Files & Data and purge cache.
findings.how_to_verify: PSI mobile: 'unused-css-rules' < 30 KB, 'unused-javascript' < 150 KB, 'render-blocking-resources' savings < 150 ms; Console 0 errors; manual tap test on a real phone: open mobile menu, popup, off-canvas, filter, booking calendar, Woo add-to-cart, language switcher; compare screenshots before/after on 3 templates (home, room/product, booking).
findings.correction: Add: LiteSpeed UCSS requires CSS Combine + QUIC.cloud and UCSS Inline disables Load CSS Asynchronously; flag CSS Print Method 'internal' (cretaforums) as a pre-flight fix; read 'render-blocking-insight' on Lighthouse 13/PSI. Risk stays medium.

findings.claim: The cookie-consent banner must never be the largest painted element or push content: on onar the Complianz banner (#cmplz-message-2-optin) IS the LCP element at 16.4 s because the real hero never painted earlier.
findings.detail: onar Lighthouse: 'largest-contentful-paint-element' = <div class="cmplz-message" id="cmplz-message-2-optin">, Render Delay 15 355 ms; the HTML also loads cookie-script.com and 158 cmplz references. vorenia's only layout shift (0.005) is 'faz-consent-container faz-box-bottom-right'. AcceleraWP case list: a chat box above the fold 'was being detected as the LCP element... Solution? Move the chat box below the fold.' wptraining.at: 'A cookie banner or notice bar that pushes the content downwards is a guaranteed CLS hit. Lay it over the content.' web.dev tags: do not deliver cookie notices through a tag manager because they 'load later than resources requested directly' and can raise LCP and CLS. Anton Smolik (2026): 'Consent tools, tag managers, chat... compete for bandwidth/main-thread time during the same window the hero needs to become visible.'
findings.breaks_when: Legal requires the banner to block the page (modal overlay) so it is always the first large paint; the banner is injected by GTM (Cookie-Script via GTM) and therefore also delayed by the delay-JS rule; three consent tools are active at once (onar: Complianz + Cookie-Script; limnoupolis: Cookie-Script via GTM).
findings.how_to_apply: One consent plugin per site, loaded directly (not via GTM), excluded from delay JS, styled as a small position:fixed bottom sheet with a fixed height and no full-screen overlay on mobile; make the hero paint first by fixing the hero (findings 2-4). Complianz: Banner > Position 'bottom' (not center/overlay) and disable the 'Cookie-Script' duplicate. FAZ: keep box-bottom-right, set explicit height to avoid the 0.005 shift. Remove unused consent plugins (audit 'dup' column).
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse LCP element is the hero image/h1, not .cmplz-* or .faz-*; 'layout-shifts' has no consent node; banner still appears without interaction and consent choices still gate GTM tags (check dataLayer consent state in Tag Assistant).

findings.claim: Field data and the local lab agree that Elementor's problem is LCP, not INP or CLS, so the plugin should rank LCP levers first and treat lab TBT spikes (limnoupolis 142 s) as secondary symptoms of the same hero.
findings.detail: PageSpeed Matters (published 2026-07-16, CrUX May 2026, ~2.1M WordPress origins, 982 553 Elementor mobile origins): Elementor passes CWV on 30.0% of mobile sites (Gutenberg 41.5%, Divi 34.5%, WPBakery 32.7%); good LCP only 44.8%, good INP 92.6%, good CLS 92.3%; authors: 'The entire problem is loading... Image optimization, reining in the number of widgets and fonts, and good page caching all move LCP directly.' Local: all five sites below 75 fail on LCP (4.4-16.4 s), CLS is <= 0.005 everywhere except the lazy-loaded limnoupolis hero (0.103); INP is not measured in lab but TBT is < 650 ms everywhere except the three.js site. wptraining.at (2026): work order 'Images first, then caching, then fonts, then scripts... sorted by diminishing return'. Smolik (2026): map each failing metric to the template/element; LCP phases (TTFB, discovery, load, render delay) decide the fix.
findings.breaks_when: not known to break
findings.how_to_apply: In the audit skill, report LCP element + its four phases first, then third-party blocking, then fonts/icons, then DOM/plugins. Gate 'done' on LCP <= 2.5 s lab (<= 1.2 s for a 100 per ThemeZhub's rule of thumb) and CLS <= 0.05, not on the aggregate score. Keep CrUX (PSI 'Discover what your real users are experiencing') as the acceptance signal after 28 days.
findings.how_to_verify: After fixes, PSI field section shows LCP p75 'Good' for the origin; lab LCP phases: TTFB < 800 ms, Load Delay ~0, Load Time < 500 ms, Render Delay < 300 ms.
findings.correction: Rank LCP first for the fleet, but gate on the metric score breakdown per site: where TBT score < 0.5 (limnoupolis, staging 1,800 ms) treat main-thread work as a co-equal lever because TBT carries 30% of the Lighthouse score.

findings.claim: Front-end request count and bytes separate fast from slow (62-64 requests / 0.7-1.6 MB vs 127-147 / 2.4-4.0 MB); raw plugin count does not: pallada runs 41 plugins and is the fastest site.
findings.detail: results.jsonl: pallada 62 requests/1579 KB, platonos 64/734 KB; limnoupolis 145/3660 KB, staging 147/4007 KB, vorenia 135/2434 KB, onar 127/2948 KB. audit-summary.json plugin counts: pallada 41, limnoupolis 30, vorenia 17, onar 28, platonos 10. What differs is what reaches the page: scripts 23 req/299 KB (pallada) vs 58 req/1729 KB (limnoupolis); stylesheets 13/23 KB vs 56/197 KB (onar). Duplicates on slow sites: TinyPNG + Converter for Media, Popup Builder + WebToffee popups, a standalone Font Awesome plugin, Complianz + Cookie-Script, Premium Addons + PRO + Dynamic.ooo. ThemeZhub recommends deactivating plugins one by one and re-running Lighthouse; ShortPixel #1 problem is 'Conflicting image optimization plugins'; Crocoblock recommends Elementor's Element Manager to switch off unused widgets (marakaki already disabled 131). OMM step 12-13: test plugins for CSS/JS and disable where not used (Perfmatters Script Manager).
findings.breaks_when: A plugin is removed that another depends on (Converter for Media serving WebP via .htaccess rewrites; Font Awesome plugin used by theme shortcodes); Script Manager disables a script site-wide that a booking page needs (use per-page or regex rules and Test Mode).
findings.how_to_apply: Audit the mobile home page's network list, not the plugin list: for every third-party or addon asset ask 'is it used above the fold on this template?'. Remove duplicate image optimizers/popup/consent/FA plugins (audit 'dup' column). Elementor > Settings > Element Manager: deactivate unused widgets (incl. addon packs). Perfmatters > Script Manager with 'Test Mode' ON, disable addon CSS/JS everywhere except where used, then publish.
findings.how_to_verify: Lighthouse mobile: requests <= 60 and transfer <= 1 MB on the home page; 'network-requests' has no asset from a plugin not used on that template; smoke-test the templates that still need the plugin (booking, forum, shop).

findings.claim: Theme choice (Hello Elementor child vs the custom Inglelandi parent/child) has no support in the agency's data as a speed lever, despite being the first recommendation in most guides.
findings.detail: pallada (86) uses hello-elementor-child; platonos (84) uses Inglelandi-child; cretaforums (74), marakaki (74), vorenia (50), onar (44) also use Inglelandi-child; limnoupolis (27) uses the Inglelandi parent. Both the best and the worst outcomes occur on Inglelandi. Guides: element.how 'Hello Theme... my personal preference... simple'; element.how 90+ tutorial measured requests 41 -> 25 on a fresh Hello install only after disabling fonts/icons/Gutenberg CSS, i.e. the gain came from settings not the theme; wptraining.at: 'the Pro version does not make your site faster'. WP Rocket's 74->99 test used Twenty Twenty-Three, not Hello.
findings.breaks_when: Switching an existing site's theme drops theme-specific template parts, hooks, custom CSS and the Polylang string translations registered by the parent theme; headers/footers must first be rebuilt in Elementor Theme Builder (element.how warns about this).
